US weighs strikes on Houthis and Iran after deadly Saudi airport attack. A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s main airport drew a Saudi vow of retaliation on Saturday, as President Donald Trump raised the possibility of joining strikes on the group and resuming attacks on Iran.

US pressure threatens Iran’s political survival but may not bring concessions. The US blockade and tighter sanctions enforcement are cutting into Iran’s oil income and targeting financial networks that sustain the Islamic Republic, but may still fall short of forcing Tehran into concessions, experts said at an Iran International town hall in Washington.

World leaders condemn Houthi attack on Riyadh airport. An attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport drew condemnation from European leaders, the United Nations and regional governments on Sunday.

Machete-wielding men at IRGC-backed rally revive scrutiny of crackdowns. Footage and images showing men wielding machetes and swords at an IRGC-backed rally in the central Iranian city of Isfahan have renewed scrutiny of the Islamic Republic's history of using unofficial armed groups to suppress anti-government protests.

Iran-US diplomacy stalls as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify. Efforts to end the war with Iran and restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained deadlocked Sunday, as military pressure continued at sea and the Iran-backed Houthis carried out increasingly deadly attacks inside Saudi Arabia.

Can US sanctions derail Iran’s China trade route?. Washington’s new sanctions are unlikely to stop a China–Iran freight train at the border, but may make the route Tehran has turned to under pressure from the US naval blockade costlier and less reliable.

Iran warns of wider risks as regional attacks intensify. Two commercial vessels were attacked near Oman on Sunday, two Indian sailors were left missing, and a drone struck an Iranian Kurdish opposition camp in Iraq on Monday, as Iranian officials warned that a renewed war could put regional infrastructure at risk.

Tehran seizes on Rubio’s Xerxes remarks to champion a past it once disparaged. Marco Rubio’s invocation of ancient Persia in a speech championing Western power has given Tehran an opportunity to present itself as a defender of Iranian identity, even as critics recall the Islamic Republic’s own record of disparaging pride in the country’s pre-Islamic rulers.

UK blames IRGC for RAF plot, vows crackdown on Iranian networks. Britain said on Monday that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had “almost certainly” directed a suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford, as it vowed to crack down on Iranian criminal networks, sanctioned two Iranian nationals and summoned Iran’s ambassador.

Over 90 killed in six months as clashes escalate in Iran's southeast - report. Armed attacks and security operations in southeastern Iran have left at least 94 people dead and 33 wounded since March 31, with fighting growing more frequent and involving heavier weapons, US-based human rights group HRANA reported Monday.

Suspect in plot to attack Iran journalists sought embassy visit, UK court hears. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists in Britain discussed an “embassy” visit with one contact and told another he had been promised £150,000 and help resolving his criminal case in Iran, a London court heard.

Meta, Google remove Iran matchmaking app after child marriage report. Meta and Google removed Iran’s “Adam and Eve” matchmaking app and related promotional accounts after an investigation found girls as young as 13 were being listed as prospective spouses, US-based rights group HRANA said Monday.

Iran hardliners back threats to strike Persian Gulf digital infrastructure. Iranian hardliners have backed security chief Mohsen Rezaei’s threat to strike data centers, undersea internet cables and artificial intelligence facilities in the Persian Gulf if the United States and Israel resume hostilities.

US military support against Houthis risks widening Iran war, expert says. Washington could support the Saudi campaign against the Houthis at little direct cost by lifting political objections to its operations, but deeper military involvement risks appearing to widen the Iran war, senior Middle East analyst Ryan Bohl told Iran International.

UKMTO warnings show 12 commercial ships attacked in one week. Twelve attacks on commercial vessels were reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf between October 5 and 11, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) warnings.

Iran officials hinted at land incursions if US resumes strikes - WSJ. Some Iranian officials have privately suggested Tehran could send forces into neighbouring countries if the United States launches new strikes, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the warnings.

‘Best advertisement for Starlink’ Iranians mock threat to subsea cables. The Islamic Republic’s threats to target undersea internet cables in the Persian Gulf drew mockery and criticism from readers who told Iran International that such attacks could deepen Iran’s isolation and damage its own connectivity.

Iran says six killed as armed clashes intensify in southeast. The Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday that five members of an alleged kidnapping cell and one of its personnel were killed near Zahedan, while separate reports said more than 20 members of an Iran-backed militia were killed or wounded in the area.

Gunfire heard as county-naming protest turns violent in central Iran. A protest over the name of a newly created county in central Iran turned violent after security forces moved to disperse demonstrators, with videos sent to Iran International capturing gunfire, tear gas and injured protesters.

Amnesty urges global action after Iran executes five protest-linked prisoners in one week. Amnesty International on Tuesday condemned Iran’s execution of five men in cases linked to the January protests within one week and called for coordinated international pressure on Tehran to halt further executions.

Houthi airport strikes carry echoes of Iran’s aviation threats, experts say. The deadly attacks on Riyadh’s main airport mirror Iranian warnings to disrupt regional air travel in response to US sanctions, analysts say, while serving the Houthis’ own goal of pressuring Saudi Arabia over its support for rival forces in Yemen.

L’accès à la mer Rouge est-il le véritable enjeu de la guerre entre l’Éthiopie et l’Érythrée ?. Quatre ans après avoir combattu côte à côte lors de la guerre du Tigré, les armées d’Abiy Ahmed et d’Issayas Afewerki s’affrontent dans le nord de l’Éthiopie. Jusqu’où cette escalade pourrait-elle aller ? Décryptage.

Denise Dusauchoy au secret à Kinshasa, le Maroc face à la rupture Algérie-Émirats arabes unis, le calendrier serré de la dette du Sénégal… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur la chute de l’influenceuse congolaise Denise Dusauchoy, décrypte les ambitions sahéliennes de Saddam Haftar, s’intéresse aux avocats qui s’imposent dans les batailles politiques ivoiriennes, analyse les conséquences de la rupture entre l’Algérie et les Émirats arabes unis pour le Maroc et évalue la crédibilité du calendrier de restructuration de la dette sénégalaise.

Tramadol en Afrique : le filon des trafiquants, l’antidouleur des pauvres. 97 % des saisies mondiales de tramadol ont lieu en Afrique de l’Ouest et en Afrique centrale. Ce trafic prospère sur un terreau : une région où l’on manque de presque tout pour soulager la douleur. Décryptage en infographies.

Maroc : ces femmes qui font l’économie. Au Maroc, les femmes occupent désormais 29 % des sièges dans les conseils d’administration des sociétés cotées. Finance, banque, industrie pharmaceutique… Elles s’imposent au sommet des plus grands groupes marocains. Portraits de six dirigeantes qui façonnent l’économie du royaume.

Le 11 octobre 1996, la Mauritanie organise ses premières élections pluralistes. Si les habitants de la « Mauritanie française » ont obtenu le droit d’élire des députés en 1946, il a fallu attendre 1996 pour que le pays organise ses premières législatives pluralistes. Un essai non transformé, mais une date importante dans l’histoire mauritanienne.

Mali : qui sont les hommes de l’ombre d’Ismaël Wagué, le général chargé de la réconciliation ?. Pour tenter de renouer les fils du dialogue dans un pays en guerre, le ministre d’État, ancien porte-voix des putschistes qui ont renversé Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta (IBK) en 2020, s’appuie sur un réseau qui va des officiers aux chefs communautaires, en passant par les religieux et les influenceurs.

Face au chômage, l’exode des jeunes Ghanéens vers le Golfe s’accélère. De plus en plus de jeunes Ghanéens jettent leur dévolu sur l’Arabie saoudite, les Émirats arabes unis ou le Qatar. Des destinations plus accessibles que l’Europe mais souvent gérées par des trafiquants et des agences de recrutement douteuses.

Cameroun anglophone : dix ans après, la guerre refuse de s’éteindre. Privés d’une partie de leurs appuis dans la diaspora, les séparatistes anglophones n’en poursuivent pas moins leurs attaques sanglantes, une décennie après le début de la crise dans les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest (Noso). Face à eux, Paul Biya, réélu il y a un an pour un huitième mandat, fait le pari de l’usure.

À Madagascar, un an après la chute d’Andry Rajoelina, la tentation présidentielle du colonel Michaël. Alors que la GEN Z, fragilisée par ses divisions internes, est marginalisée, le colonel Michaël Randrianirina doit organiser les scrutins qui mettront un terme, dans un an, à la transition qu’il préside. Et auxquels il pourrait bien participer.

Felipe VI à Ceuta et Melilla : la visite royale va-t-elle envenimer les relations Maroc-Espagne ?. Dix-neuf ans après la visite de Juan Carlos Ier, qui avait provoqué une crise diplomatique avec Rabat, c’est son successeur, le roi Felipe VI, qui se rendra les 13 et 14 octobre à Ceuta et Melilla, sur fond de crise migratoire et de tensions électorales en Espagne.

Sénégal, Gabon, croissance : les dossiers africains des assemblées du FMI et de la Banque mondiale. L’économie continentale résiste aux répercussions de la crise au Moyen-Orient. Un tournant stratégique se profile pour plusieurs pays africains dans leurs tractations financières avec le FMI.

Au moins 139 morts au large de Djibouti, l’UA appelle à « lutter contre le trafic de migrants ». L’embarcation surchargée a chaviré presque dès son départ, à quelques dizaines de mètres de la côte djiboutienne. Elle transportait 305 personnes, dont 80 ont pu être sauvées.

Gabon : Ali Bongo Ondimba à l’offensive pour récupérer ses comptes bancaires. Depuis le coup d’État qui l’a chassé du pouvoir en août 2023, l’ancien président gabonais, installé depuis plusieurs mois à Paris, n’a plus jamais eu accès à ses comptes locaux. Tandis que la banque BGFI lui oppose l’ordonnance d’un juge, lui y voit un règlement de comptes politique.

Un continent, deux modèles : comment Afreximbank défie Standard Bank sur le financement des grands projets. La banque multilatérale dispute au géant sud-africain la position de numéro un sur le terrain des mégaprojets. Un duel au sommet qui révèle surtout les failles du modèle bancaire commercial face aux besoins de l’Afrique.

La Sierra Leone sous l’emprise de la cocaïne, et de Jos Leijdekkers. La Sierra Leone serait devenue un quasi narco-État, sous l’emprise de Jos Leijdekkers, un trafiquant néerlandais qui fait désormais partie de la famille du président Julius Maada Bio.

Tchad-France : Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno attendu à l’Élysée par Emmanuel Macron. Le président tchadien atterrit à Paris en provenance de N’Djamena ce 12 octobre. Il doit rencontrer son homologue français, Emmanuel Macron, dès le lendemain. C’est déjà la troisième rencontre entre les deux hommes depuis le mois de janvier.

Côte d’Ivoire, Sénégal : le canadien Fortuna Mining peut-il réussir son pari africain ?. Après Séguéla en Côte d’Ivoire, Fortuna prépare le développement de Diamba Sud au Sénégal. Une nouvelle étape stratégique pour le groupe minier, qui cherche à étoffer ses actifs pour soutenir sa montée en puissance.

Gabon : ce qu’il faut retenir du remaniement surprise. Avec ce nouveau gouvernement, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema entérine des changements aux postes clés de l’Éducation nationale et de l’Accès universel à l’eau et l’électricité, tous deux en crise. Il propulse aussi des visages neufs au sein de l’exécutif.

Côte d’Ivoire : ce que l’on sait de la convocation de Sébastien Dano Djédjé, placé sous contrôle judiciaire. Après sa comparution ce 12 octobre à la section antiterroriste d’Abidjan, Dano Djédjé a été placé sous contrôle judiciaire, selon son avocate. Cette dernière dénonce une procédure irrégulière.

RDC : Joseph Kabila prend officiellement la tête de la rébellion, l’AFC/M23 dissoute. L’ancien président congolais a annoncé la création d’un mouvement politico-militaire, le Front pour la refondation de la nation, depuis Goma, dans l’est du pays. Ce nouveau groupe rebelle sera codirigé par les principaux chefs de l’AFC/M23.

Cameroun anglophone : vers Bamenda, une route neuve construite sur les cicatrices de la guerre. Symbole des frustrations qui ont nourri la crise anglophone commencée en 2016 dans les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest (Noso), l’axe Babadjou-Bamenda vient enfin d’être réhabilité. Mais le long de ses 35 km, les traces de dix années de conflit sont partout visibles.

Guinée : les dessous de la grâce présidentielle accordée à l’opposant Aliou Bah. Condamné à deux ans de prison pour « offense et diffamation » envers Mamadi Doumbouya, le leader du Mouvement démocratique libéral a été gracié mais pas encore libéré. Un long processus de lobbying, impliquant diplomates, autorités morales et religieuses, a précédé cette décision. Coulisses.

Alger annonce avoir arrêté 61 « saboteurs » marocains, Rabat évoque une « affabulation ». Les 61 personnes arrêtées dans la région d’Oran ont été présentées par Alger comme constituant un groupe criminel venu commettre des actes de sabotages. Pour le Maroc, il s’agit de candidats à la migration vers l’Europe.

TotalEnergies, NNPC, Conoil… Au Nigeria, comment la méga-raffinerie Dangote redistribue les cartes du marché pétrolier. Les revenus pétroliers de la Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), la compagnie pétrolière nationale, ont chuté de près de 78 % en 2025. Le lancement de la raffinerie Dangote et la libéralisation complète du marché ont déclenché une guerre des prix féroce dans l’ensemble du secteur aval.

Centrafrique : les manœuvres de Touadéra pour contenir la colère populaire contre la vie chère. À l’appel de la société civile, une journée ville morte a été organisée ce 12 octobre à Bangui, marquant la première mobilisation de ce type contre le pouvoir depuis 2023. Mais Faustin-Archange Touadéra a tout fait pour en limiter la portée.

Pourquoi Aliko Dangote accorde un délai supplémentaire pour l’IPO de sa raffinerie. Les investisseurs ont jusqu’au 27 octobre pour manifester leur intérêt. Aliko Dangote insiste sur le nombre de personnes qu’il veut voir participer à l’opération.

Au Niger, une fuite de pétrole majeure met la gestion du champ d’Agadem à l’épreuve. Une éruption de pétrole brut et de gaz secoue le nord-est du Niger depuis le 25 septembre. Le ministère du Pétrole alerte sur un incident environnemental d’une gravité exceptionnelle.

En Guinée, le calendrier des élections sénatoriales et régionales désormais fixé. Il s’agit des dernières étapes du retour à l’ordre constitutionnel : ces scrutins doivent permettre à Mamadi Doumbouya de mettre un terme à la période de transition entamée après son coup d’État de septembre 2021.

Rwanda – Jean-Guy Afrika : « La Formule 1 s’inscrit dans une ambition beaucoup plus large ». La Formule 1 signe son retour sur le continent africain en s’installant pour dix ans sur le circuit de Bugesera, près de Kigali. Pour le directeur général du Rwanda Development Board, cet investissement est cohérent avec la stratégie d’attractivité du pays.

Accords stratégiques et tensions diplomatiques : 5 questions pour comprendre la position du Somaliland dans la crise dans la Corne de l’Afrique. Reconnue par Israël en décembre 2025, la République autoproclamée s’impose dans les équilibres géopolitiques de la région, entre diplomatie sécuritaire et deals économiques. Au risque d’accentuer des tensions déjà vives.

Pourquoi des millions de contraceptifs destinés à plusieurs pays africains sont-ils bloqués en Belgique ?. Financés à l’origine par l’Usaid, ces colis humanitaires sont immobilisés depuis plus d’un an, sans qu’une solution n’ait été trouvée.

Comment la surpêche et l’industrie alimentaire vident les océans et ruinent les populations en Afrique de l’Ouest. Au Sénégal, en Mauritanie ou au Sahara occidental, des dizaines d’usines exploitent les ressources halieutiques de l’océan pour produire de la farine de poisson. Cette industrie ravage l’économie locale et pousse de plus en plus de personnes sur les dangereuses routes migratoires de l’Atlantique.

L’Erythrée demande au Conseil de sécurité de l’ONU de condamner la « déclaration de guerre » de l’Ethiopie. L’Ethiopie avait, la veille, accusé l’Erythrée, qui a déployé ces derniers jours des troupes dans le Nord éthiopien, « d’agression flagrante », dans une nouvelle escalade verbale entre les deux voisins, qui augmente le risque d’une guerre ouverte.

Le Maroc en cinq escales à portée de main et de clic. Chaque mois, La Matinale du Monde vous propose un dépaysement à moindre frais. Aujourd’hui, exploration du royaume chérifien en cuisine ou derrière l’écran.

Pourquoi Ceuta et Melilla restent un sujet de discorde entre l’Espagne et le Maroc. L’arrivée de plus de 72 000 migrants à Ceuta, en provenance du Maroc, les 30 et 31 juillet, a ravivé la question de la souveraineté de l’Espagne sur les deux villes autonomes de la côte nord-africaine. Une souveraineté revendiquée par Rabat depuis les années 1960, à laquelle la visite annoncée du roi Felipe VI, le 13 octobre, doit symboliquement opposer une énième fin de non-recevoir.

Romain Choron, historien et officier, victime expiatoire du raidissement de l’Etat français sur les archives militaires de la guerre d’Algérie. Les déboires administratifs subis par le Saint-Cyrien en raison de sa consultation d’archives classifiées sur la guerre souterraine menée par la France en Algérie, entre 1959 et 1962, ont soulevé une vive émotion chez les historiens. Ils illustrent les tentatives de l’Etat de durcir l’accès aux documents historiques sensibles.

Derrière le site complotiste Géopolitique profonde, plagiat, IA et sous-traitance à Madagascar. Ce site majeur de la complosphère française fait appel à des rédacteurs malgaches pour copier-coller des articles trouvés sur Internet et les soumettre à une intelligence artificielle chargée de leur donner une tonalité « plutôt pro-droite, pro-Trump, pro-Poutine, anti-UE ».

Au large de Djibouti, au moins 139 migrants meurent dans le naufrage de leur embarcation. Le bateau de fortune transportait 305 personnes de Djibouti vers le Yémen, selon les survivants du naufrage cités par l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations.

ICE, de la chasse à l’homme au trafic vers l’Afrique : deux documentaires implacables diffusés sur France 5 et France 24. Deux enquêtes remarquables se penchent sur les actions de cette police de l’immigration américaine encouragée par le président Trump.

L’Algérie déclare avoir arrêté 61 Marocains soupçonnés de préparer « des actes de sabotages ». La direction générale de la sûreté nationale évoque « un réseau criminel international marocain », sans donner de détails sur les actions qu’il aurait planifiées.

Les Cairotes scandalisés par l’abattage de leurs arbres. Le régime d’Abdel Fattah Al-Sissi a instauré une politique de grands travaux d’aménagement urbain au détriment des espaces verts. En réponse à une colère inédite dans la capitale égyptienne, le gouvernement tente d’ajuster sa stratégie.

Au Maroc, la consécration de Fouad Ali El-Himma, homme de l’ombre au service de Mohammed VI. Conseiller très influent auprès du souverain, qu’il a connu élève au collège royal, il est aussi le fondateur du Parti Authenticité et modernité, la formation qui va conduire le prochain gouvernement.

Tyla au Zénith de Paris : le décevant virage pop d’une chanteuse sud-africaine incontournable. Lors de son concert, lundi 12 octobre, l’interprète de « Water » présentera, notamment, le répertoire de son deuxième album paru cet été et à la dimension pop peu inspirée.

Le Sénégal peine à dépêtrer sa compagnie aérienne nationale des scandales à répétition. Le chef de l’Etat, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, mise sur Air Sénégal pour faire de Dakar un hub aérien, à quelques semaines du lancement des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse. Minée par une dette considérable, la compagnie fait face à une nouvelle affaire qui met en cause l’éthique de ses employés.

Joseph Kabila, ex-président de la République démocratique du Congo, prend la tête d’un mouvement politico-militaire incluant les rebelles du M23. Condamné à mort par contumace en 2025, l’ancien chef de l’Etat a été désigné à Goma, alors que l’opposition accuse l’actuel président, Félix Tshisekedi, de vouloir modifier la Constitution pour briguer un troisième mandat.

A Ceuta, les migrants ont opportunément disparu du paysage pour la visite du roi Felipe VI et de la reine Letizia. Les souverains effectuent une visite inédite, mardi 13 octobre, dans la ville autonome espagnole d’Afrique du Nord où les immigrés ayant déferlé du Maroc fin juillet sont encore des milliers à dormir à la belle étoile ou dans des centres d’accueil d’urgence.

Au Niger, une éruption de pétrole provoque un incident environnemental « d’une gravité exceptionnelle ». D’importantes quantités de pétrole brut et de gaz sont projetées à plus de dix mètres de hauteur, ont expliqué les autorités. Les causes de l’incident, qui a commencé le 25 septembre dans l’est désertique du pays, « ne sont pas encore totalement établies », mais la « piste criminelle ou terroriste » est écartée.

En Libye orientale, l’ascension fragile de Saddam Haftar, le fils du maréchal. Saddam Haftar, le dirigeant de la Cyrénaïque, est parvenu à prendre le contrôle du Parlement de Benghazi début octobre, consolidant ainsi son pouvoir et renforçant son statut de successeur de son père. Non sans attiser des querelles fratricides au sein de son clan.

Images. L’annonce surprise de la création d’un nouveau mouvement politico-militaire en République démocratique du Congo. Joseph Kaliba préside dorénavant le Front pour la refondation de la nation (FRN), une alliance avec les groupes rebelles AFC et M23.

Au Nigeria, le milliardaire Aliko Dangote veut faire de l’entrée en Bourse de sa raffinerie de Lagos une opération populaire. Le magnat nigérian des affaires a promis que l’entrée sur la place financière de Lagos de sa raffinerie serait « l’introduction en Bourse du peuple ». Il ambitionne de rassembler 10 millions de souscripteurs.

The resilience of the world economy is built on illusion - it's time the West woke up Submitted by Marco Carnelos on Sun, 10/11/2026 - 15:30 Record debt, a paralysed trade-dispute architecture and the normalisation of sovereign-asset seizure as a policy tool means fragility is baked into the global economic system In his Davos speech this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney recognised that powerful nations were using economic coercion to get what they want, pictured in Alberta, Canada, 1 October 2026 (Reuters/Todd Korol) Off Since 2022, a steady drumbeat of forecasts has warned that cascading military and political upheavals - war in Ukraine , conflict in the Middle East , an accelerating tariff war , the weaponisation of sanctions and the disruption of energy supplies - would eventually overwhelm the world economy’s capacity to absorb shocks. The most destructive of those scenarios have not materialised, or at least not yet. As the IMF's managing director Kristalina Georgieva stated last year, while previewing the fund's World Economic Outlook, the global economy "has generally withstood significant strains from various shocks". Although that resilience is real, on closer inspection, it is a more fragile and more contested achievement than it first appears. The adaptive mechanisms behind this resilience are visible and measurable. Trade has rerouted rather than collapsed. Energy corridors have diversified. And reserve managers have spent the past three years quietly re-engineering the architecture of the international monetary system. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); According to the World Gold Council's 2026 Central Bank Gold Reserves survey - which drew responses from 76 institutions, its highest participation in nine years - 89 percent of central banks expect global gold holdings to keep rising over the next year, with a record share planning to add to their own reserves. The result: gold has overtaken US Treasuries as the largest single component of global central bank reserves for the first time since the mid-1990s. Mother of all ticking bombs Analysts tracking the shift link it directly to a single event: reserve managers were unsettled by the seizure of the Central Bank of Russia's reserves at the start of the Ukraine war by Washington and have since been actively reducing the dollar share of their portfolios. Debt of this scale narrows the fiscal space available to absorb the next shock, military or otherwise, which is precisely what makes today's resilience difficult to extrapolate into tomorrow's This is a clear example that the economic system is not breaking under political pressure, it is adapting to it - flexibly, and crucially, without severing the interconnections that make global trade and finance function at all. In other words, central banks accumulating gold are not exiting the system; they are just hedging within it. But adaptability has a cost, and that cost is compounding. Global debt - government, household, corporate and financial combined - surpassed $365 trillion in the first half of 2026, according to the Institute of International Finance's Global Debt Monitor , the sixth consecutive quarterly record. Emerging-market debt alone rose by $6.5 trillion in the same period, breaking past $110 trillion. Georgieva has been blunt about the trajectory: speaking at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, she warned that global public debt is projected to reach 110 percent of the world's GDP by 2029. There is an evident reluctance to address what is not a crisis in any single country's balance sheet, but a structural drift that every major economy appears aware of and none is prepared to correct unilaterally. Debt of this scale narrows the fiscal space available to absorb the next shock, military or otherwise, which is precisely what makes today's resilience difficult to extrapolate into tomorrow's. In this context, there is also the mother of all ticking bombs, a nuclear one: the $40 trillion US federal debt which US Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent is desperately trying to reign in. The third strand, the onslaught of punitive political measures targeting market principles, is best illustrated by the fate of Russia's frozen central bank reserves. Roughly $300bn in Russian sovereign assets have been immobilised globally since 2022, with some €210bn ($235bn) held within the European Union. Erosion of neutrality Rather than remaining in legal limbo, these reserves have become the financial engine of a specific policy outcome: the EU's proposed €140bn ($157bn) "reparations loan" to Ukraine, structured so that Ukraine would repay it only once Russia itself pays war damages - effectively converting a sanctions freeze into a grant. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Russia's central bank has responded by suing the Brussels-based depository Euroclear , which holds the bulk of the assets, calling the manoeuvre illegal. Whatever one's view of the underlying conflict, the precedent is the point economists increasingly raise: the first large-scale use of frozen sovereign reserves as collateral for a geopolitical objective changes the calculus for every reserve-holding state watching from outside the western bloc. It is one more data pointing to the reinforcing of the gold-accumulation trend described above - and a vivid example of how political tools aimed at a single adversary can erode the perceived neutrality of the system itself. A parallel erosion is under way in trade governance. The WTO's Appellate Body (the one supposed to settle trade dispute among countries) has been non-functional since December 2019, after the United States blocked the appointment of new judges and talks on reviving or replacing it remain stuck. More than 30 appeals currently sit unresolved, and the workaround mechanism created to fill the gap - the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement - has resolved only a single case. The institution designed to prevent trade disputes from becoming purely a function of relative power has been quietly sidelined for seven years. It is then worth wondering - in such a situation - if the Global West and Global Rest see the same picture here. The evidence suggests convergence on diagnosis but real divergence on meaning. Both recognise that debt is unsustainable and that institutions are strained. But where western policymakers tend to treat sanctions, frozen assets and trade paralysis as defensive responses to external aggression. Voices from the Global Rest increasingly read the same tools as confirmation that the system was never as neutral as advertised. India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar captured this gap memorably in 2022, telling European interlocutors that Europe needed to "grow out of the mindset" that its problems are everyone's problems while the reverse does not hold. Selective status This is something many Global Rest governments had been thinking but not saying aloud: that the postwar order's claim to universality was always, in practice, more selective than it appeared. Why the EU's sanctions on Sudan's gold trade are fundamentally flawed Read More » The more honest and outspoken western leader to recognise such an unfair situation, to use an understatement, was Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier this year in Davos. None of this means the system is about to fracture. The world economy has proven more elastic than feared, absorbing shocks that a decade ago might have triggered genuine crisis. But elasticity and durability are not the same thing. The real test of this sort of "economy of resistance" is not whether it survives the next military-political storm - it plainly has, repeatedly. It is whether record debt, a paralysed trade-dispute architecture, and the normalisation of sovereign-asset seizures as a policy tool are quietly converting what is in effect a short-term adaptability into long-term fragility, especially at a moment when the Global Rest and Global West can no longer agree on what the system is actually for. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “What’s happening is that every country has now suddenly figured out that energy security is national security,” said Ajay Banga, president of the World Bank, in Bangkok, where financial officials from around the world have gathered this week for meetings. The forecast for Saudi Arabia , which was completed before recent attacks on Riyadh airport and elsewhere, estimated that the kingdom’s economy, which is more diversified, would shrink by 3.3 percent this year before growing 7.9 percent in 2027. Iran will not trade its nuclear insurance policy for worthless American promises Submitted by Ali Naghieh on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 15:45 A durable agreement to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz must make concessions progressively harder to reverse on both sides Iranian missiles are seen on display near a portrait of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, at Baharestan Square in Tehran on 28 September 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP) Off US President Donald Trump last month rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations, while hinting that talks might continue. But the fundamental barrier to a lasting agreement is Washington’s habit of rewriting the rules after the ink dries. Consider the last diplomatic opening. The June memorandum between the US and Iran promised to release frozen funds for recipients chosen by Iran’s central bank. Five days later, US Vice President JD Vance outlined a different arrangement : Washington and Qatar would approve the process, while the money would be restricted to purchases of American soy, corn and wheat. Washington was writing a shopping list with Iran’s money. That bait-and-switch highlighted a fatal flaw in American diplomacy. Washington expects Iran to trade lasting nuclear dismantlement for benefits the US can withdraw overnight. The more nuclear capacity Tehran surrenders, the more it depends on its adversary’s whims to deliver the rewards. Without enforceable, symmetrical remedies for American non-compliance, Washington’s preferred bargain leaves Iran easier to coerce precisely because it complied. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The US justified withdrawing oil and banking relief by citing Iranian attacks on shipping. But treating those clashes as the beginning of the story ignores the diplomatic sabotage that preceded them. Under the June interim agreement, Washington agreed to lift its naval blockade and grant oil waivers in exchange for a halt in hostilities and Iranian cooperation to restore Hormuz transit, pending Iranian- Omani talks over maritime administration. Tehran agreed to facilitate passage, not to surrender maritime oversight. Yet just one day later, a US-backed maritime centre recommended a southern route through Omani waters to bypass northern lanes associated with Iranian control. Washington was thus demanding Iranian cooperation, while simultaneously plotting a route to reduce Tehran’s leverage over Hormuz. When Iranian forces opened fire on 25 June on a vessel using the uncoordinated bypass route, the deal’s cooperative premise had already dissolved into a raw contest for control. Hollow promises The promised financial relief proved equally hollow. By late June, Qatar confirmed that the mechanism for releasing Iran’s frozen funds remained unresolved, while Washington’s proposed arrangement restricted the money to purchases of American agricultural goods - tying Iran’s access to its own sovereign assets to Washington’s domestic priorities. When further clashes erupted in July, the US Department of the Treasury revoked oil authorisations just 16 days after issuing them. It took no election or new administration; the same White House that granted relief quickly snatched it back. Washington treats its unilateral discretion to reverse commitments as strategic leverage. For Tehran, that discretion is precisely what makes American commitments unreliable. Washington has spent years dictating what Iran must surrender; the next deal must also ask what the US will put beyond its own discretion Iran has already experienced the consequences of substantial nuclear concessions. Under the 2015 nuclear agreement, it reduced its enriched-uranium stockpile , dismantled centrifuges, and rendered the Arak reactor vessel unusable. Trump withdrew from the deal in May 2018 , while the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed Iran’s full compliance ; Tehran waited more than a year before scaling back its commitments. Inspectors could verify the surrendered uranium and dismantled centrifuges, but they could not verify whether Washington would honour its commitments. Rebuilding a disabled reactor takes years, while reimposing US sanctions takes a single “stroke of a pen” . Regional war has transformed this imbalance into a security dilemma. For Tehran, nuclear latency - the ability to move quickly towards a weapon without actually possessing one - is increasingly viewed not simply as bargaining leverage, but as strategic insurance against catastrophic and existential escalation. Nuclear latency has not deterred conventional strikes. But the prospect of a rapid nuclear breakout forces adversaries to calibrate their campaigns: pushing for state collapse leaves a cornered Iran with no choice but to finally build the bomb. Fatal paradox Herein lies the fatal paradox of Washington’s strategy. The war might have reduced Iran’s nuclear capacity, but it also increased the value Tehran attaches to retaining a nuclear hedge . American policymakers treat military escalation as leverage to compel nuclear surrender, blind to the fact that the pressure itself makes surrender suicidal. Demanding that Tehran dismantle its hedge, without altering the threats that make it valuable, risks turning military gains into diplomatic failure. Washington can destroy facilities; it cannot expect the same campaign to make nuclear restraint more acceptable. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); If compliance leaves Tehran more exposed to the next bombing campaign, Washington is not preventing a bomb, but rather manufacturing the strategic necessity for it. Any new agreement must include restoring full IAEA access. Negotiators cannot freeze a stockpile that inspectors cannot monitor. But demanding transparency requires acknowledging Tehran’s intelligible pessimism: having watched the agency fail to unequivocally condemn attacks on its nuclear facilities, Tehran views intrusive inspections not as a routine baseline, but as a major security concession. Once stockpiles are verified and immobilised, deeper reductions, such as diluting 60 percent material , must strictly follow demonstrated American performance: actual oil sales, accessible sovereign assets, and an enduring ceasefire. This requires reciprocal irreversibility: reversible steps, such as immobilising nuclear material, should initially be exchanged for reversible measures, such as sanctions waivers. Progressively harder-to-reverse concessions, such as downblending, should be matched by progressively harder-to-revoke economic and security commitments from Washington. That means moving up a durability ladder, from flimsy presidential waivers towards normalised banking access, sovereign funds secured in independent international escrow, congressional repeal of statutory sanctions, and deeper long-term commercial integration with the global economy. Permanent Iranian nuclear concessions cannot be purchased with temporary presidential promises. Another countdown Economic relief alone cannot resolve a security crisis. Washington cannot demand that Iran surrender its nuclear hedge, while simultaneously underwriting the threat that gives that hedge much of its value. The US must formally pledge not to launch unprovoked strikes against a compliant Iran, while explicitly withholding intelligence, aerial refuelling, base access and munitions that could be used in an Israeli attack. Should Israel strike a compliant Iran anyway, the agreement must mandate an automatic suspension of specified US offensive military aid. Can Iran war deadlock be broken at the US ballot box? Read More » To enforce boundaries, dispute resolution must be independent and insulated from unilateral political vetoes. If Washington withholds earned relief, or if the US or Israel strike a compliant Iran, an independent panel established at signing should clear Tehran to halt nuclear reductions and suspend deal-specific restrictions, without losing economic relief already secured. Iran would remain bound by the baseline safeguards of the Non-Proliferation Treaty, and verified Iranian violations would trigger predetermined consequences, including a rapid sanctions snapback. Beyond the agreement itself, a durable settlement requires a transformed regional security architecture. Iran’s neighbours have legitimate concerns over maritime disruption and cross-border escalation. The nuclear pact should therefore run alongside a regional security process - one involving Iran, Iraq , and the six Gulf Cooperation Council states - that explores cooperative frameworks like a regional fuel-cycle consortium . This would allow Iran to retain domestic enrichment under shared regional ownership and oversight, thus reducing mutual threats, rather than substituting American hegemony for Iranian dominance. The objective is not simply to delay an Iranian bomb, but to reduce the strategic incentive to build one in the first place. That requires a regional security environment in which remaining without a nuclear deterrent is strategically sustainable for Tehran. No agreement can erase Iran’s nuclear knowledge, but a durable settlement can reduce the strategic value of turning that knowledge into a weapon. Washington has spent years dictating what Iran must surrender; the next deal must also ask what the US will put beyond its own discretion. If the answer is nothing, another signature will simply buy another countdown. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs395.37 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.85 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 13 (Tuesday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

‘Pakistan’s poverty rate higher than India, B’desh’. WASHINGTON: More than one-third of Pakistan’s population faces overlapping deprivations in health, education and living standards, according to the United Nations Development Prog­ramme’s (UNDP) Multidimensional Pov­er­ty Index (MPI) released on Monday. Figures released by the UNDP in New York show that 38.3 per cent of Pakistan’s population was multidimensionally poor, compared with 16.4 per cent in India and 14.9pc in Bangladesh. The estimates are based on household surveys conducted in different years and do not provide a strictly contemporaneous comparison. In Pakistan, the intensity of deprivation among those classified as multidimensionally poor stood at 51.7pc. Another 12.9pc of the population was considered vulnerable to multidimensional poverty, indicating that a substantial share of people remained at risk of falling into acute deprivation. Unlike conventional income-based measures, the MPI assesses overlapping disadvantages in areas such as nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing and household assets. UNDP estimates 38.3pc Pakistanis face multidimensional poverty The report also documents a worrying global reversal. The number of people living in multidimensional poverty has risen for the first time in 15 years, reaching 1.2 billion, as families struggle to meet their basic needs. The latest total is 51.5 million higher than the previous update. Children account for more than half of those affected, with 617m living in multidimensional poverty, while 83pc of the total live in rural areas. The global findings underline the scale of the challenge facing governments, particularly in providing essential services to disadvantaged communities. Poverty is not simply a shortage of income; it can also mean inadequate nutrition, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. South Asia accounts for a substantial share of global deprivation. The report says the region accounts for at least one-third of global deprivations in nutrition, housing, and years of schooling. It is also home to 150m poor people living in households where a school-aged child is not attending school, highlighting persistent barriers to education despite broader development gains. The UNDP’s regional figures put South Asia’s multidimensional poverty rate at approximately 19.3pc, with another 18.4pc of the population vulnerable to such poverty. Health accounts for about 29.9pc of the contribution to regional multidimensional poverty, education for 33.7pc and living standards for 36.3pc. The figures show how disadvantages in different areas reinforce one another. Poor health, inadequate education and substandard living conditions can trap families in poverty and make it difficult for them to improve their circumstances. “The rise in poverty should be a wake-up call for the world,” said UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo. “Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable.” Published in Dawn, October 13th, 2026

Super El Nino set to make 2026 record hottest year. BRUSSELS: An intensifying El Nino pattern set an all-time temperature high in a key Pacific zone in September and could help make this year the hottest globally on record, the director of the EU’s climate monitor said on Monday. Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino would likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode’s expected peak later this year. The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming. The Copernicus Clim­ate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Nino monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Nino3.4, had reached an “all-time high” of 29.70 degrees Celsius last month. This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, the EU monitor said. This year’s El Nino, which emerged in June, is “very exceptional” but it is too early to say whether it is the strongest ever observed, Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo told AFP. As climate change raises ocean temperatures, it can make recent El Nino events appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons. Copernicus said it had adopted a new index, which accounts for the warming of tropical oceans, that suggested the current event is not yet stronger than past ones. “It’s a very large event even in that metric,” Buontempo said. “This very large event today is happening in a much warmer climate.” Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino. On Friday, Japan’s weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their “strongest intensity on record”. Record ocean temperatures As El Nino gathers strength, global average sea surface temperatures hit a record 21.05 degrees Celsius for September, topping the previous high of 20.92 for the same month in 2023, according to Copernicus. Experts have warned that this El Nino, combined with human-induced climate change, could make 2027 the hottest year on record as heat stored in the Pacific is released into the atmosphere. The weather phenomenon, which typically occurs every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months, can drive world temperatures higher the year after its peak. But Buontempo said even 2026 could wind up a record breaker as this El Nino builds toward its peak. “If we follow the pattern we have seen in the past, we may have a record-breaking 2026, followed by a record-breaking 2027,” he told AFP. After a record-breaking August, the world experienced its second hottest September ever observed, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27 degrees Celsius, the EU service said. Riyadh vows ‘serious’ response amid Houthi escalation. • Saudi minister says ‘energy security can’t be taken for granted’ • Yemeni rebels warn of ‘swift, painful response’ if US joins war • Iran ‘deeply concerned’, offers to help broker talks • Riyadh airport to remain shut RIYADH: Saudi Arabia vowed a “serious” response after Houthi strikes turned Riyadh’s international airport into a target, killing 18 people in under a week and leaving the world’s biggest oil exporter facing its worst security crisis in more than a decade. “Energy security can’t be taken for granted,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told an energy conference in Riyadh. “The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious. For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people and our resilience.” The strikes have shaken the world’s biggest oil exporter, which is pursuing an expensive economic reform programme intended to att­ract foreign investment. Oil prices rose above $105 a barrel on Monday. Yemen’s civil war, in which a Saudi-led military coalition backs the government against the Houthis, has reignited months into the wider US-Iran conflict, which has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis. On Saturday, Houthi strikes killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 at King Khalid International Airport, the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade. Four people died in earlier attacks on Wed­nes­day and Thursday, and another was killed on Sunday, when Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said a fresh strike also wounded 11 people. Riyadh’s airport was not the only one to suffer an attack as authorities said Dammam airport in the east was also struck on Sunday evening. One person had been killed and 11 wounded in a strike on Dammam airport. The Saudi-led coalition said on Monday it had “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi ballistic missile heading for Khamis Mushait, a southern city that is home to a major military base. It also reported responding to drone and missile threats around Riyadh, where residents reported explosions and authorities warned of continuing security risks. The coalition has called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”. Volker Turk, the UN human rights chief, said he was “appalled by the repeated attacks” on Saudi Arabia but urged both sides to back down. US warned against joining strikes A Houthi official warned on Monday that the US would face a “swift and painful response” if it entered the war in Yemen. Donald Trump has said he is considering joining Saudi strikes against the group. “If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi political bureau, told AFP. He also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”. The campaign, he said, was intended to show the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, “that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position”. Trump condemned Saturday’s attack as “not acceptable” and said he would speak to the crown prince about the possibility of joining strikes against the Houthis. Fighting in Taiz Elsewhere in Yemen, Houthi fighters have tightened their siege of Taiz, where more than 60 people were killed in 24 hours, military sources from both sides told AFP. A military source loyal to the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government said the Houthis had blocked all exits and launched several attacks overnight. The dead included 22 pro-government fighters and at least 40 Houthis, the sources said. The Houthis continued fighting despite Saudi airstrikes and were sending reinforcements. Yemen’s health ministry warned on Sunday of a “humanitarian catastrophe” in the city, where medicine, medical equipment and fuel were “on the verge of running out”. Regional reaction Iran said it was “deeply concerned” about the escalating attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia and offered to help broker talks. “We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula,” the foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baqaei, told a weekly news conference. Tehran was ready, he said, “to use our good offices to help facilitate dialogue between the parties”. Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, called for stronger Gulf security cooperation. “It is necessary to revive joint action by the Gulf countries, particularly in security and defence, and to strengthen the collective security system,” he wrote on X, adding that shortcomings in regional security had encouraged further attacks. The UAE, which has long been at odds with Saudi Arabia over Yemen, expressed its “full solidarity” with the kingdom. China also condemned the attacks on Saudi airports and energy infrastructure. “China condemns the attacks that caused heavy casualties and expresses serious concern over the intensification of the conflict,” said the foreign ministry spoke­swoman, Mao Ning, who urged all parties to avoid escalation and resolve disputes through dialogue. Flights disrupted Authorities have extended the closure of King Khalid international airport until Saturday, and airlines have cancelled flights after the repeated attacks. A notice to airmen showed the airport would stay closed until 2100 GMT on Oct 17. Flightradar24 showed aircraft avoiding Riyadh on Monday, although flights continued through Saudi airspace towards Jeddah. The aviation analytics firm Cirium said cancellations across Saudi airports had reached 46.4pc. Etihad Airways cancelled flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah, while Gulf Air suspended services to Riyadh. Lufthansa and Air France-KLM also extended suspensions. Delta Air Lines postponed its planned Atlanta-Riyadh service, due to start on Oct 23, until March 2027. US aviation regulators urged airlines to exercise caution, and the American embassy warned citizens of security risks. “This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented,” said Mark Zee, the founder of the aviation safety organisation Opsgroup. Published in Dawn, October 13th, 2026

AJK leaders call for peaceful resolution of Poonch crisis. PTI’s protest call draws lacklustre response in Peshawar. PESHAWAR: With riot police and prison vans deployed across the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, only a handful of Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) workers stepped out on Monday to stage brief protests in different areas of the city. What the PTI had called a “flash protest” was staged in Nishtarabad, Hashtnagri and Sikandarpura, attracting just 15-20 workers. No former minister, MPA or MNA turned up. PTI Peshawar district president Irfan Saleem had called for the protest on Sunday night. The workers would emerge from streets, shout slogans against the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in the province and disperse upon approaching the riot police. Only handful of workers stage brief protests A senior PTI leader wondered how the workers could stage a protest if thousands of police personnel were deployed on all roads and intersections of the city. He told Dawn that the police did not allow workers to demonstrate and that the party leadership had categorically instructed them to avoid clashes with the police and security forces. Asked about the future course of action, the PTI leader said the Tehreek Tahafuz Ayeen-i-Pakistan (TTAP) had convened a meeting today (Tuesday) to decide the next steps. Following the proclamation of emergency in the province, the PTI’s local cabinet met on Monday, with senior vice-president Senator Noorul Haq Qadri in the chair. During the meeting, the party’s deputy general secretary, Nawaz Shangla, presented a declaration that was adopted by the participants. The meeting strongly condemned what it described as the federal government’s undemocratic measures, including the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in the province. It termed the removal of an elected government an attack on the public mandate and democratic values. Police personnel arrest a PTI worker during a protest in the provincial capita.l— AFP/Shahbaz Butt The arrest of former chief minister Sohail Afridi, PTI provincial president Junaid Akbar Khan, provincial assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, former Gilgit-Baltistan chief minister Khalid Khurshid and other party leaders was also condemned as shameful. The participants demanded the immediate release of Sohail Afridi and other arrested leaders. They also praised Mr Afridi for refusing to make any compromise on people’s mandate. The party’s provincial cabinet further condemned the governor’s maiden address to the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, describing its tone as dictatorial. It instructed party workers to hold peaceful protests across the province against the federal government’s “illegal actions”. Students return home as educational institutions in Peshawar remained closed. — AFP/Shahbaz Butt The participants said the PTI would continue its struggle for democratic rights, constitutional supremacy and the protection of the public mandate. They also called for an end to political victimisation and reiterated their commitment to safeguarding the democratic system, constitutional rights and political stability in the province. A small demonstration was held in Landi Kotal following the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency. India youth shift tactics as police clamp down on election protest. From Batman masks to offline maps, young Indian protesters have responded to one of New Delhi’s toughest security crackdowns with improvised tactics designed to evade surveillance and keep demonstrations alive. As police and protesters engage in a high-stakes game of cat and mouse, social media savvy students are turning ingenuity into a form of resistance. With tens of thousands of security personnel deployed in key parts of the capital to block the main protest site of Jantar Mantar, protesters turned to holding flash demonstrations elsewhere, taking authorities by surprise. Protesters have been undeterred by thousands of reported detentions during demonstrations over the weekend in the capital. Many have since been released. They are seeking the resignation of the head of India’s election commission, accusing it of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party — which the constitutional body has denied. Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters shout slogans during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter roll irregularities linked to the “special intensive revision” (SIR), in New Delhi on October 12, 2026. —AFP Meghnad S., a 36-year-old content creator, is on a mission that resembles a crowd-sourced rescue service. Armed with little more than smartphones, his group of about 170 volunteers spent the weekend tracking police vehicles. As soon as volunteers identified where detainees had been taken, information was fed into a digital dashboard matching them with volunteer drivers. “Once we get to know where the detainees are, we have a WhatsApp group where we ask if any volunteer driver is around, what car they have, if it is stocked with food, water, fuel,” Meghnad told AFP . Sometimes a doctor would join the ride. “Once those checks are done, we try and get a doctor in our network to join the driver on the way, in case the detainees need medical assistance.” Dodging surveillance cameras Popular student leader Neha Bora became a viral sensation after a case of mistaken identity led to police detaining her lookalike. The real Bora, 29, managed to slip through the security cordon and make a dash towards central Delhi before eventually being detained. She later posted a photograph with her doppelganger, joking that the resemblance was “pure coincidence, not strategy”. All India Students’ Association (AISA) President Neha Bora raises her fist inside a bus, as opposition parties march to the Supreme Court in protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has sparked days of unrest, in New Delhi, India on October 12, 2026. —Reuters It was not just Bora — police were also seen struggling to catch up with sprightly young protesters on streets. “They have big bellies, they can’t run,” a protester told reporters. “They pant after running just 50 metres,” she said. In other dramatic scenes, protesters were seen holding on to one another as they were dragged to waiting buses — only for them to later wriggle out from the driver’s seat or the rear window. Police personnel detain supporters of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter roll irregularities linked to the “special intensive revision” (SIR), in Ahmedabad on October 10, 2026. —AFP AFP also met several demonstrators who wore Batman masks to avoid being identified. Bollywood actress Richa Chadha, meanwhile, offered other tips to avoid detention while filming herself drawing on her face with make-up on Sunday. “Dear protesters, since you’re being filmed without your consent, try using make-up to dodge surveillance/facial recognition cameras,” she said on social media.
