Pakistan condemns Israeli actions in Syria, calls for withdrawal. UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan has condemned continued Israeli military actions in Syria, calling for Israel’s withdrawal from all occupied Syrian territory and full respect for the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement. Speaking at a UN Security Council briefing on the humanitarian and political situation in Syria on Monday evening, Pakistan’s Acting Permanent Representative, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, said Israeli actions violated international law and Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, undermining prospects for regional peace and stability. He reaffirmed that the occupied Syrian Golan remained Syrian territory under international law and relevant UN Security Council resolutions, including resolutions 338 and 497. Ambassador Jadoon also reiterated Pakistan’s support for Syria’s political transition, national reconciliation and economic recovery, stressing the importance of preserving the country’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity. Welcoming renewed diplomatic engagement and efforts to restore national institutions, he expressed optimism about Syria’s future. He backed the Syrian government’s efforts towards an inclusive political transition and welcomed progress in engagement with the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). He called for outstanding challenges, including the situation in Suweida, to be addressed through dialogue and peaceful engagement, with full respect for Syria’s unity and territorial integrity. Emphasising the need for sustained international support, Ambassador Jadoon said reconstruction, economic revival and continued humanitarian assistance were essential to meeting the needs of the Syrian people. He noted that sanctions relief, increased investment and stronger regional and international economic partnerships could provide fresh impetus to Syria’s recovery. The Pakistani envoy also stressed the need for continued vigilance against Daesh and other terrorist groups, including foreign terrorist fighters. He expressed support for Syria’s efforts to strengthen its security and national institutions. Reaffirming the longstanding ties between Pakistan and Syria, Ambassador Jadoon said Islamabad would remain a steadfast friend and partner, committed to strengthening bilateral relations and advancing peace, stability and prosperity for the Syrian people. Last month, a UN commission investigating Syria expressed alarm over Israel’s military activity inside Syrian territory, warning that some actions, including the detention of civilians, could amount to war crimes. In August, eight Israeli airstrikes hit an airbase in northwestern Syria, Syrian state media reported, in what the US envoy for the region called an “unnecessary escalation”. In the months after Assad was toppled, Israel seized ground in southwestern Syria and struck much of the Syrian military’s heavy weapons and equipment, as Israeli officials expressed alarm over the background of Syria’s new rulers.

'No choice': IMF says developing countries must cut spending despite Iran war shock. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned on Tuesday that while low-income developing countries were dealing with the disproportionate impacts of the Iran war-fuelled energy shock , many had “no choice” but to cut spending or potentially face debt restructuring. Speaking to AFP on the sidelines of the organisation’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, IMF deputy director of research, Petya Koeva Brooks, said that the heavily indebted oil-importing countries were facing the worst of the energy shock, and had difficult choices in helping their citizens through the crisis. “Unfortunately, after years of the global economy being hit [by] shock after shock, debt levels have increased quite a lot, and at the same time, inflation has become a problem,” she said. The US war on Iran has plunged the Middle East into conflict and sent global energy prices soaring , as Tehran’s retaliatory action targeted Washington’s Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies. Those prices have begun to bleed into other goods, with the crisis also having an effect on crucial fertiliser supplies. The IMF has called on countries to offer narrow, targeted subsidies in the wake of the crisis, while also recommending all governments work to rebuild fiscal buffers and address rising debt after years of fighting economic shocks since the pandemic. “Our messages indeed apply to most countries, but again, the trade-offs and the choices that have to be made are much more difficult for the most vulnerable countries,” Koeva Brooks said. The IMF’s World Economic Outlook , released on Tuesday, identified low-income developing countries that are net oil importers and are not exposed to the ongoing artificial intelligence technology investment boom as being the most vulnerable to the shocks from the Iran war. “For those countries that are most vulnerable, this is where the consumption basket is heavily weighted towards energy and food, and so indeed it is much much more difficult,” she said. “But unfortunately there is no other choice.” The senior IMF official added that “many” low-income countries were in debt distress, or close to it, and that they should seek debt restructuring if they were not able to address the issue. “Where debt is not sustainable, then resolving that debt and having orderly and timely restructuring is always better than waiting, because then the cost of restructuring down the road is going to be much higher,” she said. ‘Domino effect’ In its World Economic Outlook, the IMF raised its forecast for 2026 global growth, largely on the back of advanced economies enjoying a boost from AI-related investments and economic activity. Growth outcomes were highly uneven across economies, depending on their exposure to the war and whether they were integrated into AI supply chains. The world’s advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1 per cent in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain such as Taiwan and South Korea posting significantly higher figures. Koeva Brooks told AFP that if AI investment activity were to slow, the world economy “would see a negative impact on output, not only in advanced countries like the US but again through trade linkages also in Asia”. In the IMF’s worst-case scenario — of AI not delivering promised productivity gains — global GDP forecasts for 2028 would fall by as much as 0.4pc. Climate-related risks were another key part of the World Economic Outlook this year, and Koeva Brooks told AFP that some of the effects of a particularly intense El Niño phenomenon had already been taken into account in higher prices for certain food items. The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Niño raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming. “We have a significant increase in beverage prices, in the prices of rice, and so on,” said Koeva Brooks. “Of course, it could turn out that the domino effect is even bigger than what we currently have.”

5 of a family found dead inside locked flat in Karachi's Bin Qasim. Five members of a family were found dead on Tuesday in a locked one-room apartment in Karachi’s Bin Qasim Town, police said. Those dead included a middle-aged couple, along with their two daughters under the age of six, and the husband’s sister who was in her early 20s, according to Bin Qasim Station House Officer (SHO) Faisal Rafiq. Police said the apartment in Gulshan-i-Falaknaz Block J was locked from the inside. The SHO said the couple had suffered fatal injuries, adding that a pistol was recovered from the incident site. Sindh Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar and the provincial police chief ordered that the deaths be probed from all possible angles. The Edhi rescue service said the bodies had been transferred to Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC). Home minister takes notice Taking notice of the incident, the home minister sought details from the Malir senior superintendent of police (SSP). In a statement, Lanjar directed that the incident be investigated from all angles and that “every possible measure” be taken to bring the facts and motives to light. “The elements involved in the incident should be identified and action should be ensured according to the law,” Lanjar was quoted as saying. He ordered officials to keep him updated on progress in the case. Meanwhile, Sindh Inspector General of Police (IGP) Javed Alam Odho sought a detailed report from the east deputy inspector general, a statement issued by his office said. “A transparent and impartial investigation covering all aspects of the incident must be conducted, and the actual causes of the deaths determined,” IGP Odho said. He also directed officers to ensure immediate evidence collection and fulfilment of legal requirements, including forensic analysis. He added that potential criminal angles should be probed and directed officers to keep him updated on the investigation. Last month, a middle-aged doctor, his wife and their three underage daughters were found dead at their Ahsanabad apartment in Scheme-33 off Superhighway. IGP Odho had established a high-powered body to investigate the incident.

Pope Leo heads to Rome hospital for lung operation. Pope Leo XIV was due to be admitted to hospital in Rome on Tuesday for surgery to remove a nodule on his lung, an operation experts say is generally low-risk. The 71-year-old will head to the Gemelli hospital in the late morning, Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni told AFP . The surgery to remove a pulmonary nodule, or small growth of tissue in the lung, will mark the pope’s first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025. On Sunday, in a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers, Leo told faithful in St Peter’s Square that doctors had discovered the nodule “at a very early stage” during recent medical checks. “The doctors believe it would be right to intervene,” he said, addressing the crowds from a window of the Apostolic Palace. The Vatican was historically very secretive about papal health, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo’s predecessor Francis , an Argentine who freely discussed ailments. The pope’s recovery time could be about a week, the Vatican said. His audiences have been cancelled until October 20. Rome’s Gemelli hospital is where popes are usually treated, and Leo is expected to stay in a special top-floor suite, under high security. He will likely be accompanied by his personal nurse Massimiliano Strappetti, who looked after Leo’s predecessor Francis during several stays at the Gemelli hospital before his death last year . ‘Coin lesion’ Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health. Marco Scarci, a thoracic surgery expert in the UK, told AFP it was not “a particularly risky operation” and he expected Leo’s recovery to be quick, though “it might take up to three months to return to his pre-surgery fitness level”. Leo is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Most pulmonary nodules are benign, or non-cancerous, but a small percentage can be an early indication of lung cancer. The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks, and there were no symptoms that led to checking the pope’s lungs. A small nodule is called a “coin lesion” because on X-rays it looks like a coin, Professor Federico Venuta, head of Thoracic Surgery at the Policlinico Umberto 1 hospital in Rome, told AFP . Small nodules tend not to cause symptoms, but larger ones can cause shortness of breath, chest pain and persistent coughing — sometimes with blood. Such nodules “could be a whole range of benign lesions — inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, or congenital — or they could be malignant,” Venuta said. Outlook ‘positive’ Removing the nodule can take place under general anaesthetic with the patient breathing through a tube. “Often, the lesion can be accessed from the outside or inside, for instance, via image-guided biopsy or endoscopy, but sometimes this is not possible,” Venuta said. Even if the nodule should turn out not to be benign, the pope’s outlook would be “very positive”, he said. “For a generally healthy person, the prognosis for lung cancer caught at such an early stage — specifically a pulmonary nodule with no distant spread — is absolutely favourable,” he said. In terms of the Latin American trip, Venuta said that “generally, the rule is to avoid air travel for about 20 days following these surgeries, though there is obviously some flexibility”.

New Delhi police detain top 'cockroach' leaders after flash protest at Jantar Mantar. India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) said on Tuesday that key leaders had been detained after entering an iconic protest site in New Delhi blocked by police. Opposition parties and supporters of the movement have taken to the streets in recent days, defying a security clampdown to demand the resignation of the head of India’s election commission, accusing it of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing. Delhi Police said on Monday that Jantar Mantar in the heart of the capital had been taken off the list of designated official protest sites. The site has been sealed off for several days by yellow metal barricades and guarded by a heavy police presence . But a video posted online by CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke on Tuesday showed protesters clambering over the barricades, running into the empty space and waving the national flag — before police chased and detained them. View this post on Instagram “CJP sneaks inside to reclaim Jantar Mantar,” the group said in a post on social media, adding that those detained included leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde. “All of them have been detained by Delhi Police,” it added. View this post on Instagram Delhi Police had announced three official sites on Monday as alternatives to Jantar Mantar, where protesters have gathered for decades — including CJP demonstrations that led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal in July. “You cannot denotify the resistance,” Dipke said, tagging Modi in his post. View this post on Instagram Modi, in comments at a business conference in New Delhi on Tuesday, called India the “mother of democracy”, but did not refer directly to the protests. “In our country, people openly debate a wide range of issues and discuss different perspectives,” he said.

President Zardari approves foreign visits of SC, FCC chief justices. On the advice of the prime minister, President Asif Ali Zardari has approved ex-Pakistan leaves and issued no-objection certificates (NOC) for the chief justices of the Supreme Court (SC) and the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) to make upcoming foreign visits. In a press release issued late on Monday, the Presidency said that President Zardari has approved the trips of Chief Justice of Pakistan (CJP) Yahya Afridi and FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan. CJP Afridi would visit the “United Kingdom, South Korea and Japan from Oct 14 to 21 and from Oct 27 to Nov 4”, the Presidency said. Justice Aminuddin would visit Azerbaijan from Oct 19 to 22 to attend TÜRK-AY – a conference of constitutional courts and bodies exercising constitutional jurisdiction in the Turkic world. The FCC was admitted as an observer to TÜRK-AY in July this year, about four years after the forum was established. The president is the competent authority to grant leave to the SC and FCC chief justices under Rule 14 of the 1997 and 2025 orders regarding leave, pension and privileges for the respective court. Under the same rules, the chief justice of each court is the competent authority to grant or refuse leave, or to revoke or curtail leave already granted to other judges of their court. In April 2025, CJP Afridi headed a delegation to the 20th Con­­ference of Chief Jus­ti­ces of the Supreme Courts of Shanghai Cooperation Organisation member states in Hangzhou, China. In June this year, Justice Aminuddin represented Pakistan at the 14th St. Petersburg International Legal Forum in Russia.

Pakistan’s growth during FY27 projected at 3.5pc, inflation at 9.9pc: IMF. ISLAMABAD: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Pakistan’s economic growth at 3.5 per cent during the current fiscal year and inflation to remain close to double digits for another year, notwithstanding global growth rebounding to 3.4pc. In its flagship World Economic Outlook, released at the launch of the World Bank-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, the fund estimated Pakistan’s current account deficit to widen to 1pc of GDP from a surplus of 0.5pc in FY2025. Headline inflation is projected to rise significantly to 9.9pc from 7.1pc last year. However, the Washington-based lending agency projected Pakistan’s unemployment rate to decline to 6.5pc this year, compared with 6.9pc last year and 7.1pc a year earlier. The fund, which concluded its review of Pakistan’s economic situation last week, did not explain the projected decline in unemployment despite the rising population and its other economic forecasts, including higher inflation and a widening current account deficit. The fund’s growth projections are significantly lower than the government’s 4pc target for the current year and the 3.8pc forecast by the World Bank last month. Its estimated 3.5pc growth rate for Pakistan is slightly lower than the 3.6pc recorded last year but higher than the 3.2pc in FY2025. Saying global economic activity had proved resilient despite multiple challenges, the international lender projected global growth to slow to 3.1pc in 2026 before rebounding to 3.4pc in 2027. Global headline inflation is projected to rise notably to 4.7pc in 2026 before easing to 4.1pc in 2027, it added. The IMF attributed global economic resilience to the technology upturn, buffers and adaptations that helped mitigate the damage from geopolitics-driven disruptions. “In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events. The pandemic and the ensuing disruptions to global supply chains; the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, with the consequent sharp increases in the prices of energy and other commodities; and significant changes in trade barriers and trading relations have tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets, and governments,” it said. “Individually, each of these major developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary. Yet, despite this barrage of shocks, the global economy has held up,” the IMF said. It added that labour markets had remained unexpectedly strong, financial systems had broadly withstood the shocks and the sharpest monetary tightening in half a century, while inflation had receded from its peaks in many economies, although it remained persistent in some cases. The IMF warned that energy-importing economies like Pakistan, which have limited links to the technology value chain, face the most difficult outlook. The margins of adjustment that have helped sustain resilience, however, are not limitless, and risks are skewed to the downside. Further escalation in conflicts, a reassessment of expectations surrounding artificial intelligence (AI), renewed trade tensions and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken growth. On the upside, stronger momentum in AI investment and productivity gains from AI, or a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions, could strengthen growth, it said. The fund advised its members that fiscal frameworks must deliver better results in dealing with disruptive shocks and build policy space through revenue measures. During cost-of-living crises, governments should preserve price signals and rely primarily on temporary, targeted income support for the most vulnerable, it said. The stable global aggregate masks a reallocation of growth across economies. Countries with limited direct exposure to the war shock and strong participation in the technology upturn are seeing activity hold up or strengthen. Energy exporters outside the immediate conflict zone are benefiting from favourable terms of trade. Conversely, energy-importing economies with little connection to the technology value chain face the most difficult combination of higher import costs and exchange rate pressures, weaker real incomes, more constrained fiscal space and fewer offsetting demand impulses. Many low-income and vulnerable countries belong to this latter group, increasing the risk that recent shocks will widen income gaps across and within countries. The IMF projected world trade volume growth to slow in 2026 and stabilise in 2027, reflecting the drag from tariffs, adjustments in production chains and continued strength in technology-related trade. Global imbalances are expected to decline only modestly over the medium term, as large fiscal deficits, limited domestic rebalancing, technology-driven capital flows and differing demand compositions across major economies under current policies continue to sustain external gaps. The medium-term growth outlook remains lacklustre by historical standards and uneven across countries, partly reflecting varying degrees of AI preparedness and the robustness of energy mixes. Risks are skewed to the downside, the IMF warned, adding that a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East could keep energy and food prices elevated and volatile, revive inflationary pressures, worsen fiscal and external balances, and weigh on growth. Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyberattacks or extreme weather events could amplify these effects. A day earlier, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb told Reuters that the government expected the economy to grow by more than 4pc this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices. He also said the government was looking to privatise five to six entities during the year, potentially raising more than $1 billion. Pakistan’s economy remains vulnerable to a prolonged conflict in the Middle East because of its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region.

Sohail Afridi’s brother approaches Peshawar High Court to trace his whereabouts. PESHAWAR: The brother of non-functional Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Tuesday approached the Peshawar High Court (PHC) to trace his whereabouts. On October 11, the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP, invoking Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution. On the same day, the PTI claimed that the Afridi, along with some of his cabinet ministers and party leaders, had been abducted. The next day, officials, however, confirmed that Afridi and some of his cabinet members were in preventative custody . The state minister for interior had stated that those against whom cases were pending would be charged and tried, while the others would be released. Muhammad Amir, Afridi’s brother, filed a petition in the high court, seeking multiple directives for the respondents, including the KP inspector general of police (IGP), Peshawar capital city police officer (CCPO) and others, to immediately take all lawful and effective measures to trace and recover his brother and, if he was found to be in custody, produce him before the high court so that the legality of his detention could be examined in accordance with Article 199(1)(b)(i) of the Constitution. The petition was filed through senior counsel Bashir Khan Wazir. He contended that the impugned detention and disappearance of the abductee were “wholly illegal, unlawful, without lawful authority and of no legal effect”, as the respondents had “failed to disclose any lawful order, warrant, abduction order or other legal authority under which the abductee was taken into custody”. Amir also sought further directives requiring the respondents concerned to submit a comprehensive report on the whereabouts, present condition and legal status of the abductee, along with details of the steps taken to trace and recover him. The petitioner requested the court to direct the CCPO to submit a detailed report on the alleged incident that took place at around 2pm on October 11, 2026, at the Chief Minister’s House in Peshawar. The report would include the circumstances in which the abductee was allegedly taken away, the security arrangements in place, the persons present and the action taken immediately afterwards. Afridi’s brother asked the court to direct the respondents to “ensure the preservation and lawful examination of all relevant CCTV footage, security logs, entry and exit registers, duty rosters, vehicle access records and other contemporaneous material relating to the incident, including footage from the relevant entrances, exits and adjoining routes”. Furthermore, he sought the registration of a first information report (FIR) and a direction for a “prompt, impartial and effective investigation” into the alleged abduction, disappearance and illegal detention of the abductee. The petitioner requested the court to direct the release of the abductee if he was found to be in unlawful or improper custody. The petitioner also sought interim relief, requesting the court to direct the respondents, pending the final decision on the instant writ petition, to immediately ascertain Afridi’s whereabouts and submit a preliminary report within a timeframe set by the court. He also requested the court to direct the respondents to produce the abductee before it if he was found to be in the custody or control of any person or authority, so that the legality of his detention could be determined. The petitioner claimed that on October 11, 2026, at approximately 2pm, the non-functional chief minister was “illegally detained” at the Chief Minister’s House and subsequently “abducted from the premises by unidentified armed and masked individuals in the presence of the capital city police officer (CCPO)”. Afridi’s brother stated that the precise sequence of events, the identities of the persons involved and the circumstances in which he was taken away require immediate verification through the relevant official record, eyewitness accounts and other available evidence. He stated that the incident took place at the premises of the Chief Minister’s House, and, according to the information available to the petitioner, occurred in the presence of the CCPO. “The circumstances in which the abductee was taken away from such a sensitive public institution, despite the reported presence of a senior police officer, raise grave and legitimate concerns regarding the security arrangements, the response of the concerned authorities and the safety and liberty of the abductee,” the petition said. The petition maintained that the petitioner had reasonable grounds to apprehend that the abductee might have been taken to an undisclosed location and might be held there against his will. He contended that Afridi’s whereabouts and present condition needed to be immediately ascertained through lawful means. Afridi’s brother further stated that the identity of the alleged abductors, the means used to remove the abductee from the premises, the vehicles, if any, involved in the incident, and the subsequent route taken by the alleged abductors were matters requiring immediate investigation. The emergency follows heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the PTI-led KP government. The Centre and opposition have been at odds over various issues, particularly the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons cited by both parties behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . The governor’s rule also coincided with the PTI’s long march to Islamabad, which was being led by Afridi and remained limited to KP. While the party has vowed to continue with its planned protest, the provincial police have been directed to thwart any such move.

Govt says people of KP ‘welcomed’ governor's rule as it gave them ‘hope’. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Tuesday claimed that the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had “welcomed” the federal government’s move to impose governor’s rule and emergency in the province, saying the measures had given them “hope”. The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency in 12 districts of KP, and placed the province under governor’s rule, taking note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. On Tuesday, Attaullah addressed a joint press conference alongside Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar in Islamabad. Attaullah noted, “Had the people of KP supported the pro-terrorist stance of the PTI government, you would have seen millions on the street.” He went on to claim that “barely a dozen” people had gathered in protest. Defending the move, the information minister said: “The people of KP have welcomed the step because they believe there is now hope for them. They believe they will now be provided with safety and security, their lives and livelihoods will be protected, and this political-crime nexus will be eliminated.” At the outset of the press briefing, the law minister noted that the province in the recent past had witnessed a hike in terrorist incidents, noting a “195 per cent” rise, with 8,600 terrorist attacks recorded in 2024-2026 compared to 2,900 in 2020-2024. Azam emphasised that it was essential that counterterrorism efforts taken by federal and provincial agencies be “harmonised”, adding that such an approach was standard practice globally. “All these arrangements are made to run the country in a way that people feel safe,” he remarked. At this, the law minister noted the “non-serious” attitude of the previous PTI-led KP government, which he said, “has now ceased to exist”. He recalled that the PTI, allegedly using government resources, “launched an onslaught on the capital”. However, at the time, the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency did not come under discussion. Describing the situation on the ground in the province, the law minister said: “The KP police were under attack, armed forces deployed in the province were under attack […] innocent people lost their lives.” “You cannot shut your eyes after receiving such reports and seeing this rise in terrorist activity,” Azam added. Recalling the events leading up to the federal government’s decision, Azam said the government had held “constant engagement” with the provincial authorities. “Unfortunately, their response was somewhat different. Maybe their politics were more important to them than having the national interest at heart,” he said. He maintained that the federal government had exhausted “all possible avenues” to resolve the differences. Azam said the provincial government should have intervened amid “internal disturbances or the likelihood or apprehension of such disturbances”. Referring to Article 232, under which the emergency was imposed, Azam said it “deals with internal disturbances where the law and order situation is such, and the onslaught is of a nature that the provincial government cannot fight against it”. Referring to the PTI, he said, “Your priorities were not to curb terrorism or to fight against it”. “In such grave conditions, your priority should be to protect the people, not to pursue political gains.” Azam said it was against this backdrop that the prime minister brought the matter before the federal cabinet, and a decision was subsequently made. On being asked why similar measures could not be enacted in Balochistan, despite the prevailing security situation in the province, Azam said: “Look at the conduct of the Balochistan government; the chief minister is on his toes [..] he is trying hard.” He noted that whenever there is a terrorist incident in Balochistan, the CM visits the area himself and personally oversees relief efforts. ‘Total breakdown of governance’ Attaullah, during the presser, reiterated that the federal government did not have a political agenda against the PTI-led provincial government; instead, it was pursuing “a unified policy on counterterrorism”. “You cannot have a government in the country that sympathises with terrorists, supports terrorism or has a policy that enables terrorists to carry out their operational actions,” he said. He questioned how one country could have two separate counterterrorism policies. “As the [law] minister explained, the framers of the constitution included these clauses (232 and 234) for a time like this,” citing a “complete breakdown” of law and order in KP. The minister went on to question why resources allocated to the provincial government via the National Finance Commission Award were not utilised to strengthen security-related infrastructure and equip KP police. The information minister reiterated that the PTI-led government was facilitating the terrorists, describing it as a “political-terrorist nexus”. He further said there was a “total breakdown of governance” in KP, noting a lack of reforms in education, health, and public services. Vawda touts ‘reboot’ Separately, Independent Senator Faisal Vawda reappeared on television following the recent political developments and touted the governor’s rule as the beginning of a “reboot” of the country’s governance. Addressing a press conference at the National Press Club in Islamabad, the former PTI member described the new set-up in KP as a “good cabinet”, but also stressed that it must show its performance before its 180-day tenure. “It will be performance-based; if they are not able to perform, better ones will come,” Vawda said. “Failure is no option,” he emphasised, saying the governor-run administration will face even stricter scrutiny. Vawda remarked, “Through this province, God willing, in the story of Pakistan … we are looking into the option of reboot, not that boot but the mobile one.” Responding to a query about his “reboot” metaphor, the senator said such a format usually entails “deletion, subtraction and addition” of individuals. Referring to the eight PTI leaders in preventative detention, he said, “Eight men were with me in the last 48 hours, including their cabinet members.” However, he claimed, “All of them are involved in the arrests; all of them staged a drama.” Addressing PTI leaders, he said, “Some of them will be left, some of them will be picked up, some will be washed away. The party is already scattered; it’s all over. The show is over.” Later in his media talk, Vawda declared: “PTI, as of now, does not exist anymore; neither will.” Vawda also rejected allegations against Maulana Fazlur Rehman — who made efforts to reduce tensions between the Centre and PTI — that he “trapped” Sohail Afridi by inviting him to talks at CM House. Asked about his thoughts on ex-premier Imran Khan’s future, the former PTI leader said the former taught him politics. “It is the same politics that I am doing today,” he added. Emergency over terrorism concerns On Sunday, the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and governor’s rule under Article 234. The decision came during a meeting of the federal cabinet, which deliberated on the security situation in PTI-led KP and noted the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Subsequently, the prime minister sent a summary to the president, who approved the move. Soon after, the Centre also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. Meanwhile, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre sought to explain that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. On Monday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar defended the governor’s rule, saying it was not politically motivated but instead taken to curb terrorism. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

Army conducts successful test launch of hypersonic Fatah-2 extended range missile: ISPR. The Pakistan Army successfully test-launched the Fatah-2 extended range (ER) hypersonic ballistic missile, the military’s media wing said in a statement on Tuesday. According to Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the Fatah-2 ER is equipped with advanced navigation and state-of-the-art avionics. “It is capable of engaging targets with high precision and defeating [the] enemy’s missile defence systems due to its unique trajectory and manoeuvrability features,” it added. “Fatah-2 ER, with its extended range, will further enhance [the] army’s reach and capability of engaging deep targets.” The test launch was witnessed by Army Rocket Force Command (ARFC) chief Lt Gen Nauman Zakaria, senior army officers, scientists and engineers. The ARFC commander “appreciated the dedication and technical prowess of scientists and engineers”, ISPR said. It further said the president, prime minister, and the chief of defence forces congratulated the scientists and engineers on the successful test launch of the “extended range version of Fatah-2 weapon system”. Last week, the indigenously developed extended version of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile also underwent a successful test launch . In a statement, ISPR said, “Equipped with advanced avionics and state-of-the-art navigational aids, the weapon system is capable of engaging targets at extended ranges with high precision and lethality.” “The test also validated additional technical parameters of various sub-systems incorporated for improved accuracy and enhanced survivability,” it added.

Nasa's Perseverance rover breaks record for off-planet driving on Mars. Nasa’s robotic Perseverance rover has now driven farther than any other vehicle on the surface of any world other than Earth, racking up 45.2 kilometres since arriving on Mars in 2021, the US space agency said on Tuesday. The car-sized, six-wheeled rover reached the milestone 5-1/2 years into its mission to explore if conditions conducive to microbial life ever existed on Earth’s neighbour. In doing so, it is visiting some of the most ancient terrain ever encountered in the solar system. “Perseverance’s engineering hardware and instruments are in excellent shape with all redundant systems still available,” Steven Lee of Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, told Reuters . “A recent assessment of all systems concluded that they are capable of operating well into the 2030s, likely beyond,” added Lee, the project manager for Nasa’s two Mars rovers, Perseverance and Curiosity . Perseverance has exceeded the previous figure of 45km driven on the Martian surface by Nasa’s Opportunity rover from 2004 to 2018. Both also exceeded the driving distances of any lunar rover. Traversing Jezero Crater Perseverance, with its suite of scientific instruments, has focused on the Jezero Crater, a region in the northern hemisphere of Mars believed to have been flooded with water and home to a lake basin billions of years ago. The rover set the milestone in a journey toward an area called Idubi, through the region off the crater’s western rim nicknamed Lac de Charmes. View this post on Instagram Its companion rover, Curiosity, rolls along in the Gale Crater near the Martian equator. Perseverance is showing no signs of slowing down, Lee added. Its mobility system mechanisms are being tested to show it can drive 100 km or more, he said, with the hardware to be tested to the equivalent of 150km to 300km in the effort. Nasa attributed a major role in Perseverance’s success to its self-driving capability, an autonomous navigation system called AutoNav. Lee said 90 per cent of its drives are done autonomously, with no human intervention. “Perseverance takes stereo images of the terrain ahead, generates a 3D software map, and selects the safest path towards a drive goal,” he said. Another key component is the Vision Compute Element, a fast co-processor computer that allows the rover to process images and run its self-driving software very quickly, almost continuously during drives, Lee added. That contrasts with previous rovers, which needed to pause to “think” before each drive segment, he said. “Perseverance builds on the 29-year legacy of our past Mars rovers — Sojourner , Spirit , Opportunity and Curiosity — each incorporating prior lessons and improving our ability to drive on another world,” Lee said. Potential biosignature Lee said the rover’s biggest achievement was almost certainly its discovery, unveiled last year, of a potential biosignature , or possible sign of ancient microbial life. This was found in reddish rock believed to have formed 3.2 billion to 3.8bn years ago in a river channel feeding the lake that once filled Jezero Crater. The Lac de Charmes terrain, Lee said, may yield clues to early planetary geological processes, such as the effects of large meteorite impacts. Jezero Crater was formed by such an impact early in Martian history. Lee cited orbital evidence that some areas of the rim were once hydrothermal systems with warm or hot groundwater. “These areas may once have provided a warm, watery subsurface environment conducive to life,” he added. “Indeed, some palaeontologists hypothesise that life on Earth began in such environments.” The rover’s original mission envisaged just 20km of driving. Nasa recently approved an extension of its mission to explore the crater rim until roughly the end of 2028. The rover’s plutonium-based power system is performing as expected, Lee said, adding it has “many years of useful energy still available”.

Violence in response to a woman's refusal to marry 'profound shame' on society's conscience: Supreme Court. ISLAMABAD: Criticising patriarchal customs and gender-based violence, the Supreme Court (SC) on Tuesday said it was a profound shame on the conscience of any civilised society when a man, having failed to win a woman’s affection, answered her refusal with violence rather than acceptance. “The sole reason he takes her life is to appease his wounded ego, as he was unable to secure her hand and marry her,” regretted Justice Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar in a nine-page judgment he authored. The observation was made by a three-member bench, which also included Justices Salahuddin Panhwar and Ishtiaq Ibrahim. In its judgment, the bench rejected a criminal review petition by Muhammad Kamran, who sought the commutation of his death sentence to life imprisonment. Kamran, who has already served around 15 years of his sentence in the death cell, was convicted for murdering a woman after she and her family rejected his marriage proposal. Dismissing his review plea, the court ruled that a condemned prisoner could not claim, as a matter of right, that him having served 14 or 15 years of his sentence placed him in the same position as a person sentenced to life imprisonment. “The latter entered prison under a sentence of life imprisonment; the former entered it under a sentence of death. The distinction does not lie in the number of years already spent in prison, but in the sentence which the court actually imposed,” the judgment emphasised. Woman’s consent considered irrelevant, regrets SC The court further observed: “Marriage is a mutual, voluntary covenant that necessitates free consent of both parties. But in a variety of patriarchal systems, it is accepted that men have the exclusive right to select, demand and enforce possession over a woman, irrespective of her wishes.” The judgment stated that a woman “challenges the suitor’s perceived ownership when she exercises her fundamental right to say ‘no’”. “Under a patriarchal mindset, this rejection is taken by that man as a blow to his ‘honour’ ( ghairat ), which results in stalking, home invasion, acid violence or femicide,” the judgment added. The judgment also referred to several customs, such as that of ghag , to illustrate the manifestation of this mindset. Ghag (proclamation in Pashto) is an archaic customary practice where a man unilaterally claims a woman as his bride without her or her guardians’ consent. The court observed that historically, ghag was executed by firing gunshots outside the woman’s residence or making a public declaration. “ Ghag acts as an informal seal or taboo intimidating other perspective suitors away, holding a woman’s marital status hostage as if she is a territory, which is now marked by this man,” the judgment said, adding if the woman or her family resisted, the suitor would frequently employ violence to enforce his claim. As a result, a woman may remain unmarried for years, or even decades, solely due to a declaration that was never followed by a legal or religious ceremony, engagement, or marriage, the court said. It added that the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Elimination of Custom of Ghag Act, 2013, had already declared the custom a cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable criminal offence. The judgment then referred to the customs of suara , also known as vani or badal-e-sulh , which it said operated differently from ghag , despite the fact that both portrayed situations where the decision to marry a woman was made by others for a purpose that was not in accordance with her own desires nor benefit. Suara involves a girl or young woman from a family that has committed an offence, such as homicide, given in marriage to a man from the victim’s family as a form of compensation through decision made by a jirga , and serves as a substitute for a criminal proceeding or financial compensation, the court observed. The practice was criminalised through Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2004 and further solidified by Prevention of Anti-Women Practices Act, 2011, it noted. Similarly, there was the custom of watta-satta — another example where the setting of marriage was at the cost of the bride’s well being, the judgment said. Watta-satta , which translates to “give-take”, is a “reciprocal marriage that is prevalent in our country involving a brother and sister from one family marrying a sister and brother from another family”, the judgment said. “The common thread that unites all of these customs is that in this male-dominated society having patriarchal customs and traditions, a woman’s assent to her own marriage is considered irrelevant,” the court regretted. It further stated that it is impossible to reconcile this mindset with Islam, which required woman’s free assent as a prerequisite for a valid nikah . Any adult person, either a man or a woman, was equally entitled to decide whether, when and with whom they would marry, the judgment said. That entitlement, the judgment said, was not a concession that her family, tribe or society, as a whole, had granted to her, the judgment emphasised, adding that a woman possessed this privilege in her own right. “There is no excuse for such behaviour, regardless of whether it is committed in the name of honour, custom, injured pride, or emotions.” The judgment further highlighted that Pakistan was party to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW). Its Article 16 obliged states to ensure that a woman had the same right to freely choose a spouse and to enter into a marriage only with her free and full consent, the court noted. “A domestic custom or such prevalent mindset that nullifies this choice by force cannot be permitted to survive under the guise of local practice,” the judgment said. In the case at hand, the petitioner, who murdered a woman in cold blood, seemed to have “suffered from the mindset which led to beliefs that a woman is a commodity and it was the right of the suitor to have her, with no possibility of refusal because commodities cannot express”, the court held. The court further said that the attempt to present a woman’s lawful refusal as “provocation” or as a mitigating circumstance was a very “absurd ground” for the plea at hand because no individual had the right to deprive another of their life just because of refusing a marriage proposal. Accepting such an argument would constitute judicial endorsement of the notion that a woman’s will was subordinate to a man’s preference, the court declared. The court held that the petitioner had failed to point out any error to justify the SC’s review jurisdiction under Article 188 of the Constitution. “The submissions advanced are, in substance, a request to rearrange and reweigh matters, which this court, sitting in review, cannot undertake,” it said.

Pakistan make four changes for third T20I as Sri Lanka win toss, elect to bowl first. Pakistan made four changes to their line-up for the third and final Twenty20 International against Sri Lanka, who won the toss and decided to bat first at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Tuesday. Razaullah, who made his debut in the first T20I was brought back to the XI while spinner Sufyan Moqim, all-rounder Arafat Minhas and batter Abdul Samad were also handed playing time. Seniors Shadab Khan, Saim Ayub, Naseem Shah and Abrar Ahmed were benched. For Sri Lanka, spinner Maheesh Theekshana — who had an outing to forget in the second T20I — was replaced by younsgter Vijayakanth Viyaskanth. The hosts are looking to complete a clean sweep of the three-match series. After winning the opening T20I by four wickets and securing a convincing 82-run victory in the second match, Pakistan have established a commanding position heading into the series finale. The second T20I saw Pakistan deliver an impressive all-round performance with both bat and ball. Young opener Maaz Sadaqat played a crucial role with a brilliant 96 off 51 deliveries, while captain Sahibzada Farhan contributed 73 runs to help Pakistan post a formidable total of 215 for three. The bowlers then maintained control of the contest, restricting Sri Lanka to 133 for seven to seal a comprehensive victory. For Sri Lanka, the third T20I presents an opportunity to bounce back and finish the tour on a positive note. Captain Kusal Mendis and his teammates will be eager to address their shortcomings, particularly with the bat, after struggling to keep pace with Pakistan’s aggressive approach in the previous encounter. Pakistan, meanwhile, will aim to maintain their momentum and use the final fixture to further strengthen their combinations. The performances of the top-order batters, the effectiveness of the bowling attack and the contributions of the all-rounders could once again prove decisive. With the series already secured, Pakistan will enter the contest with confidence, while Sri Lanka will be determined to avoid a whitewash. PM Shehbaz, EU official discuss Pakistan's efforts to curb migrant smuggling. ISLAMABAD: European Union Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday to discuss strengthening Pakistan-EU cooperation in migration and mobility, one of the eight pillars of the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan 2019. Welcoming Commissioner Brunner on his first visit to Pakistan, the prime minister underscored the importance Pakistan attaches to its partnership with the EU, according to a press release by the PM Office. The premier highlighted Pakistan’s sustained efforts to curb irregular migration and combat migrant smuggling and human trafficking through legislative reforms, institutional strengthening, effective enforcement and international cooperation. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening cooperation across all pillars of the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan. PM Shehbaz emphasised that efforts to address irregular migration should be complemented by practical opportunities for safe, orderly and regular migration. He noted that expanding legal pathways for Pakistani skilled workers and professionals would help meet the labour market needs of European countries while reducing prospective migrants’ vulnerability to smuggling networks. Brunner appreciated the measures taken and cooperation extended by the government of Pakistan, PMO said. He expressed confidence that these efforts would contribute to expanding legal migration pathways and promoting mutually beneficial labour mobility between Pakistan and the European Union. Naqvi, EU commissioner discuss border security Separately, Brunner also met with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi in Islamabad, where they discussed enhancing cooperation in border security, legal migration and border management. The meeting was followed by delegation-level talks. Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s measures against illegal migration, describing the 64 per cent reduction in illegal migration to Europe resulting from the country’s efforts as commendable. He said the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) had demonstrated professional competence despite limited resources, which was commendable. He added that the decline in illegal migration would pave the way for legal migration. Naqvi said Pakistan had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards illegal migration. “After a 64 per cent reduction in illegal migration, our next target is its complete elimination,” the interior minister said, describing illegal migration as a serious global issue. The two sides also discussed the promotion of legal migration and enhancing opportunities for skilled workforce between Pakistan and the European Union. Both sides agreed to further strengthen cooperation in immigration, institutional coordination and border management, and to work together on the EU’s Eastern Corridor Initiative to eliminate illegal migration. They also discussed increasing mutual cooperation to enhance the capacity of Pakistan Coast Guards and agreed to increase collaboration to promote border security and legal migration. Brunner assured Pakistan of all possible cooperation in this regard. The meeting was attended by the interior secretary, special and additional interior secretaries, FIA director general, Federal Constabulary inspector general, NCCIA director general, passports director general, Islamabad chief commissioner and other officials. Last month, Naqvi said Pakistan had recorded a 64pc reduction in illegal migration to Europe, describing the achievement as challenging despite limited resources. He said Pakistan’s next target was to eliminate illegal migration completely, stressing the need to expand legal migration opportunities, adopt modern technology and strengthen institutional capacity. In February, Pakistan and three European countries — Italy, Spain and Greece — reached a consensus on promoting legal pathways to “effectively combat illegal migration”. The three countries endorsed Naqvi’s proposal to establish legal pathways as a strategy to combat illegal migration and human smuggling during a conference.

'We're not giving up': Activist Thunberg joins France student protests. Thousands of protesters marched through central Paris on Tuesday as part of nationwide demonstrations supporting high school pupils who have been protesting for better classroom conditions, with Swedish activist Greta Thunberg taking part. With just six months to go before elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron, French authorities had been hoping that the protests were easing ahead of half-term holidays starting at the end of this week. But teenagers at high schools called lycees — backed by university students, teachers, unions and the far-left opposition party France Unbowed (LFI) — have said their demands have not been met. French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon was seen among the crowd of demonstrators in Paris. Outside the Paris city hall, demonstrators — mostly university students — gathered in the early afternoon to the tune of an orchestra playing the The Rebel Fanfare from the Star Wars movies. “I’m expecting a surge of solidarity,” said 20-year-old Patricia, not wishing to give her surname. “We’re not giving up the fight, whether it’s for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence,” she added, referencing multiple allegations of police brutality against protesters in recent weeks. The education ministry said 214 schools were closed on Tuesday. Most of these were high schools out of the country’s 3,700. University student union l’Union Etudiante reported that 90 per cent of universities had closed nationwide to show support. Thunberg, who became famous as a teen for school strikes to demand action on climate change, stood among pupils demonstrating outside a school in the capital’s largest suburb, Saint-Denis. “Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us,” the 23-year-old told reporters outside the Paul Eluard high school. ‘Country without a future’ French students say they are determined to press their demands for solutions to too many absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded class schedules and other grievances. The protests, launched late last month, have seen teenagers pile up dumpsters and security barriers outside hundreds of lycees. Rallies were also underway in other cities on Tuesday. In the western city of Nantes, thousands marched behind a banner reading “Schools without money, a country without a future”. “I think there are a lot of us in France who are still motivated,” 16-year-old Mariolino said. “Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don’t get it.” In the northeastern city of Strasbourg, Adeline Ferier, 42, a middle school French teacher, said she was demonstrating to support her 16-year-old daughter. “I think it’s great that young people are aware of inequalities and are getting involved,” she said. More than 70,000 people took to the streets last Thursday in the last major event of the movement. Protesters hold placards and banners during a demonstration of high-school students in Lyon, southeastern France on October 13, 2026, as part of a nationwide high school mobilisation. — AFP ‘Issues that deserve time’ The demonstrations in recent weeks have mostly been peaceful, but clashes have occasionally broken out with police. More than 6,800 people — largely minors — have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests, according to the justice ministry. Police have opened internal investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators. Some 147 teaching staff members have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said. Authorities said fireworks fired through tubes on Monday injured two school workers in Reims, one school worker in a Paris suburb and a police officer outside a school in Marseille. Tuesday’s demonstrations supporting the students were to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living . Macron, speaking to reporters at a car show on Monday, urged restraint from protesters. “These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect,” Macron said just months before elections to replace him. This photograph shows a banner which reads as ’Macron, You break scholl! — AFP After last week’s nationwide demonstrations, the government promised that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools. The education minister said on Tuesday that 35pc had already been assigned. High school students are demanding a 10 billion-euro ($11 billion) boost for lycees.

PTI seeks production orders for 'detained' MNAs ahead of NA, Senate sessions. ISLAMABAD: The PTI requested the National Assembly speaker to issue production orders for its nine “detained” MNAs ahead of NA and Senate sessions on Tuesday. In a letter to NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq, Chief Whip Amir Dogar claimed that the nine MNAs were “currently detained” and requested him to issue production orders for them to enable them to attend the 30th session starting today. The lawmakers comprised Haji Imtiaz Ahmad Choudhry (ΝΑ-68), Muhammad Jamal Ahsan Khan (NA-89), Mian Ghous Muhammad (ΝΑ-170), Sanaullah Khan Mastikhel (NΑ-91), Dawar Khan Kundi (NA-43), Junaid Akbar (NA-09), Amjad Ali Khan (NA-02), Fazal Muhammad Khan (ΝΑ-25) and Adil Khan Bazai (NA-262). “As the speaker of the National Assembly of Pakistan, the impartiality of your esteemed office requires that production orders be issued for all detained members, irrespective of their political affiliation, to ensure that no constituency remains unrepresented during the proceedings of the House,” the letter read. It requested Sadiq to issue the production orders under Rule 108 of the 2007 Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the National Assembly. President Asif Ali Zardari had summoned the sessions after he and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif agreed on it during their weekend meeting on the country’s political and security situation. The sessions also follow the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and emergency in 12 of its districts, for which the Centre cited the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. President Zardari had approved the measures under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, which pertain to the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule, respectively. According to Article 232, in case the president “acts on his own” — which was not the case for KP as he acted on PM Shehbaz’s advice — the proclamation of emergency is to be placed before both houses of Parliament for approval by each house within 10 days. It also empowers Parliament “to make laws for a province, or any part thereof, with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Federal Legislative List” during emergency. In the upper house, Senator Kamran Murtaza of the Jamiat Ulemai-i-Islam–Fazl (JUI-F) had submitted a resolution on Monday opposing the imposition of governor’s rule in KP. More to follow

5 killed, several injured as Peshawar-bound train derails in Punjab's Multan district. LAHORE: Five people were killed and several others were injured when the Peshawar-bound Rehman Baba Express derailed near Sher Shah Railway Station in Multan district on Tuesday, officials said. Pakistan Railways (PR) Chief Executive Officer Muhammad Hafeezullah confirmed the death toll to Dawn , adding that more than 40 had been injured. According to an initial investigation report by the PR, the derailment was likely caused by a fault in a passenger coach. Minister for Railways Hanif Abbasi has appointed the federal government inspector of railways (FGIR) as the inquiry officer. “We have appointed the FGIR to probe the incident,” Abbasi told Dawn . Passengers sit with their belongings next to derailed coaches of the passenger train Rehman Baba Express on the outskirts of Multan on October 13, 2026. — AFP Speaking to Dawn , train driver Rizwan Abbas said the train was travelling at 100 kilometres per hour. “The signal was clear, and as I was passing through the Sher Shah station area, I suddenly felt a push,” he said. He said he applied the brakes and managed to bring the train to a stop. “When I got out of the locomotive and looked back, I saw that the passenger coaches had derailed and were lying off the tracks. It was horrible,” he said. Abbas maintained that the train was in working order. In an earlier statement, the railways minister expressed grief over the loss of life, saying he shared the sorrow of the bereaved families, according to an official statement. He directed the authorities to ensure the provision of the best possible medical facilities to the injured passengers and said compensation would be paid to the deceased and injured in accordance with the Pakistan Railways insurance policy, as per the statement. Meanwhile, a replacement train for the Rehman Baba Express, carrying more than 500 passengers, departed from Sher Shah Railway Station, according to a statement. Buses were also arranged in coordination with the Multan district administration for passengers wishing to continue their journeys by road. The statement added that all field formations of the Commercial Department were on high alert to facilitate passengers. Multan Commissioner Amir Karim Khan also met the affected passengers and their families and assured them of all possible assistance. Rescue workers search for the victims following the derailment of passenger train Rehman Baba Express on the outskirts of Multan on October 13, 2026. — AFP For its part, the PR set up round-the-clock information and help desks at all major stations to guide and assist passengers following the accident. Divisional commercial officers (DCOs) were also directed to arrange alternative travel options and ensure ticket refunds wherever necessary. Ministry working to resolve issues Speaking to the media later, the railways minister acknowledged that it was his responsibility to ensure safe journeys for passengers. “Before this, no one even tried to focus on the mechanical condition of trains,” he said. “Even today, there are five or six trains, such as the Karakoram Express, Millat Express and Awam Express, that you cannot even look at because they seem ancient.” He described freight wagons as “dummies” because, he said, they did not have brakes. Abbasi added that his ministry was working to address problems with locomotives, coaches and wagons, setting Dec 31 as the deadline for the work to be completed. “All of this work will be completed by Dec 31,” Abbasi said. Asked whether he would resign, the minister said: “Have some patience. We need to investigate the incident first, and those responsible will be held accountable. In fact, I was just on a call with the prime minister. We are trying to prevent such incidents and making efforts to that end. Giving up and running away is not in our nature.” Abbasi expressed sorrow over the loss of lives, saying there could be no substitute for those who had died and that the incident should not have happened. President, PM express condolences President Asif Ali Zardari, in a statement on X, expressed concern over the incident, extending “heartfelt condolences and sympathy” to the bereaved families. He also expressed best wishes for the injured passengers’ early recovery. “The President directs relevant authorities to ensure assistance to the affected passengers and provision of all possible facilities. Transparent investigations should be conducted to determine the causes of the accident,” Zardari said. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the deaths caused by the derailment. The premier took notice of the incident and instructed the relevant authorities to expedite rescue and relief operations, according to state-run Associated Press of Pakistan . He also called for providing immediate and the best possible medical facilities to the injured. “PM Shehbaz prayed for peace for the departed souls and strength for the bereaved families to bear the loss, besides sympathising with the affected families,” APP reported. Lack of maintenance There have been a series of train derailment incidents over the past year, raising concerns over possible negligence and deep-rooted issues of Pakistan Railways (PR) over maintenance of trains and tracks across the country. On October 1, two passenger trains, Shalimar Express and Pakistan Express, narrowly escaped major accidents after derailing, while a third minor accident also occurred on Jaffar Express on the track near Gujar Khan. At the time, PR Chief Executive Officer Hafeezullah said the accidents happened due to a lack of maintenance in the last five years, while claiming that a series of maintenance measures had been undertaken. In August, the Yousafwala coal train derailed near Firoza Railway Station (between Khanpur and Liaqatpur) after it ran into the sand hump on the loopline, apparently due to weak brakes or the driver not applying the brakes in time. The same day, a passenger train (Rawal Express) derailed near Kala Gujran in Jhelum district on the Main Line-1 (Lahore-Rawalpindi track), disrupting railway operations. On Aug 4, the Havailian-bound Hazara Express also met with an accident when its driver reportedly overshot and hit the sand hump, causing loss of rolling stock and other infrastructure. Similarly, Aug 5 saw another derailment as the Bulleh Shah Passenger train derailed. On July 28, the Lahore-bound Tezgam derailed between Hyderabad-Kotri sections while on the same day, Thal Express’s engine broke down near Muzaffargarh. On July 5, the Karachi-bound Shalimar Express had derailed near Khanewal. A Bulleh Shah passenger coach derailed in Lahore on July 20, while July 22 saw another major derailment when Hazara Express’ four passenger coaches derailed near the Karachi Cantt Railway station.

Patrick T. Fallon / AFP Commentary / United States 01 October 2026 20+ minutes Five Energy Market Factors That Could Tip the Scales in the Middle East War Oil, gas and fuel prices are central to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, with Washington striving to lower them and Tehran to keep them high. With both sides determined to prevail, five market-shaping developments in particular could affect whether fighting ramps up or de-escalates. Share BlueSky E-mail Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Salva Stampa Related Tags Global Order and Peacemaking United States Iran Israel/Palestine As Iran and the United States trade blows in the Gulf, they are both trying to sway at least one shared audience: global energy markets. The public and private companies that produce, refine, move and consume oil and gas around the world are listening rapt to what the belligerents say and watching every move they make in an attempt to understand where the war is headed. These commodities have many prices: for instance, what a barrel of crude oil is fetching today; how much customers are paying for derivative products like diesel or jet fuel in major markets like East Asia, the European Union or the U.S.; and what future delivery of such items is projected to cost. Together, these actual and estimated prices serve as a rough indicator of what the market thinks about the conflict’s likely trajectory. In turn, the price fluctuations are monitored in both Tehran and Washington, which factor them into strategy. U.S. President Donald Trump is plainly keeping one eye on the markets at all times. In June, when he signed a now defunct memorandum of understanding meant to end the war, he noted a market motivation, saying, “We run out of [oil] reserves at about four weeks”. On 13 August, with November’s midterm elections getting closer, Vice President JD Vance cited low fuel prices as Washington’s main war aim, saying “That’s goal number one – keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country”. Preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – Washington’s ostensible motive for launching its airstrikes in February – was apparently, at least for a time, goal number two. Iran, for its part, is trying to maintain the clout it obtained by asserting control of the Strait of Hormuz, for which it is willing to pay a big price. The Iranian economy is being hammered by intensifying sanctions and a resumed U.S. naval blockade that has halted exports from Iran’s southern coast. Washington has repeatedly hailed the impending death of Iran’s oil industry, due to lack of export and storage capacity. While these predictions were overblown, Iran is still reeling economically. As both the U.S. and Iran pin their hopes on being able to manage prices, the energy markets have proven unpredictable. Despite disruptions, the markets have displayed unexpected resilience, helping dilute the conflict’s economic consequences. Apocalyptic prophecies that oil would reach $200 a barrel have so far been incorrect. Instead, the price of the global benchmark, Brent crude, has risen from below $75 before the war to peaks that have not yet topped $130. These prices are high, but adjusted for inflation, they pale in comparison to previous spikes. Part of the explanation owes to buffers that have kept the markets from careening out of control. It helps that the world had an oil surplus when the war began, the U.S. had a few hundred million more barrels in its federal stores, Russia had more functional refineries and export terminals, China was building up rather than depleting its reserves and the Red Sea was largely open to tanker traffic. Since the war began, higher prices have pushed demand lower and raised production in some countries while new workarounds – in part orchestrated by the U.S. and Gulf states like the United Arab Emirates – and growing risk tolerance are sending a significant amount of oil through Hormuz despite Iran’s attacks. [T]he question remains whether the U.S. or Iran will outlast the other in what has become an endurance test. Still, the question remains whether the U.S. or Iran will outlast the other in what has become an endurance test. The feared tipping point at which a shortfall in oil supply causes a rapid price increase until demand falls has seemingly been forestalled by greater crude flow through Hormuz. But surging diesel and other fuel prices may now matter more than crude oil alone. U.S. retail diesel prices are soaring to record highs, generating support for a 90-day U.S. diesel export ban and even a measure of dissent from the war among members of Trump’s Republican Party (in many other parts of the world, rising fuel prices are already stoking significant public anger). Iran is cognisant of the correlation between fuel prices and the Republicans’ political fortunes; with the November midterm elections approaching and major Republican losses a significant possibility , Iran may think that such a result would produce new constraints on Trump’s war-making, in the form of more vigorous oversight from a Congress controlled by opposition Democrats. For this reason, many Iran watchers believe Tehran, along with its allies, will seek to prevent the U.S. from stabilising prices, even if it involves a mutually hurting re-escalation of the conflict. Indeed, in September, the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels advanced in Yemen, positioning themselves to more effectively threaten shipping in the Red Sea, a major energy corridor. But while Iran looks for ways to keep oil and gas bottled up in the Middle East, Washington and its partners continue to work on means of getting these items out, with the outflow of crude through the Strait of Hormuz reportedly hitting its pre-war baseline by the end of September, though refined products like fuel lagged far behind. Efforts are under way to keep raising this Hormuz outflow, and land routes add a few million more barrels. The U.S. conundrum now is that crude needs to reach refineries, and the resulting products to hit global markets, for the world to get out of its growing fuel crisis. As the U.S. increasingly looks to others to help manage the fallout of its war with Iran, it is also pursuing a number of costly mitigation measures, whose sustainability is questionable. This Crisis Group analysis examines the relationship between global energy markets and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. It looks at the cushions that have helped absorb war-related shocks to oil markets so far and the extent to which they are under pressure. It identifies five particular factors that could contribute to re-escalation or de-escalation of the conflict. U.S. concerns began with crude oil, but diesel may be the Trump administration’s undoing. Only Beijing knows how quickly and by how much China’s oil imports and fuel exports will recover.
