B. Border Tensions With maritime tensions simmering, friction increased along the land border. On 13 February 2025, a group of Cambodians visited the disputed Ta Muan Thom/Tamone Thom temple, reportedly escorted by Cambodian soldiers, and sang a patriotic song. Thai soldiers objected to the implicit assertion of sovereignty, which contradicted the “gentlemen’s agreement” governing the area since 2011, and asked the group to leave. 43 The arrangement permitted villagers from both nations to visit the temple but prohibited political or nationalist demonstrations. William J. Jones, “Cambodia undermines ASEAN centrality in 2025 border conflict”, Geopolitical Monitor , 29 January 2026. Video of the incident went viral. 44 “Thai-Cambodian tensions over anthem at temple”, Bangkok Post , 17 February 2025. Two weeks later, on 1 March, a pavilion in the Cambodia-Laos-Thailand tri-border area, built to commemorate neighbourly relations among the three countries, burned down. 45 “Thailand and Cambodia to discuss pavilion fire”, Bangkok Post , 6 March 2025. While the Thai military officially called it an accident, rumours circulated that Cambodian troops had set off the blaze. 46 Crisis Group interview, retired senior Thai military officer, Bangkok, June 2026. See also “Thailand and Cambodia to discuss pavilion fire”, op. cit. The situation escalated on 28 May, when Thai and Cambodian troops exchanged fire in a disputed area between Chong Bok in Thailand’s Ubon Ratchathani province and Cambodia’s Preah Vihear province, killing a Cambodian soldier; both sides claimed the other shot first. 47 “One killed after Thai and Cambodian soldiers briefly clash in a disputed border area”, Associated Press, 28 May 2025. A week earlier, Thailand had alleged that Cambodian troops had been digging trenches and building fortifications in disputed territory in the area but had agreed to withdraw after talks between local commanders. “Thai, Cambodian troops hold talks over border patrol dispute”, The Nation , 18 May 2025. Prime Minister Paetongtarn spoke to Hun Manet the same day. “We don’t want this to escalate”, she told the media. 48 “Paetongtarn discusses with Hun Manet after Thai-Cambodian border clash”, The Nation , 29 May 2025. The countries’ army chiefs met two days later and agreed to pull back their troops. 49 “Army chiefs try to resolve Thai-Cambodian border dispute”, Bangkok Post , 30 May 2025. A welter of developments ensued in June. On 4 June, more than a week after the clash with Cambodian troops, Paetongtarn’s government released a statement affirming “unwavering commitment to safeguarding sovereignty and territorial integrity”. 50 “Statement by Thai Government on Thailand-Cambodia Border Situation”, Thai Government Public Relations Department, 4 June 2025; “Thailand, Cambodia mobilise troops, evacuate villages”, The Nation , 5 June 2025. Two days later, Thailand’s National Security Council delegated full authority to military commanders to administer all border crossings; within a day, the army halved the opening hours at Ban Khlong Luek-Poipet, the main checkpoint along the frontier. 51 “Thailand enforces border controls to safeguard communities amidst rising tensions”, The Nation , 7 June 2025; “Early border closure in Sa Kaeo strands thousands”, Bangkok Post , 7 June 2025. In mid-June, Hun Sen called on Cambodian workers in Thailand – more than 1.5 million people – to come home, while Hun Manet ordered border provinces to prepare for a wave of returnees. 52 “Hun Sen calls upon Cambodian workers to return home from Thailand, before Thai authorities expel them”, Khmer Times , 14 June 2025; “Cambodia braces for mass deportation, mobilises to welcome workers home”, Cambodianess , 14 June 2025. In 2024, Thailand recorded some 459,863 documented Cambodian workers. Estimates of the total, including undocumented persons, range between one and two million. “Cambodia CTIP and Thailand CTIP”, Winrock International, September 2024, p. 4. Satellite imagery of three Khmer Empire-era temples: Ta Moan Thom/Ta Muen Thom (top), Ta Moan Toch/Ta Muen Toch (left) Ta Krabey/Ta Khwai (right), along the Cambodia-Thailand border. Source: Google Earth / CRISIS GROUP As tensions rose, the two sides convened a meeting of the Joint Boundary Commission – the first since 2012. 53 “Press conference on the 6th meeting of the Thailand-Cambodia Joint Boundary Commission”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 15 June 2025. The JBC affirmed agreement on the position of 45 of 73 boundary markers and revised the 2003 Terms of Reference to incorporate light detection and ranging technology in aerial photographic maps. 54 Light detection and ranging is a remote sensing method that determines distance by emitting laser pulses at a target and measuring how long the reflected light takes to return to a receiver. Airborne light detection and ranging units can accurately measure and map ground elevation across large areas. Galen Scott, “Lidar: Lasers, Airplanes and Drones!”, The Earth Scientist , vol. 40, no. 3 (2023), pp. 3-4. Experts said it was a breakthrough, because these instruments can quickly produce accurate 3D terrain maps. 55 William J. Jones and Narut Chareonsri, “The Sovereignty Straitjacket: Cambodia-Thailand Relations, Withdrawal from Memorandum of Understanding 2001 and Regional Security”, Kyoto Review of Southeast Asia , no. 42 (March 2026). Nevertheless, the two sides issued contradictory statements, with Cambodia asserting that the JBC had agreed to use the 1:200,000 scale map annexed to the 1907 treaty, while Thailand’s foreign ministry denied that any such discussion had transpired. 56 “Cambodia categorically refuses to recognize the map drawn unilaterally by Thailand as a basis for border issues”, Khmer Times , 15 June 2025; “Tension lingers following Thailand-Cambodia JBC talks”, Prachatai English , 17 June 2025. On 15 June, Cambodia formally petitioned the ICJ to determine the sovereignty over four disputed sites, three of which encompass Khmer Empire-era temple ruins that nationalists on both sides have imbued with cultural and political significance. 57 The sites are Ta Moan Thom, Ta Moan Tauch, Ta Krabei temple and Mom Bei/Chong Bok. “Cambodia turns to World Court over Thailand border disputes”, Reuters, 15 June 2025. Two weeks earlier, Hun Manet raised the possibility of Cambodia and Thailand seeking a joint ICJ referral, but Bangkok rejected it, having withdrawn recognition of the court’s compulsory jurisdiction in 1960. “Hun Manet calls for urgent border talks with Thailand, proposes ICJ resolution for disputed areas”, Khmer Times , 2 June 2025; “Thailand urges positive engagement after Cambodia threatens to take dispute to World Court”, Reuters, 5 June 2025. The move antagonised Bangkok, which has long maintained that the dispute should be settled bilaterally. 58 “Thailand’s position in response to Cambodia’s submission on 15 June 2025 of a letter to the International Court of Justice related to the Emerald Triangle (Mom Bei), Ta Moan Thom, Ta Moan Tauch and Ta Krabei temples”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 16 June 2025. C. The Fateful Telephone Call On 15 June, Prime Minister Paetongtarn had a telephone conversation with Hun Sen, a nine-minute recorded excerpt of which was made public three days later. 59 Hun Sen acknowledged that he had recorded the call and shared it with some 80 party officials, suggesting that one of them leaked the audio. He later released the full seventeen minutes on his Facebook page. “Hun Sen admits to recording phone call with Thai PM and sharing with 80 officials”, The Nation , 18 June 2025; “Cambodian-Thai tensions escalate on diplomatic and economic fronts”, Khmer Times , 23 June 2025. It revealed that, in her efforts to de-escalate, she was deferential to Hun Sen, addressing him as “uncle” and seeking his understanding regarding the precarious political situation the border dispute had created for her government. Most damagingly, she described the 2nd Army Area commander, Lieutenant General Boonsin Padklang, who was in charge of the areas where clashes had occurred, as belonging to “the opposite side”, a reference to the Thaksin/conservative divide. For his part, Hun Sen asked her to prevail on the Thai military to reopen the border. 60 Nattan Casey Plewissara, “The leaked call shaking Thai politics: Translated”, The Asia Cable (blog), 22 June 2025. The leaked audio roiled Thai politics, confirming the open secret of dissension between government and military, already exacerbated by popular perceptions that the Pheu Thai-led government had been slow in dealing with Cambodia. In contrast, the military, and especially Boonsin, gained public support for adopting an uncompromising stance. 61 “A general at ease: Lt Gen Boonsin’s quiet weekends amid Thai-Cambodian tensions”, Bangkok Post , 14 June 2025. As an analyst put it, the government’s response “accidentally [made] Thai nationalism cool again”. 62 Ken Lohatepanont, “Thai government fails to meet the nationalist moment”, The Coffee Parliament (blog), 8 June 2025. For Thaksin’s critics, the telephone call also appeared to confirm longstanding suspicions that the Shinawatra clan was ready to collude with Hun Sen and “sell out” the country for personal gain. 63 Susannah Patton, “A border skirmish and leaked phone call sees the Thailand-Cambodia dispute surge back to life”, The Interpreter , 20 June 2025; “Thai protesters vent their exasperation with the prime minister”, The New York Times , 28 June 2025. In their view, the call also showed Paetongtarn – Thailand’s youngest-ever prime minister – to be out of her depth in a crisis and thus ripe for unseating. 64 Crisis Group interviews, officials and journalists, Bangkok, April and June 2026. The political consequences unfolded rapidly. The day the recording was exposed, Deputy Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul pulled his Bhumjaithai Party out of the coalition government and called on Paetongtarn to take responsibility for harming the nation’s honour. 65 “Bhumjaithai party announces withdrawal from government coalition”, The Nation , 18 June 2025. The Constitutional Court suspended her from office on 1 July while it considered a petition submitted by 36 senators that she had breached constitutional ethical standards. 66 Deputy Prime Minister Phumtham Wechaiyachai became acting prime minister. “July legal battles fuel momentum for political reset”, Bangkok Post , 25 June 2025; “Constitutional Court suspends Paetongtarn as PM because of Hun Sen’s clip”, The Nation , 1 July 2025. The Pheu Thai Party-led government ... adopted a firmer stance toward Cambodia, highlighting its role as a hub of transnational crime. The leaked audio also had bilateral repercussions, strengthening the Thai military’s hand. 67 Paul Chambers, “The 2025 Thai-Cambodian Conflict from Thailand’s Perspective”, Asia Policy , vol. 21, no. 2 (April 2026), pp. 18-19. On 23 June, the army spokesman announced the closure of all border checkpoints. 68 “Military seals border with Cambodia”, Bangkok Post , 24 June 2025. The Pheu Thai Party-led government also adopted a firmer stance toward Cambodia, highlighting its role as a hub of transnational crime, particularly industrial-scale fraud in scam compounds. 69 “Thai PM seeks international crackdown on Cambodia-based scams”, Bangkok Post , 23 June 2025. On his own social media accounts, meanwhile, Hun Sen kept up a steady stream of invective directed at Thaksin. He spoke of betrayal by the Shinawatras, recalling his hospitality to Thaksin, Thaksin’s sister Yingluck and their supporters; he also predicted that Thailand would have a new prime minister within three months. 70 “Hun Sen: ‘I predict that Thailand will have a new prime minister within the next three months, and I already know who it will be’”, Khmer Times , 25 June 2025. Why Hun Sen severed his longstanding relationship with Thaksin in this way remains a matter of speculation, but analysts in Phnom Penh attribute it to unhappiness that Thaksin had not delivered on joint development of maritime hydrocarbon deposits. 71 Crisis Group interviews, analysts and academics, Phnom Penh, February 2026. See also Gregory V. Raymond, “Patronage Networks, Personal Relationships and the Return of the Thai-Cambodia Border Conflict: A Nontraditional Account”, Asia Policy , vol. 21, no. 2 (April 2026). Others point to Paetongtarn’s plans to legalise gambling in Thailand, which would undercut Cambodia’s casinos, or the intensifying Thai campaign against scam centres across the border, which by one rough estimate generate one quarter to two fifths of Cambodia’s GDP. 72 Crisis Group interviews, analyst, Phnom Penh, February 2026; former government official, Phnom Penh, February 2026. The GDP share estimate appears in Jacob Sims and Bopha Phorn, “The Scam Economy in Cambodia”, Southeast Asian Affairs , 2026, p. 78. Many in Cambodia also believe it was an emotional decision, as Hun Sen was irritated by Paetongtarn calling Hun Manet “unprofessional” for issuing statements on social media. 73 Crisis Group interviews, former official, academic, Phnom Penh, February 2026; Western diplomat, Phnom Penh, May 2026. Thailand’s Constitutional Court removed Paetongtarn from office on 29 August, as it had done with all five Thaksin-aligned prime ministers since the 2006 coup. 74 On 9 September 2025, the Supreme Court sentenced Thaksin to serve the prison term he had avoided upon returning from exile in 2023. He was released the following 11 May. Anutin was elected prime minister a week later, promising fresh elections within four months. 75 Anutin dissolved parliament on 12 December 2025, and the general election took place on 8 February. IV. Fighting and Ceasefires The balance of power between Cambodia and Thailand is lopsided. Thailand dwarfs its neighbour in population (roughly 70 million to 17 million), gross domestic product ($577 billion to $51.2 billion in 2025), military spending ($5.7 billion to $1.3 billion in 2024) and armed forces (360,850 active personnel to 124,300). 76 World Bank data; “The Military Balance 2025”, International Institute for Strategic Studies, pp. 238; 302-303. These asymmetries weighed heavily on the battlefield, especially during the protracted December fighting in which Thailand gained the upper hand. A. Round One Tensions rose sharply after landmines wounded eight Thai soldiers on 16 and 23 July 2025 on the border area of Nam Yeun district, Ubon Ratchathani province. 77 “Landmine dispute escalates tensions between Thailand and Cambodia”, Reuters, 22 July 2025; “New mine blast inflames border tensions”, Bangkok Post , 23 July 2025. Thailand said the mines were newly laid; Cambodia said they were remnants of earlier conflicts. 78 Cambodia is among the countries most affected by landmines and other explosive remnants of war, with an estimated contaminated area of 1,856 sq km as of January 2024. See the Cambodian Mine Action Centre website. Thailand then expelled Cambodia’s ambassador and withdrew its own. The Preah Vihear temple has long been at the centre of the border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand. Renewed fighting along the border in 2025 killed at least 150 people and displaced almost a million more. Sources: UN OCHA Humanitarian Data Exchange, Subnational Administrative Boundaries (Cambodia, Thailand); OpenStreetMap; Google Earth satellite verification / CRISIS GROUP On 24 July, fighting broke out between ground troops near Ta Muen Thom and Ta Krabei temples, between Thailand’s Surin and Cambodia’s Oddar Meanchey provinces, with each side accusing the other of firing the first shot. 79 “Thailand launches airstrikes on Cambodia as border clash escalates”, Washington Post , 24 July 2025. The combat escalated quickly to unprecedented levels. Cambodian BM-21 rockets hit civilian areas in Thailand’s Kantharalak district, killing seven people, including two children, at a petrol station some 20km from the border. 80 “Strikes on civilians a ‘war crime’”, Bangkok Post , 25 July 2025. Thailand launched airstrikes on military targets in Preah Vihear, the first use of airpower across the Thai-Cambodian border since the early 1970s. 81 “Thailand and Cambodia exchange fire in new border clashes that kill at least 1 civilian”, Associated Press, 24 July 2025. Altogether, in five days, the exchanges killed at least 48 people and displaced some 300,000 civilians. 82 “Thailand-Cambodia border calm as military commanders hold talks”, Reuters, 29 July 2025; “Thai police fire tear gas at Cambodian protesters at a disputed border village”, Reuters, 18 September 2025. On 24 July, Malaysian Prime Minister and acting ASEAN chairman Anwar Ibrahim appealed for a ceasefire. 83 “Thailand, Cambodia must ‘stand down’ over border clash: Malaysian PM”, Thai PBS World, 24 July 2025. China also pushed for negotiations. Phnom Penh was ready for dialogue, but Bangkok was reluctant until the U.S. also weighed in. President Donald Trump stated that if the two countries did not negotiate, he would suspend trade talks with both. As Thailand was eager to use these talks to secure lower tariffs on exports to the U.S., Trump’s threat was sufficient to bring it to the table with Cambodia. 84 “Exclusive: Trump’s call broke deadlock in Thailand-Cambodia border crisis”, Reuters, 31 July 2025. On 28 July, acting Prime Minister Phumtham Wechaiyachai met Hun Manet in Putrajaya and agreed to a ceasefire, as well as a meeting of regional military commanders the next day and a meeting of the General Border Committee in early August. 85 “Joint Press Release on the Special Meeting Hosted by Malaysia to Address the Current Situation between Cambodia and Thailand”, Malaysian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 28 July 2025. The prime ministers also agreed to Anwar’s proposal for ASEAN observers to monitor the ceasefire. 86 Crisis Group interview, retired senior military officer, Bangkok, June 2026. See also “ASEAN chair deploys observer team to monitor Thai-Cambodian ceasefire”, The Nation , 28 July 2025. B. Interregnum The ceasefire was fragile from the start, with allegations of violations soon emerging from both capitals. 1. Developments on the border The situation was particularly fraught at Ban Nong Chan and Ban Nong Ya Kaeo in Khok Sung district, Sa Kaeo province abutting Cambodia's Chouk Chey and Prey Chan villages, where thousands of Cambodians had settled as refugees in the 1980s, on land Thailand claims. The Thai military, reportedly impatient with the government’s failure to evict these people, pressed it to act. 87 “Thai military increases pressure on govt, Cambodia to relocate encroachers”, The Nation , 2 September 2025. Thai riot police scuffled with Cambodians at Ban Nong Ya Kaeo on 17 September, injuring 23 with tear gas and rubber bullets; Thai officers also reportedly sustained injuries. 88 “Thailand gives Cambodia 30 days to withdraw after border clashes”, Khaosod English , 17 September 2025; “Thai police fire tear gas at Cambodian protesters at a disputed border village”, Reuters, 18 September 2025. In early October, Thailand began stacking up shipping containers to build walls, cordoning off parts of Ban Nong Chan to prevent Cambodians from entering. 89 “Cargo containers arrive in Ban Nong Chan to reinforce border wall”, Thai PBS World, 10 October 2025. The situation was particularly fraught at Ban Nong Chan and Ban Nong Ya Kaeo, Sa Kaeo province, abutting Cambodia’s Chouk Chey and Prey Chan villages, where thousands of Cambodians had settled as refugees in the 1980s. Sources: UN OCHA Humanitarian Data Exchange, Subnational Administrative Boundaries (Cambodia, Thailand); OpenStreetMap; Google Earth satellite verification / CRISIS GROUP Amid these confrontations, bilateral border mechanisms kept functioning. On 27 August, a Regional Border Committee meeting affirmed the ceasefire and pledged cooperation on demining and crime suppression. 90 “Second Army outlines 11-point RBC, Cambodia defers demining and scams to GBC”, The Nation , 27 August 2025. On 10 September, at a special General Border Committee meeting convened in Koh Kong, Cambodia, the parties agreed to remove heavy weapons from the border, develop terms of reference for ASEAN Observer Teams on each side of the border and cooperate on demining. They also said they would refer the matter of Chouk Chey/Nong Chan to the next JBC meeting as a priority for joint survey and demarcation, “peacefully manag[ing] the situation on the ground” in the meantime. 91 “Joint Press Statement of the Special General Border Committee Meeting, Koh Kong, Cambodia”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 10 September 2025. Despite the positive tone, tensions lingered, as Thai conservative activists whipped up nationalist sentiment. On 10 October, with the Thai military’s permission, social media celebrity Kanthat Pongpaiboonwet began broadcasting piercing, “ghostly” noises through loudspeakers at Ban Nong Chan and Ban Nong Ya Kaeo to intimidate Cambodians. 92 “Thai army defends psych-ops along Cambodian border”, Bangkok Post , 12 October 2025. Earlier, in late August, Kanthat had brought fourteen sewage trucks to Ban Nong Chan. He had intended to spray protesting Cambodians with sewage, but authorities prevented him from doing so. “Thai social media star stages sewage stunt at tense border”, Bangkok Post , 28 August 2025. The Thai military put a stop to the stunt after a week, but prominent figures who spoke out against it had to seek police protection after receiving death threats. 93 “Army orders halt to ‘sound war’ against Cambodians in Sa Kaeo province”, Thai PBS World, 19 October 2025; “Action urged after border comment death threats”, Bangkok Post , 21 October 2025. 2. International peace efforts Meanwhile, in an 8 October letter, President Trump urged Thailand’s new prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, to reach a peace deal with Cambodia. 94 “Thailand snubs Trump’s mediation, tells Cambodia to remove border troops”, Bloomberg, 9 October 2025. Trump agreed to attend the forthcoming ASEAN summit on the condition that he could preside over a peace accord signing ceremony. 95 “Trump seeks peace ceremony spotlight at ASEAN summit”, Politico , 6 October 2025. Anutin responded that Trump should press Cambodia to meet four conditions: withdrawing heavy weapons, removing landmines, eliminating scam centres and relocating Cambodian settlements on Thai territory. 96 “Anutin to notify Trump, urging Cambodia to comply with Thai conditions”, The Nation , 9 October 2025. As the ASEAN summit approached, Thai officials suggested that peace prospects hinged on a JBC meeting and the second Special GBC meeting, both scheduled for 20-23 October. 97 “Anutin chairs security meeting ahead of GBC-JBC talks”, The Nation , 20 October 2025. These achieved a measure of success: the JBC assented to expediting the joint survey in the Chouk Chey-Nong Chan and Prey Chan-Nong Ya Kaeo area, while the GBC delegations produced an in-principle agreement to withdraw heavy weapons, clear mines and cooperate against scam centres. 98 “Border talks agree to repair markers, review land holdings”, Bangkok Post , 23 October 2025. On 26 October, Trump presided over the signing of a joint declaration by Prime Ministers Anutin and Hun Manet, endorsed by Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim, on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Kuala Lumpur. Despite the fanfare, the joint declaration amounted to a recommitment to the terms of the 28 July ceasefire: withdrawing heavy weapons, coordinating demining and border demarcation, and desisting from dissemination of false information and “harmful rhetoric”. 99 Thailand also committed to promptly release eighteen Cambodian prisoners of war. “Joint Declaration by the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Cambodia and the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Thailand on the outcomes of their meeting in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia”, White House, 26 October 2025. Speaking at the summit, Anutin sought to reassure the Thai public, saying the agreement would not put Thailand at a disadvantage. He specified that the 1:200,000 map was not discussed and that light detection and ranging technology had rendered the Annex I map obsolete. 100 “PM claims joint declaration with Cambodia won’t disadvantage Thailand”, Thai PBS World, 26 October 2025. C. Round Two Just two weeks after the Kuala Lumpur accord, the ceasefire began to unravel. On 10 November, Prime Minister Anutin said Thailand would stop observing the joint statement after a landmine wounded four Thai soldiers in Kantharalak district. 101 “Anutin halts Thai-Cambodian peace declaration after Thai troops hit landmine again”, The Nation , 10 November 2025. The four incidents that wounded sixteen Thai soldiers in 2025 all involved recently laid PMN-2 antipersonnel mines, of which Cambodia has stocks. All the incidents occurred on customary patrol routes in contested territory previously known to be safe and often used by both armies. According to an independent analysis, “these incidents [have] the appearance of a targeted military activity”. “Investigation into New Use of Antipersonnel Landmines on the Thai-Cambodia Border”, Landmine Monitor, 1 March 2026, p. 20. On file with Crisis Group. The U.S. briefly tried to intercede, saying it would suspend talks about a reciprocal trade framework agreement – which would have meant higher tariffs – if Bangkok did not reverse course. 102 “US halts trade talks with Thailand over peace pact compliance”, Bangkok Post , 15 November 2025. But Thai officials learned that no such penalty was forthcoming. Within a month, troops exchanged fire in the same district, and fighting soon spread. 103 “Thai-Cambodia border clash injures two Thai troops, triggers evacuation”, Khaosod English , 7 December 2025; “Briefing to the Diplomatic Corps and International Organizations on Developments on the Thailand-Cambodia Border Situation”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 8 December 2025. Thai officials made clear that this round of combat would differ from the first. “The aim of the Thai army is to disable Cambodia’s military capability for a long time, for the sake of our children’s safety”, army chief of staff Chaiyapruek Duangprapat explained. 104 “PM Anutin says no more negotiations with Cambodia”, Thai PBS World, 8 December 2025. On 9 December, Anutin said Thailand was determined to push ahead, notwithstanding calls for dialogue: “We can’t stop now. We’ve already given our commitment to the armed forces that they can fully carry out the planned operations”. 105 “Border battle expands as Thailand and Cambodia clash for second day”, Reuters, 9 December 2025. At its height, the fighting had displaced over 600,000 people in Cambodia and some 400,000 in Thailand. Combat continued for twenty days, including rocket and artillery exchanges and Thai airstrikes that hit targets deep inside Cambodia. 106 “Cambodia counts the cost of its border war with Thailand”, BBC, 19 December 2025. At its height, the fighting had displaced over 600,000 people in Cambodia and some 400,000 in Thailand. 107 Roughly 84.5 per cent of the displaced in Cambodia were women and children. “Situation Report 20 – Displacement Crisis as a Result of the Cambodia-Thailand Border Conflict”, op. cit. At least 101 people were killed, including 26 Thai soldiers. Cambodia did not release military casualty figures, but media estimates put the toll at roughly 130 killed. 108 “Cambodian deaths exceed 110 in December border conflict with Thailand”, Nikkei Asia , 13 January 2026. Reported Thai military estimates of the number of Cambodian troops killed range from 200 to 500. “Army places district out of bounds”, Bangkok Post , 16 December 2025; “Thailand carries out more airstrikes on Cambodia as deadly border conflict flares”, Associated Press, 18 December 2025. Again, Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar played an important role in ending the hostilities. 109 “Anwar calls Thai, Cambodian leaders to discuss border clashes”, Thai PBS World, 10 December 2025. As ASEAN chairman, he convened a special foreign ministers’ meeting that called for an immediate ceasefire, withdrawal of troops under the watch of interim ASEAN Observer Teams and bilateral dialogue. 110 “ASEAN Chair’s Statement Special ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on the Current Situation between Cambodia and Thailand”, 22 December 2025. Washington urged talks, but Thailand was less inclined to respond to U.S. pressure than it had been in July, as the Trump administration had not imposed the higher tariffs it threatened after Bangkok stopped observing the ceasefire in November. 111 “On Fighting on the Cambodia-Thailand Border”, press statement, U.S. State Department, 9 December 2025; “Thailand says US trade talks to proceed despite Cambodia dispute”, Reuters, 15 November 2025. China, meanwhile, played a more prominent mediating role in December. 112 Immediately after the first ceasefire agreement, China’s vice minister for foreign affairs, Sun Weidong, hosted Cambodian and Thai officials for an “informal consultation” in Shanghai. “China vows to continue Thailand-Cambodia peace efforts after ‘informal’ post-truce talks”, South China Morning Post , 30 July 2025. Foreign Minister Wang Yi called his Cambodian and Thai counterparts directly, and Deng Xijun, Beijing’s special envoy for Asian affairs, visited both countries. 113 “Special Envoy for Asian Affairs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Makes Another Shuttle-Diplomacy Trip for Peace between Cambodia and Thailand”, Chinese Foreign Ministry, 25 December 2025. Cambodia and Thailand eventually agreed to a ceasefire at a special GBC meeting on 27 December. Key provisions include commitments to resume “at the earliest” efforts to survey and demarcate the border using the JBC’s existing mechanisms, as well as to refrain from building up forces along the border. 114 The two parties also agreed to cooperate against scam centres. “Joint Statement of the 3rd Special General Border Committee between the Kingdom of Thailand and the Kingdom of Cambodia at Ban Pak Kard (Chanthaburi Province of Thailand)-Prum (Pailin Province of Cambodia) International Point of Entry”, 27 December 2025. The day after the agreement was signed, Wang Yi hosted Foreign Ministers Sihasak Phuangketkeow and Prak Sokhonn in Yuxi, Yunnan province. 115 “Foreign Ministers of China, Cambodia, and Thailand Hold Trilateral Meeting”, Chinese Foreign Ministry, 29 December 2025. According to a Thai official, China played a constructive role outside the media glare: “They are fair, not trying to impose a solution”. 116 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Thai Foreign Ministry, Bangkok, April 2026. V. Not Turning the Page Following the December ceasefire, relations have remained tense with little movement toward restoring normal diplomatic relations or delimiting the land border. Instead, the two governments have remained locked in a contest for international public opinion amid regular border provocations and fears of a third round of war. A. A New Status Quo When the dust settled from the December fighting, the Thai military had most of the high ground. Thailand now holds not only territory in contested areas, but also land that is indisputably Cambodian, beyond Bangkok’s proposed border line. Bangkok justifies its action by arguing that the ceasefire froze the conflict where it stood on 27 December, citing point 2 of the joint statement, which says, “Both sides agree to maintain current troop deployments without further movement”. 117 “Joint Statement of the 3rd Special GBC”, op. cit. Following the same logic, Thai troops have built walls of stacked shipping containers and barbed wire in disputed areas, notably those from which they forcibly repatriated Cambodian refugees who had settled there in the 1980s. 118 The areas in question are Ban Nong Chan/Chouk Chey and Nong Ya Kaeo/Prey Chan, in Thailand’s Khok Sung district, Sa Kaeo province and Cambodia’s O’Chrov district, Banteay Meanchey province. Thailand has also built container walls in Bang Tha Sen, Muang district, Trat province/Thma [Thmor] Da, Pursat province; and Chong An Mah, Ubon Ratchathani/An Seh village, Choam Ksan district, Preah Vihear province. According to Cambodian officials, Thailand expelled 1,200 families from these areas. 119 “A tale of two villages: Cambodians lament Thailand’s border gains”, Agence France-Presse, 7 February 2026. The Thai military, which has also destroyed homes in these locations, describes the barriers as a “reorganisation” needed for security, strictly in accordance with the 27 December joint statement. 120 “Cambodia says Thai troops still occupy civilian areas, testing December truce”, Reuters, 14 January 2026; “Army denies blocking return of displaced”, Bangkok Post , 29 March 2026. An independent non-governmental organisation in Cambodia determined that Thailand’s destruction of Cambodian homes in disputed areas of Ban Nong Chan/Chouk Chey and Nong Ya Kaeo/Prey Chan may violate international law. “Post-ceasefire Razing of Cambodian Villages Likely Violates International Law”, LICADHO, 20 January 2026. In January, Thai Defence Minister Natthaphon Narkphanit said Thai soldiers would stay deployed along the border for at least a year, adding that veterans may be allowed to settle in formerly restricted zones. 121 “Troops to man border for ‘at least one year’”, Bangkok Post , 11 January 2026. Many in Cambodia worry that Thailand is moving toward de facto annexation of the disputed areas and Cambodian territory it currently controls. Cambodia has objected to this new status quo. On 2 January, less than a week after the ceasefire, its foreign ministry issued a statement identifying fourteen areas held by Thai troops that are “unequivocally within Cambodian territory”, accusing Thailand of “intensifying demolition of Cambodian civilian and cultural structures”, and condemning “an unlawful and continuing occupation … brought about and sustained through the threat and use of force”. 122 “Statement of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Cambodia’s Protest against Thai Violations”, 2 January 2026. The statement specified the following areas: In Banteay Meanchey province, Prey Chan, Chouk Chey and Boeung Trakuon; in Pursat province, Phluk Domei and Thmor Da International Point of Entry (Chrok Chey Chomneas); in Preah Vihear province, An Ses, Ta Thav and Phnom Trap; and in Oddar Meanchey, O’Smach, K’nar Temple, Ta Krabei temple, Tamone Thom temple, Chob Angkhun and Chok Krous. It is not clear how much Cambodian territory Thailand holds, but it likely amounts to several square kilometres. The Banteay Meanchey governor said Thai troops held 7.6 sq km of territory in Prey Chan, Chouk Chey and Boeung Trakuon. “Thai forces illegally occupying nearly 800 hectares of Cambodian territory in Banteay Meanchey, says governor”, Khmer Times , 24 February 2026. This estimate may include disputed areas, however. Crisis Group interview, Western analyst, Phnom Penh, May 2026. Many in Cambodia worry that Thailand is moving toward de facto annexation of the disputed areas and Cambodian territory it currently controls. 123 Crisis Group interviews, analysts and government officials, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. See also “Cambodia doubles down on bid to spotlight Thai occupation”, Khmer Times , 25 February 2026. Phnom Penh organises regular visits by the ASEAN Observer Team and foreign dignitaries to these areas. See, for example, “Cambodia doubles down on legal efforts to counter Thai military encroachment”, Phnom Penh Post , 27 March 2026. Bangkok denies such accusations. But the government has repeatedly organised media trips to a casino resort it seized in the Cambodian border town of O’Smach, which it presents as evidence of Cambodia’s role in permitting scam operations to flourish, prompting Phnom Penh to accuse Thailand of seeking to justify its continued occupation of the site. 124 “Cambodian scam compound yields trove of fraud evidence, Thai military says”, Reuters, 2 February 2026; “Thailand exposes scam city in O’Smach, invites international scrutiny”, Khaosod English , 7 April 2026; “Cambodia: Thai military’s border media stunt is ‘direct breach’ of UN Charter”, Agence Khmer Presse, 30 June 2026; “Thailand shows observers alleged O’Smach scam and military sites”, The Nation , 8 September 2026. On 8 February, the Thai general election gave a convincing victory to the Bhumjaithai party, previously the third largest in parliament, led by caretaker prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul. The party positioned itself as a reliable ally of the conservative establishment and pledged a hard line on Cambodia. 125 The Bhumjaithai party won 191 seats in the 500-seat lower house, the progressive People’s Party 120 seats and Pheu Thai 74. Bhumjaithai formed a coalition with Pheu Thai and fourteen other parties. “Thai poll body certifies election results, clearing path for new parliament”, Reuters, 4 March 2026. Faced with December’s military setbacks and loss of territory, the Cambodian government took steps to bolster its international standing and domestic legitimacy. Authorities intensified a rolling nationwide crackdown on scam centres, with a senior official declaring on 27 August that large-scale operations had been “brought fully under control”. 126 “Cambodia declares ‘large scam compounds’ eliminated as criminal networks shift into homes, cafés”, Phnom Penh Post , 29 August 2026. The large compounds have closed, but the crackdown has targeted the premises, not the landlords, officials and financiers who run the scams, so the industry is dispersing into smaller, hidden locations rather than disappearing. Crisis Group interviews, analysts, diplomats and researchers, Phnom Penh, February-September 2026; Crisis Group observations, Sihanoukville and border casino towns, July-August 2026. In May, former opposition leader Kem Sokha, convicted of treason in 2023, received a royal pardon. His daughter, Kem Monovithya, accepted an appointment in August as a special envoy in Hun Manet’s government, specialising in border affairs and trade. 127 “Kem Monovithya’s new role raises questions over political reconciliation and opposition’s future”, Cambodianess , 19 August 2026. B. The Diplomatic Impasse Since the 27 December ceasefire agreement, Phnom Penh has pushed for resuming talks under the JBC, which last convened on 22 October 2025, after the first round of fighting. 128 “Thai minister sees ‘progress’ toward Cambodia peace deal”, Bangkok Post , 23 October 2025. Between January and April, it made three separate requests for the body to hold a special meeting, but Bangkok demurred each time. 129 Bangkok first cited the coming general election, then the formation of a new cabinet and finally the need to appoint a new chief delegate to the commission. “Foreign ministry decries Thai efforts to stall JBC demarcation work”, Phnom Penh Post , 13 March 2026; “Thailand not ready for border talks with Cambodia: Sihasak”, Bangkok Post , 12 April 2026. On 12 April, Hun Manet announced that Cambodia would focus on direct talks to resolve disputes with Thailand. 130 “Cambodia shifts border resolution priorities: ‘From ICJ to bilateral negotiations’”, Phnom Penh Post , 12 April 2026. It amounted to a concession, given Thailand’s longstanding insistence on resolving differences bilaterally, and a tacit admission that Cambodia’s ICJ gambit in June 2025 was futile, given that Bangkok does not consent to the court’s jurisdiction. Hun Manet said bilateral talks would be faster, but the change in tack likely also reflected a recognition that another round of fighting could threaten his government’s legitimacy. 131 Crisis Group interview, analyst, Phnom Penh, May 2026. In another glimmer of potential progress, the two countries’ foreign ministers met on the sidelines of the ASEAN-EU ministerial meeting in Brunei on 27 April, where they discussed border issues among other subjects. 132 “Cambodian, Thai FMs discuss border issue in Brunei”, Xinhua, 28 April 2026; “Cambodia, Thailand reaffirm ceasefire as rights groups decry arrests over border dispute”, CamboJA News, 28 April 2026. Anutin and Hun Manet then met at the ASEAN summit in Cebu, the Philippines, where they tasked their foreign ministers with developing confidence-building measures. 133 “Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Attends the Trilateral Meeting between the Leaders of Thailand, the Philippines and Cambodia on the Sidelines of the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu, the Republic of the Philippines”, press release, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 7 May 2026. [Thailand and Cambodia] have fallen into a pattern of recriminations, with each side attempting to load responsibility for the stalemate on the other. These minimal efforts at improving relations have not been fruitful, however. Instead, the two countries have fallen into a pattern of recriminations, with each side attempting to load responsibility for the stalemate on the other. Phnom Penh has sought to focus international attention on what it calls Thailand’s illegal actions along the border. It has lodged dozens of formal protests, and senior officials have pointed to what they call violations of sovereignty and efforts to establish a new border line by force. 134 Between the 27 December ceasefire and 22 June, Cambodia’s JBC delegation lodged nine diplomatic notes with its Thai counterpart and issued 32 formal protest notes about Thai activities. “Cambodia’s JBC sent nine diplomatic notes to Thailand, lodged 32 protests over alleged illegal activities: government spokesperson”, Agence Kampuchea Presse, 22 June 2026. “PM takes Thai border dispute to global parliamentary stage, warns of ‘fait accompli’ attempts”, Phnom Penh Post , 27 August 2026; “Hun Sen declares Thais used ‘scam excuse’ to invade Cambodia, warns of ‘collapse of world order’”, Phnom Penh Post , 27 August 2026. In response to these protests, Bangkok has said it is in compliance with existing bilateral agreements and international law, while characterising Phnom Penh’s rhetoric as an impediment to resolving the border issue. 135 “JIC warns threats to arrest Anutin and use force could harm talks”, The Nation , 27 August 2026. Foreign Minister Sihasak has publicly warned Cambodia not to criticise Thailand at international forums and repeatedly called for it to demonstrate sincerity, portraying its diplomatic manoeuvres as efforts to “internationalise the conflict and undermine prospects for peace”. 136 “Sihasak warns Cambodia against raising bilateral disputes at UNSC”, The Nation , 24 May 2026; “Land border ‘priority’, FM says”, Bangkok Post , 27 April 2026; “Thailand rejects Cambodia’s claims at UN”, Bangkok Post , 25 February 2026. In late August, Sihasak explained Thailand’s rationale for not convening the JBC, arguing that progress on border security, including cooperation on demining and combating criminal networks, must precede survey work and demarcation. 137 Sihasak Phuangketkeow, “Setting the stage for border talks”, Bangkok Post , 31 August 2026. More recently, the foreign minister denounced Cambodia for “playing the role of a victim with a sense of self-righteousness aimed at claiming the moral high ground”. 138 “Thailand’s statement at the first meeting of UNCLOS Conciliation Commission”, 15 September 2026. Bangkok’s reaction to the visit to Cambodia by a UN special rapporteur on human rights, Tom Andrews, exemplifies its defensive stance. Andrews issued an end-of-mission statement on 31 July noting that roughly 650,000 Cambodian civilians had been displaced by the border fighting and more than 20,000 remain unable to return to their homes, as well as highlighting the plight of some 900,000 Cambodian migrant workers who have returned from Thailand. 139 “Tom Andrews, UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Cambodia, End of Mission Statement, 31 July 2026, Phnom Penh, Cambodia”, 3 August 2026. Bangkok swiftly objected to the statement, saying the number of displaced included refugees from the 1970s who had “encroached on Thai territory”, adding that Thailand did not compel the workers to leave. 140 “Statement: Regarding the Statement by Mr. Tom Andrews, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Situation of Human Rights in Cambodia”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 1 August 2026. Foreign Minister Sihasak argued that Andrews had not consulted his government, labelling the statement one-sided for failing to mention Thai losses. 141 Thailand formally submitted its objections to the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and the UN Human Rights Council. “Thailand rejects UN expert’s Cambodia report, cites lack of balance”, Khaosod English , 3 August 2026; “UNCLOS conciliation chair to be named this week”, Bangkok Post , 12 August 2026. Andrews stated that he had sent a draft of his statement to Thailand two days before it was issued but had received no response. “UN envoy says Thailand received draft but did not respond”, Khaosod English , 8 August 2026. C. Nationalism as Policy Constraint Thailand’s policy appears to be conditioned by consideration for the views of ultranationalist Thais, including serving and former military officers, who espouse the narrative of lost territories and oppose even the appearance of conciliation. 142 Crisis Group interviews, analyst; senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. “The land border has grown into an emotional issue”, a senior security official said. “The government can’t back down”. 143 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Bangkok, April 2026. In November 2025, Anutin was compelled to apologise to the public for suggesting that Thailand had encroached on Cambodian territory, pledging that “that there is no possibility that Thailand will lose any territory, sovereignty, honour or dignity”. 144 “PM sorry for border gaffe”, Bangkok Post , 3 November 2025. Privately, Thai officials acknowledge that Bangkok finds the status quo acceptable. 145 Crisis Group interviews, senior official, Bangkok, April 2026; retired senior Thai military officer, Bangkok, June 2026. As one put it: “For domestic political reasons, this works well. There’s no strong desire to normalise [relations]”. 146 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, April 2026. According to a Thai analyst, when the government cites “public sentiment” as a justification for a hard line on Cambodia, it may be understood as a euphemism for “military sentiment”. 147 Crisis Group interview, analyst, Bangkok, July 2026. In the campaign for February’s general election, Anutin rode a wave of Thai nationalism generated by conflict with Cambodia. Aware that Thai nationalists have been criticising the two border memoranda since 2008, he proposed a referendum on cancelling both MOU 43 (land border) and MOU 44 (maritime border). He eventually dropped the referendum idea after the Council of State found that it might be unconstitutional, but he nonetheless pledged to withdraw from MOU 44, while keeping the option open on MOU 43. 148 “Anutin government plans referendum on Thai-Cambodian MoUs”, Thai PBS World, 25 September 2025; “Council of State clarifies referendum on MOU termination after House dissolution violates constitution”, The Nation , 17 December 2025; “Anutin pledges to scrap maritime MOU in final election rally push”, The Nation , 7 February 2026. 1. MOU 43 Thai critics of MOU 43 argue that it failed to end Cambodian encroachment and that it disadvantages Thailand by relying on the French 1:200,000 scale map. 149 “Not the right path to peace”, Bangkok Post , 28 June 2025; “Govt ‘has legal grounds’ to end MoU with Cambodia”, Bangkok Post , 9 October 2025. Before Anutin dissolved parliament in December 2025, the army asked the government to assess whether MOU 43 remained apposite. 150 Crisis Group interview, senior official, April 2026. See also “New government faces MOU 43 dilemma as Cambodia pushes JBC talks”, The Nation , 2 January 2026. Anutin suggested that progress had been made under its provisions in demarcating portions of the border. 151 “PM calls for border MoU updates”, Bangkok Post , 11 January 2026. In May, Anutin declared that “for Thailand, the 1:200,000 scale no longer exists”, raising questions about Thailand’s adherence to the 1907 treaty. 152 “Thai PM firm on sovereignty, declaring colonial-era maps ‘no longer exist’ for Bangkok”, The Nation , 27 March 2026. Thai political scientist Surachart Bumrungsuk notes that the colonial-era maps are the only legal tools available for resolving conflicts over the border. Rejecting them is tantamount to rejecting the treaties themselves, which is “practically impossible and historically flawed”. 153 “Surachart Bumrungsuk, ‘Respectfully submitted to the prime minister: Subject: Map demarcating the land border between Thailand and Cambodia’”, Matichon Weekly , 31 May 2026. While some Thai nationalists object to the Annex I map, there is no clamour for revoking the Franco-Siamese treaties. Nor is there a practical mechanism for doing so. Moreover, the 1:50,000 scale Thai military map has no legal standing under international law. Surachart warned that Thailand risked falling into a “legal trap” should the issue be adjudicated again by the ICJ. 154 Surachart also notes that the Thai military map is printed with the words “boundary representation is not necessarily authoritative”. Ibid. Meanwhile, a Senate ad hoc committee examining MOU 43 recommended on 24 March that Thailand withdraw, citing six reasons, including its reference to the Annex I map of the 1907 Treaty. Importantly, it also mentioned the changed circumstances following the fighting in December 2025: the committee’s chairman, Noppadol Inna, said the fact that Thai troops had “recovered” fifteen disputed areas weighed heavily in the committee’s decision. 155 “Senate panel urges end to MOU 43 over repeated Cambodian breaches”, The Nation , 24 March 2026. In his reasoning, the 27 December joint statement provision that troops must remain where they are supersedes MOU 43, which says neither side may “carry out any work resulting in changes of environment of the frontier zone”. 156 Ibid.; MOU 2000, Article V. 2. MOU 44 In December 2025, the same senate committee had also recommended withdrawing from MOU 44. Anutin, who had promised to annul it during his campaign, included the decision in his government’s policy statement following the February election, which the National Security Council endorsed on 23 April. 157 “Anutin pledges to scrap maritime MOU in final election rally push”, op. cit.; Mongkol Bangprapa, “Security Council scraps MoU 44, citing stalled talks, rising tensions with Cambodia”, Bangkok Post , 23 April 2026. Two weeks later, the government formally withdrew from MOU 44. 158 “For Thailand, MoU 44 no longer exists, Thai PM says”, Thai PBS World, 5 May 2026. Anutin has since been at pains to explain that the decision was unrelated to the Cambodia conflict, but instead based on the memorandum’s failure to produce results after only five meetings over 25 years. 159 “Fence project under way – Thailand moves to secure vulnerable crossings”, The Nation , 24 April 2026. Cambodian officials had warned that Thai withdrawal from MOU 44 would leave them with “no choice” but to pursue compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS. 160 “Cambodia to pursue compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS if Thailand revokes MoU”, Phnom Penh Post , 4 May 2026. In announcing the decision to invoke compulsory conciliation on 2 June, Hun Manet said it would “[bring] dialogue into a structured international framework recognised by both countries”. 161 “UNCLOS underway; Cambodia lodges formal request for maritime reconciliation”, Phnom Penh Post , 2 June 2026. Established under UNCLOS Annex V, compulsory conciliation is a dispute settlement mechanism in which parties select two experts each to sit on a commission, who then select a fifth to chair the body; the resulting recommendations are non-binding but serve as a basis for negotiations. Bangkok has acquiesced to compulsory conciliation, but made its dissatisfaction clear, with Foreign Minister Sihasak noting it would “unavoidab[ly] … affect talks on restoring relations, border security and … boundary issues”. 162 “Thailand to join UN maritime arbitration with Cambodia, halts other two-way talks”, Reuters, 5 June 2026; “Sihasak warns Hun Manet’s maritime move could shut door on wider Thai-Cambodian talks”, The Nation , 3 June 2026. Thailand appointed Rüdiger Wolfrum (Germany) and Albert J. Hoffmann (South Africa) as its two conciliators, while Cambodia appointed Peter Taksøe-Jensen (Denmark) and Jean-Marc Thouvenin (France). In mid-August, these experts selected Australian diplomat Katrina Cooper as the commission’s chairperson. Anutin later affirmed that Thailand would suspend participation in the JBC and GBC. He added that Bangkok would not discuss renewing relations until conciliation concludes. 163 “Thailand to join UN maritime arbitration with Cambodia, halts other two-way talks”, Reuters, 5 June 2026; “PM appoints Sihasak to lead UNCLOS process, vows to freeze JBC and GBC talks with Cambodia”, Thai PBS World, 5 June 2026. A Thai analyst observed that, as there was no legal rationale for linking compulsory conciliation with discussions of the land border, this stance reflected Bangkok’s anger with Cambodia. 164 Crisis Group interview, Thai journalist, Bangkok, June 2026. The compulsory conciliation process commenced on 15 September in Singapore, with opening statements by the two foreign ministers. Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn called the process “a means to rebuild trust”, expressing hope that the commission could help the parties “turn a new page for their mutual benefit”. 165 “Opening statement of the agent of the Kingdom of Cambodia, first meeting of the Conciliation Commission”, 15 September 2026. His counterpart Sihasak’s remarks struck an uncompromising note, citing the “broader context” of Cambodian provocations as the cause of the breakdown in relations. 166 “Thailand’s statement at the first meeting of UNCLOS Conciliation Commission”, 15 September 2026. VI. Averting a Third Round Demarcating the land border is essential if the two countries are to remove disputed territory as a source of conflict, leading to the loss of hundreds of lives over the past eighteen years. The means of specifying the land border already exist: the JBC has already demarcated three quarters of it. The main impediment is not technical complexity – the revised 2003 Terms of Reference and advantages offered by light detection and ranging should suffice – but rather the mistrust between Bangkok and Phnom Penh. Given events of the past year, there are genuine worries on both sides that a third round of fighting is likely – a former high-ranking Thai officer even called the prospect “inevitable”. 167 Crisis Group interviews, diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; journalist, Bangkok, April 2026. See also “Ex-deputy commander of Second Army Area warns third round of fighting ‘will happen’”, The Nation , 28 January 2026. Ideally, third-party mediation would make the necessary compromises more politically palatable. As Hun Sen noted in June 2025, any Cambodian or Thai leader who retreats from maximalist positions at this point would risk incurring public disapproval. 168 “Selected Comments of Samdech Akka Moha Sena Padei Techo Hun Sen, President of the Senate, on the Cambodia-Thailand Border Issue”, 2 June 2025. A disinterested third party could shield decision-makers from some of the political costs of compromise. The most logical candidate to play such a role remains the ICJ. Even if many in Thailand regard the ICJ’s 1962 ruling on Preah Vihear as unjust, it does not establish a binding precedent for other disputed areas of the land border. If Cambodia and Thailand agreed to have the court rule on all these areas, it could very well lead to an equitable resolution. 169 William Roth, “Tackling Thai-Cambodian border row”, Bangkok Post (editorial), 12 November 2025. Unfortunately, such a path is, for now, politically untenable in Thailand, both because of bitterness over the 1962 ruling and the establishment’s objections to internationalising the conflict. The reality of heightened nationalism is that the Thai government is unlikely to attempt to sell the public on trading even a small amount of territory for peace. 170 Jones and Narut, “The Sovereignty Straitjacket”, op. cit. Prime Minister Anutin was rewarded at the polls for maintaining a hard line on Cambodia. In turn, he is intent on keeping the Thai military’s support. He also does not wish to run afoul of right-wing nationalists who perceive bargaining as a betrayal of sacrifices, military and civilian, in the 2025 fighting. 171 “New government faces MOU 43 dilemma as Cambodia pushes JBC talks”, The Nation , 2 January 2026. Furthermore, conflict with Cambodia has allowed the Thai military to burnish its image, which had been sullied by its overt political role, including coups d’état. 172 Crisis Group interviews, journalist, Bangkok, April 2026. In this charged environment, those advocating compromise risk being labelled traitors. 173 Crisis Group interviews, Western diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. The costs of conflict are not high enough to impel [Thai and Cambodian] leaders toward a resolution. More broadly, political elites in both countries perceive benefits from the conflict, principally from popular support arising from nationalism and as a distraction from domestic economic and political problems. For decision-makers, especially in Thailand, these benefits continue to outweigh the conflict’s costs, whether economic or reputational. In any event, the costs of conflict are not high enough to impel leaders toward a resolution. Cambodia adapted to the border closure better than many anticipated, though it has compounded pre-existing economic pressures as time goes by, contributing to a marked slowdown in growth. 174 Crisis Group interview, government minister, Phnom Penh, February 2026. See also “IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Cambodia”, International Monetary Fund, 28 September 2026. The IMF projects growth to slow to 3 per cent in 2026, from 5.3 per cent in 2025. In any case, disruptions of bilateral trade have been damaging, but not bad enough to trigger a policy change. 175 Closure of the land border caused trade to decline by 40 per cent to $1.3 billion for the first half of 2026, year-on-year, according to Cambodian government data. “Cambodian economy suffers as Thai conflict blights bilateral trade”, Nikkei Asia , 24 July 2026. Some 900,000 Cambodian migrant workers returned from Thailand in 2025; two thirds of them found employment, though generally lower-paid. The UN estimated remittance losses at $277 million in 2025 and $665 million in 2026. “Socio-economic Impact Assessment of Cambodia–Thailand Border”, UN, April 2026, p. 10. Perhaps the most significant obstacle is that, for now, political elites in Bangkok appear to see greater reward in hardline policies than in the risks of reconciliation. Cambodia’s leadership likewise sees benefit in confrontation, in the form of popular nationalist fervour, though another round of fighting could shift Phnom Penh’s calculus, as further military setbacks could fracture the Hun family’s coalition. 176 Crisis Group interviews, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. Hun Sen told local officials that the CPP’s policy on the border dispute would be a campaign issue in the 2027 commune elections. “Ruling CPP to use border dispute issue as 2027 commune election campaign material”, CamboJA News, 1o June 2026. In these circumstances, reconciliation in the near term is unrealistic. Some argue that the conflict cannot be resolved until politics in both countries become more pluralistic and democratic, thereby weakening the hold of established elites. 177 Crisis Group interviews, academic, Phnom Penh, February 2026; journalist, Bangkok, April 2026. Yet, given the dismal state of bilateral ties, modest steps toward improved relations are as imperative as they are difficult. Until the land boundary is agreed upon, the issue will remain a potential trigger for war. Even in the absence of further combat, the border closure and suspension of trade is immiserating people living along the frontier, depriving both countries of revenue and eroding ASEAN cohesion in a period of major-power competition and flux in the international order. Delaying border demarcation [between Thailand and Cambodia] only heightens the risk of renewed fighting. To begin with, Bangkok and Phnom Penh should restore normal diplomatic relations by exchanging ambassadors, signalling a desire to improve the relationship, enhance communication and start rebuilding trust. Secondly, the JBC should resume its work as soon as possible, and the GBC should convene as necessary. 178 In July, Prime Minister Anutin appointed retired General Somsak Rungsita, a former director of the National Security Council, to lead Thailand’s JBC delegation. Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. The December 2025 ceasefire commits both parties to “refer to the Joint Boundary Commission to resume, at the earliest, the survey and demarcation works … to achieve lasting peace along the border”. 179 “Joint Statement of the 3rd Special GBC”, op. cit. Given the prohibition on the use of force in determining international boundaries, there is no legitimate alternative to jointly negotiating the boundary line and withdrawing Thai troops from areas that are indisputably Cambodian territory. Delaying border demarcation only heightens the risk of renewed fighting. Thirdly, the neighbours have a politically acceptable platform for cooperation on demining and disposing of explosive remnants of war, which is a priority for both countries. 180 Thailand acknowledged using cluster munitions in 2025, defending their use as directed at military targets. The Cambodian Mine Action Centre estimates that Thai M42, M46 and M85 submunitions affected nearly 300,000 hectares in 349 villages. Neither Cambodia nor Thailand is party to the 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions. “Cluster Munition Monitor 2026”, Cluster Munition Coalition, September 2026, pp. 24-25; “Third Review Conference condemns cluster munitions use, CMAC chief highlights impact of Thai shelling”, Agence Kampuchea Presse, 29 September 2026. The December 2025 ceasefire agreement stipulates that the two countries “work together to make timely progress on demining efforts along the border”. 181 “Joint Statement of the 3rd Special GBC”, op. cit. To date, however, no such cooperation has taken place. 182 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. To some extent, Thailand has lessened the urgency by unilaterally clearing mines in the disputed areas it holds, but nevertheless the two sides should undertake whatever joint efforts they can. Cambodia should destroy any remaining antipersonnel mine stocks, reaffirm to its forces that mine use is prohibited and report these steps in its annual transparency reports under Article 7 of the Mine Ban Treaty. 183 “Investigation into New Use of Antipersonnel Landmines on the Thai-Cambodia Border”, op. cit. These actions could help build trust with Thailand. Both governments would serve their own interests by toning down statements that have hardened opinion and narrowed the room for compromise. Cambodia, in particular, would benefit from speaking with one voice on the border. Hun Sen’s statements, especially in 2025, attacked Thai leaders personally and raised tensions. Hun Sen often speaks before the prime minister, setting a line from which Hun Manet cannot easily depart. 184 Crisis Group interviews, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. Leaving border matters to the prime minister, the foreign ministry and the bilateral mechanisms would give Cambodia a more coherent posture and Hun Manet room to seek a new relationship with Bangkok. Restraint is also needed on the Thai side, where senior military officers accused Hun Sen of lying and labelled him the real commander of Cambodian forces during the December fighting. 185 “RTA says Hun Sen lied, ordered provocative acts against Thailand”, The Nation , 10 December 2025. Such charges may play well at home, but they make it harder for Thai officials to treat Hun Manet as the preferred counterpart. 186 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, September 2026. International bodies and foreign states lack sufficient leverage to push [the Thai and Cambodian officials] to the negotiating table. International bodies and foreign states lack sufficient leverage to push the sides to the negotiating table or otherwise decisively influence the course of events. U.S. diplomats remain engaged, but Washington is preoccupied with the Middle East war and shows little appetite for leading mediation efforts. 187 “US to provide $45m for Thailand-Cambodia ceasefire”, Nikkei Asia , 9 January 2026. For its part, China is unlikely to risk souring its relationship with either country by attempting to impose an agreement touching on the sensitive issue of sovereignty. Beijing should nevertheless intensify its Track II efforts, which have provided a welcome platform for civil society engagement and could furnish creative ideas for mending people-to-people ties. 188 “Summary Report: The Second China-Cambodia-Thailand Track II Dialogue, 20-21 April 2026, Beijing, China”. On file with Crisis Group. For its part, ASEAN should play a greater role. Ceasefire monitoring could help build confidence between the two sides, but the current configuration of the ASEAN Observation Teams leaves that potential unrealised. The teams, staffed by military attachés and ASEAN representatives based in Bangkok and Phnom Penh, can observe border areas only with the host country’s permission and coordination. 189 “Domestic pressure holds Thailand-Cambodia peace deal hostage”, Thai PBS World, 30 October 2025. Consequently, the teams have become implicated in the rival information strategies, with both Bangkok and Phnom Penh using site visits to cast blame on their adversary. 190 Crisis Group interview, analyst, Bangkok, April 2026. See also “Can ASEAN keep the Thailand-Cambodia peace?”, South China Morning Post , 5 July 2026. Both sides should permit observers greater independence. 191 Crisis Group interviews, diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. VII. Conclusion The fighting in 2025 has given way to an uneasy ceasefire that leaves Cambodia and Thailand no closer to resolving the underlying border dispute. With nationalism running high on both sides, political elites in Bangkok and Phnom Penh perceive greater rewards in hardline posturing than in compromise. To prevent the recurrence of a conflict that has already caused hundreds of deaths and displaced over a million people, Cambodia and Thailand will eventually have to survey and demarcate the land border, requiring compromise on both sides. Current prospects for a rapprochement are poor, however, and foreign states lack the leverage or commitment to impose a settlement. In the near term, the priority should be modest steps: restoring normal diplomatic relations by returning ambassadors, resuming the JBC’s technical demarcation work without preconditions and expanding cooperation on demining. The two sides should also permit ASEAN Observer Teams a more independent monitoring role. None of these measures will resolve the territorial dispute, but they could help rebuild the trust and communication needed to manage tensions and reduce the risk of renewed violence while a comprehensive settlement remains politically out of reach. In this episode of Hold Your Fire! , Richard is joined by Crisis Group’s Horn of Africa director, Alan Boswell, to discuss the fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, the risk of direct war between Ethiopia and Eritrea and what may prevent further escalation. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Horn of Africa Ethiopia/Eritrea This week on Hold Your Fire! , Richard is joined by Alan Boswell, Crisis Group’s Horn of Africa director, to discuss the fighting in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region and the risk of an all-out war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. They examine federal forces’ recapture of Tigray’s capital Mekelle and what has changed since the previous war. They explore Eritrea’s calculations in backing its former enemy, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, and whether Ethiopian advances toward the Eritrean border could bring the two countries into direct conflict.
