AFP / Fadel Senna Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 09 October 2026 17 minutes The U.S. and UN Will Need More Patience to Resolve Western Sahara Conflict Talks between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front over Western Sahara have hit a wall, with U.S. and UN representatives pushing for Rabat’s autonomy plan as the centrepiece of negotiations. If they are to broker a compromise, the mediators will have to slow down. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Riccardo Fabiani Project Director, North Africa https://twitter.com/ricfabiani Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy Western Sahara Morocco Mauritania For some time after October 2025, it seemed that the long diplomatic stalemate over Western Sahara might have been broken. This desert territory is claimed by Morocco but sought by the Algeria-based Polisario Front as the home of an independent state for the Sahrawi people. A UN Security Council resolution passed in October 2025 strengthened international backing for a Moroccan autonomy proposal while remaining vague enough to allow for the possibility of other outcomes. Working together with the UN envoy to Western Sahara, Washington used this narrow opening to bring Morocco and the Polisario back into direct discussions for the first time since 2019. Algeria and Mauritania, both neighbours of Western Sahara, also joined. Three rounds of talks in Washington and Madrid allowed the parties to explore practical elements of a possible settlement without forcing either Morocco or the Polisario to abandon its stance on Western Sahara’s sovereignty, autonomy and self-determination. But the opening is now in danger of closing. The U.S. and UN tried to move too fast, from exploratory discussions to negotiations centred on Morocco’s autonomy proposal, meeting with firm resistance from the Polisario, which insists on a self-determination vote. Meanwhile, a series of diplomatic and military incidents sullied what had been a constructive atmosphere. Washington has responded by applying increasing pressure on the Front, entertaining alternative Sahrawi interlocutors and considering changes to the diplomatic framework. Uncertainty about the U.S. position on the future of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) adds another complication. The U.S. concededly has a difficult diplomatic task. It needs to show both resolve and a capacity for patience if it wants to coax the parties toward progress – and right now the balance is off. Why the U.S. decided to become so seized of this issue is unclear, but if the objective is a quick diplomatic win, then it is looking at the wrong file. Indeed, there is a significant risk that, if the administration persists in trying to force a quick settlement, it will risk deepening the mistrust that has long impeded progress in negotiations. Rather than searching for shortcuts, the U.S. and UN should seek to rebuild confidence among the parties, preserve an open negotiating framework and gradually create the political conditions under which substantive compromises might eventually become possible. Creating Space for Talks The Western Sahara conflict dates to 1975, when Spain withdrew from the territory and Morocco and Mauritania moved to divide it between them. The Polisario Front, backed principally by Algeria, launched an armed struggle for independence. Thousands of Sahrawis fled to Algeria. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 envisaged a referendum on self-determination, but disagreements over who should be able to vote have prevented it from taking place. Morocco has instead promoted a plan that would devolve powers to an autonomous Western Sahara under Rabat’s sovereignty, while the Polisario continues to demand a route to independence. The ceasefire collapsed in 2020, though fighting has remained limited. That same year, during President Donald Trump’s first term, the U.S. recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, in exchange for Morocco’s normalisation of relations with Israel; during Trump’s second term, the administration has strongly endorsed Rabat’s autonomy plan. In October 2025, the UN Security Council agreed to renew MINURSO’s mandate for another year, with new language more explicitly supporting Morocco’s autonomy plan. As the penholder, the U.S. had tabled a first draft that called autonomy “the basis” for future negotiations and “the most feasible solution”; but consultations among Council members led to watered-down language. The final version’s ambiguously (and awkwardly) worded text says autonomy will be taken “as basis” for negotiations and represents “a most feasible solution”. The Council thus gave its strong backing for the autonomy plan, while leaving the door ajar for discussion of other proposals. While both the Polisario and Algeria said the resolution’s final version improved upon the first draft, they rejected it. While both the Polisario and Algeria said the resolution’s final version improved upon the first draft, they rejected it. The former reiterated its demand for a self-determination referendum to settle the conflict, while the latter – then an elected member of the Council – took the politically unsurprising but exceptionally rare step of not voting on the resolution to register its opposition to a reference to “Moroccan sovereignty” in one of its preambular clauses. Nonetheless, U.S. Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos used the resolution’s ambiguity to press Algeria and the Polisario to return to negotiations. In the weeks after the Council vote, Boulos signalled to both actors that, though Washington clearly supported autonomy, the UN resolution did not preclude another solution if the conflict parties agreed to it. At the time, a Polisario official told Crisis Group that “Boulos’s language is more neutral than the UN Security Council resolution” – an expression of growing confidence in Washington’s role. Between January and February 2026, ministerial-level delegations from Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and the Polisario gathered twice in Washington and once in Madrid, the first direct meetings between the conflict parties in seven years. The co-chairs were Boulos, U.S. Ambassador to the UN Michael Waltz and UN envoy Staffan de Mistura. These rounds differed from previous efforts in at least three ways. First, Washington was directly involved in the discussions, marking a break from its traditional role as the UN envoy’s external supporter, with U.S. officials both driving the conversation and giving de Mistura space to help do the same. Secondly, Algeria and Mauritania participated in the talks – though only as ostensible “observers”. For years, Rabat has wanted Algiers and Nouakchott involved in negotiations, claiming that the Polisario is an Algerian proxy and that, to be durable, any agreement will have to be part of a grand bargain with countries abutting Western Sahara. Algeria and Mauritania have countered that they are merely neighbours interested in the conflict’s resolution (hence their insistence on “observer” status). Thirdly, ahead of the talks and responding to a demand repeatedly put forward by the U.S. and its European partners over the years, Morocco expanded its four-page autonomy proposal floated in 2007 into a comprehensive 40-page blueprint to guide negotiations. The co-chairs insisted on confidentiality from the participants to protect discussions from political pressures at home. Though news broke that the four parties were talking, the contents of the three rounds have remained mostly secret, with Morocco’s expanded autonomy plan still under wraps. That said, diplomatic sources have told Crisis Group that the talks, which apparently touched upon organising elections and reintegrating Sahrawi refugees, among other things, went well overall. In a conversation with Crisis Group, a Polisario official was keen to stress that these exchanges were “a discussion, not a negotiation”. The open-ended format seemed to suit both sides, making it possible for them to re-engage with each other, however warily. From Progress to Stalemate The talks subsequently hit a wall, however. After the three meetings, the U.S. and UN repeatedly asked the Front to offer its comments on Rabat’s plan with the aim of kickstarting a more substantive discussion of how to end the conflict. The Polisario baulked, with an official explaining to Crisis Group that the Front “has not accepted the Moroccan autonomy plan as the basis for negotiations and the UN Security Council does not require us to accept it”. While this position should not have been surprising – the talks gained momentum only because of the ambiguity that the U.S. had managed to create around this key issue – U.S. and UN diplomats seemed both frustrated and bewildered by the Front’s attitude. A U.S. official noted that “Algeria showed much more flexibility than the Polisario” by encouraging the Front to respond to Morocco’s autonomy plan, rather than rejecting the proposal out of hand. Between May and June, relations between the parties – as well as between the U.S. and the Polisario – quickly deteriorated. On 5 May, after a long period of quiet, the Front fired rockets at the city of Smara, in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, wounding a civilian and damaging a number of buildings. The U.S., France and several other countries, along with the EU and UN, immediately condemned the attack, calling it an attempt to undermine negotiations . The next day, U.S. Ambassador to Morocco Duke Buchan III visited Dakhla, in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, reiterating the Trump administration’s recognition of Rabat’s sovereignty and criticising the Polisario. On 7 May, the Polisario issued a statement denouncing Buchan’s visit and justifying the Smara attack as legitimate resistance to colonialism. Things took a turn for the worse after an exchange of letters between Ambassador Waltz and Polisario leaders failed to restore mutual confidence. Things took a turn for the worse after an exchange of letters between Ambassador Waltz and Polisario leaders failed to restore mutual confidence. According to several U.S. and European diplomats, Waltz wrote to ask whether the Front’s leaders were still committed to a negotiated solution after Smara. The Polisario reportedly responded with a long missive about the dispute’s complexity that Washington saw as obfuscatory. At that point, a number of administration insiders turned against the group. Tensions escalated further when, on 7 June, Moroccan forces killed Lahbib Abdelaziz, son of former Polisario leader Mohamed Abdelaziz and a potential future leader of the Front. His killing shocked pro-independence Sahrawis, who complained that (in contrast to the outcry that followed the Smara attack) there was precious little international condemnation. Then, on 8 June, Sahrawi activist Naama Asfari – who was arrested in 2010 in connection with protests at Gdeim Izik – began a hunger strike , which lasted 47 days and ended only after Rabat granted him a transfer to a jail closer to his family. By late June, U.S. frustration with the Polisario had begun to show. On 30 June, Waltz met with a delegation of the Sahrawi Movement for Peace (MSP), founded in 2020 as a self-styled moderate alternative to the Polisario, expressing willingness to negotiate with Morocco over autonomy. Waltz praised the MSP as an organisation committed to “peace, compromise and a durable solution” that “the world should hear”. Another meeting between a U.S. embassy official and an MSP delegation followed on 28 July. With these steps, the U.S. was breaking with a well-established practice of recognising the Polisario as the representative of the Sahrawi people (even if there was some dispute over whether it should be considered the sole, exclusive representative) and raising the spectre that it might bypass the Front absent greater cooperation. The Front reacted dismissively. A Polisario official told Crisis Group that U.S. officials “should come on the ground and see who really represents the Sahrawis. The Polisario comes from the people and remains representative. The groups they want to promote are nothing”. Summing up the U.S. approach, a Western diplomat told Crisis Group that Washington believes the Polisario’s choice is between “the hard way and the harder way”, meaning that continued resistance by the movement to engaging with Morocco’s plan will bring more adverse consequences upon it. In another sign of tougher steps to come, and in parallel to the talks, a group of U.S. members of Congress introduced two bills that would require the Secretary of State to designate the Polisario as a foreign terrorist organisation (FTO) due to its alleged links with Iran and Lebanese Hizbollah. For legal and political reasons, it is hard to imagine these bills passing into law and being enforced, and the administration has expressed no support for them. But the administration could be working with Congressional allies to signal what might come next should the impasse persist. Searching for Alternatives Faced with a diplomatic deadlock ahead of the expiry of MINURSO’s mandate at the end of October, U.S. officials have been weighing other options, including replacing the Polisario with more flexible Sahrawi representatives, such as the MSP, in the talks. A Western diplomat observed that Washington could use the mandate renewal to try including new language that creates space at the negotiating table for the MSP and others (eg, elected Sahrawi officials who reside in Morocco) – for instance by referring to “Sahrawi representatives” rather than “the Polisario Front” when describing the concerned parties. That said, not all U.S. officials seem ready to drop the Front or give up on the current format. In a 25 September interview with France 24 , Boulos stressed that the U.S. was still hoping the Polisario would engage in talks, praised Algeria’s stance and highlighted that more work was needed to achieve a mutually acceptable settlement. The pro-Polisario media welcomed these remarks. In his 28 September speech to the UN General Assembly, Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf reiterated his country’s rejection of any shortcut to a deal: “Algeria warns that any attempt to bypass this framework of reference or marginalise the holders of the inalienable right, the people of Western Sahara and their sole, legitimate representative, the Polisario Front, will not contribute to resolving the conflict; rather, it will further exacerbate tensions”. Meanwhile, Morocco has been assiduously currying favour with the Trump administration, even if it has not openly backed the idea of opening negotiations to other Sahrawi groups. In July, King Mohamed VI announced that the Tiznit-Dakhla road connecting Morocco to Western Sahara would be renamed the Donald J. Trump Highway as “a personal expression of my high regard”. On 15 September, Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and U.S. Ambassador Waltz agreed in New York on upgrading Israel-Morocco relations by appointing ambassadors and working toward a series of economic agreements to be signed by year’s end. In their official statement, the three countries reaffirmed Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and support for the autonomy plan. “The tripartite agreement with the U.S. and Israel is an essential part of Morocco’s approach to Western Sahara”, a Moroccan expert told Crisis Group. “The diplomatic upgrade is a gesture addressed to Washington, as we need the U.S. on our side ahead of the next Security Council meeting”. According to Moroccan and European sources, Rabat is hoping that the MINURSO renewal will, among other things, include clearer backing for the autonomy plan as “the only basis” for resolving the conflict. MINURSO’s future remains up in the air. At this stage, MINURSO’s future remains up in the air. In October 2025, Washington tried to shorten the mission’s mandate to three months, hoping that more frequent Security Council involvement might increase pressure on the parties to reach a deal, thus allowing MINURSO to wind down, in line with the U.S. agenda of reducing spending on peacekeeping missions. Eventually, the U.S. settled for a twelve-month renewal in parallel with a strategic review conducted by the Secretary-General. Meanwhile, in anticipation of U.S. requests to trim peacekeeping spending, MINURSO underwent cuts , removing 23 civilian posts, reducing flying hours and slashing its own budget by 11.5 per cent. In an April Senate hearing , Waltz mentioned MINURSO as a mission that – in the Trump administration’s eyes – has outlived its purpose. Several European diplomats told Crisis Group that they suspected Washington would once again push for a major cut in the mission’s expenses or (less likely) its termination during the next renewal debate. MINURSO’s political mandate has changed beyond recognition since its inception, insofar as it presently plays only a marginal role in diplomacy. But European officials who spoke to Crisis Group share the conviction that its presence remains critical to avoiding escalation. In 2022, Morocco made clear that, should MINURSO withdraw from the UN buffer zone separating the territory held by Rabat from the Algerian and Mauritanian borders, the kingdom would occupy this strip of land. If that were to happen, the Polisario would likely attack Moroccan installations from Algeria or Mauritania, rather than using the buffer zone as its launchpad, as is now the case. In turn, Rabat might decide to pursue Polisario units into Algerian or Mauritanian territory, potentially dragging its neighbours into conflict. Rebuilding Confidence among the Parties With the October deadline for renewing the MINURSO mandate fast approaching, U.S. officials could be tempted to either strong-arm the Polisario into accepting Morocco’s autonomy plan or replace the Front with a more accommodating alternative. They may hope that this small organisation will eventually buckle under Washington’s pressure, fearful of the consequences of continued obduracy, which might range from being cast aside to being designated as an FTO, with the severe attendant sanctions. For an administration keen to secure quick deals to end wars, ending the Western Sahara conflict might look like low-hanging fruit. Taking this tack would be highly risky. Since the breakdown of the UN-organised referendum scheme in the early 2000s and, in particular, the resumption of hostilities in 2020, confidence between Morocco and the Polisario has been running low, a by-product of the conflict’s five-decade duration, the accumulation of failed diplomatic initiatives, competing legal and historical narratives, and repeated periods of military confrontation and political deadlock. The two sides continue to approach negotiations from fundamentally different premises: Morocco sees autonomy under its sovereignty as the sole viable end state, while the Polisario insists on a process that preserves the option of independence. In addition, since the 2021 diplomatic rupture between Algeria and Morocco, the conflict has been nestled within a regional dispute , further complicating efforts to resolve it. U.S. pressure alone is unlikely to yield a substantive breakthrough, certainly not without simultaneous confidence-building measures. U.S. pressure alone is unlikely to yield a substantive breakthrough, certainly not without simultaneous confidence-building measures. The Polisario regards self-determination for all practical purposes as an existential issue, meaning that it is more likely to dig in than concede in the face of coercion, with much of the cost of any standoff being borne by vulnerable Sahrawi refugees. In such a scenario, the risk of escalatory violence would also increase. For leaders on both sides to make difficult concessions, and for public opinion to accept them, at least some preliminary steps are needed. Otherwise, both will view negotiations as a zero-sum game, dimming prospects for a resolution. “We need a minimum of trust”, a Polisario official commented to Crisis Group. Against this backdrop, Washington should drop any illusion of reaching a swift deal. Instead, it ought to embrace a more patient approach that, for now, focuses on clearing the air among parties whose relations have soured. The co-chairs should look to four confidence-building measures that might create a better atmosphere for future talks. They should: First, press Morocco and the Polisario to allow Sahrawi families in Algerian refugee camps to visit Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, and vice versa, resuming a program that was suspended in 2014. These exchanges would create regular, low-risk cooperation among Morocco, Polisario and the UN in service of a concrete humanitarian need, while reconnecting people divided by the conflict and helping reduce both mistrust and the political cost of engagement; Secondly, urge Morocco to release some or all the Sahrawi prisoners it has held since the 2010 Gdeim Izik protests – or at least to honour prisoners’ requests for transfer to jails closer to their families; Thirdly, push the Polisario to declare a unilateral truce in return. Even though the Front rejects returning to the 1991 ceasefire, it might be persuaded to temporarily suspend its attacks to avoid undermining talks; and Finally, arrange for U.S. and UN officials to visit the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, meeting the Polisario leadership and holding town hall-style meetings with refugees to listen to their concerns. The co-chairs also should revise their diplomatic approach to get out of the current cul-de-sac. Rather than pushing the Polisario to respond to Morocco’s autonomy plan – which it rejects as a sole basis for negotiations – they should revert to the format of the three rounds held in Washington and Madrid, thus creating space for the parties to continue a less structured exchange of views on their respective plans. The co-chairs could facilitate these conversations and advance bridging proposals on the specific issues discussed. The most difficult questions relating to sovereignty should be left for the end. Over time, such an approach – pursued on the basis that “nothing is agreed until everything is agreed” – might eventually allow for more in-depth discussions. Algeria has made clear it would not participate in a dialogue that does not include the [Polisario] Front. Crucially, the U.S. should stop suggesting it might replace the Polisario with other Sahrawi representatives in the talks. Algeria has made clear it would not participate in a dialogue that does not include the Front. Besides, any settlement reached with such alternative groups would almost certainly lack popular buy-in and would fuel tensions among Morocco, the Polisario, Algeria and Mauritania. That said, the co-chairs might create a purely consultative parallel track bringing together other Sahrawis, from elected officials in Morocco to the MSP to civil society groups from the Tindouf camps – all of whom might have more political flexibility to put ideas on the table than Morocco and the Polisario. These Sahrawis could contribute their ideas on specific issues such as elections, natural resource management and refugee reintegration – as well as on the sovereignty-related endgame issues. For its part, the Polisario should engage more earnestly in the process. Whatever the Front thinks of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign, both the Polisario and Sahrawi refugees would benefit from seeing it defused. Showing some flexibility would have the dual advantage of helping stave off this threat while taking advantage of U.S. engagement to advance diplomacy. For example, the Polisario could present a new proposal based on a 2003 plan advanced by James Baker, the former U.S. secretary of state who was then UN envoy. Under that plan, which combined autonomy and self-determination, Western Sahara would have had five years of substantial self-rule, with an elected local executive and legislature, while Morocco would have retained responsibility for foreign affairs and defence. After that transitional period, the UN would have held a referendum on the territory’s final status. At the time, the Front accepted the plan, while Rabat rejected it. Such a counteroffer would at least provide the co-chairs with a document they could use in trying to bridge the gap between the two sides’ positions. Morocco should also find ways to show flexibility. While one concrete way to do that might be releases of Gdeim Izik prisoners, it will also need to set something of a different tone in negotiations, resisting the temptation to treat autonomy as an outcome that can be fast-tracked. A more durable settlement will require Rabat to accept a long, difficult negotiating process in which trust gradually is rebuilt and the terms of any eventual compromise are worked through with the Polisario, rather than presented as a fait accompli . Meanwhile, the UN Security Council should refrain from sunsetting MINURSO and ensure that any effort to streamline its mandate or reform the mission preserves its military monitoring component to manage the risk that fighting will spill into Algerian or Mauritanian territory. Washington may reasonably seek to review the mission’s costs and functions, but reforms that significantly weaken or eliminate this military role could remove one of the few remaining stabilising mechanisms in Western Sahara. Finally, Washington should maintain a balanced approach to regional diplomacy – engaging regularly with both Algeria and Morocco, as it has sought to do during the current diplomatic effort, rather than allowing its closer ties with Rabat to feed perceptions that it is taking sides in an increasingly polarised regional competition. Maintaining credible channels with both capitals could help contain bilateral tensions, limit the Western Sahara dispute’s entanglement in wider rivalries and protect the political space needed for an eventual negotiated settlement. Should U.S. diplomats instead choose to intensify pressure on the Polisario and its backers in hopes of forcing rapid acceptance of Morocco’s autonomy framework, they are likely to find – potentially at high cost to the parties and to the region – that a conflict more than five decades old is unlikely to be resolved through coercion alone. Online Event Tuesday, 20 October 2026 10am Washington, DC | 4pm Brussels | 5pm Tel Aviv Please register here if you would like to attend this online event. The Knesset elections on 27 October could be the most consequential in Israel’s short history. After four years of hard-right government under Benjamin Netanyahu, and three years of war on multiple fronts since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Israelis head to the polls with starkly different hopes for their future. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the threshold needed to enter the 120-seat parliament. Two main blocs, of nearly equal weight according to polls, face off against each other: an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud party, and an opposing camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar, a centre-right party he founded last year. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Whichever bloc comes out on top, a question hangs over the vote: has the Israeli political “centre” shifted so much that even new leaders may not bring real change – at least, not on big issues that matter to the rest of the world, such as accommodating the 7.5 million Palestinians that live under Israeli rule? In this online event, Crisis Group brings together leading Israeli political analysts who will tackle this and other questions. It is not too late to avert disaster. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Ethiopia Eritrea Horn of Africa Ethiopia and Eritrea stand perilously close to all-out war as heavy fighting inches close to their shared border. The threat of resurgent interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa follows several weeks of fighting between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an armed rebellion on 23 September. The Ethiopian military has gained the upper hand in those clashes, moving northward after capturing Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 3 October. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and deploying military personnel on its soil, a claim that has been backed up by media reports and other accounts, though it appears that Eritrea subsequently pulled its troops back toward the border in the face of an Ethiopian advance and reported drones strikes on its forces. The effects of these cross-border movements could be dire: they could trigger a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea that, in turn, could spiral into a wider conflagration along Eritrea’s Red Sea coast. A push at the highest political and diplomatic levels to prevent this budding confrontation is a matter of extreme urgency. The Resurgence of Conflict The risk of direct conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea has risen sharply since late September as war has engulfed Tigray. On 20 September, the TPLF and six other groups announced a new “alliance for survival” aimed at toppling Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, which they see as authoritarian and bent on centralising power. Two days later, Ethiopia conducted a large drone raid on sites in southern Tigray, where officials believed the TPLF was massing for an attack. On 23 September, the TPLF mounted large-scale offensives against the federal government. It was apparently trying to join forces with two of its allies, the Amhara Fano and Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front, which commenced their own assaults on Ethiopian military positions near Tigray’s boundaries. This first wave of attacks made gains, but Ethiopian forces quickly regrouped. They have steadily pushed the Tigrayans back since then, recording a string of battlefield victories and capturing most of Tigray. On 3 October, federal forces and their allies took Mekelle without a fight. As the TPLF withdrew, the war’s front line shifted toward the group’s strongholds in the northern mountains, near the border with Eritrea. At the same time, tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea reached fever pitch in the wake of reported Eritrean troop deployments to northern Tigray in support of the TPLF’s rear guard. For the first time since 2000, when Ethiopia and Eritrea ended their last war, the two neighbours now seem poised to engage in frontal combat. For the first time since 2000, when Ethiopia and Eritrea ended their last war, the two neighbours now seem poised to engage in frontal combat. Frictions between the two are neither sudden nor surprising, even if the present rift between them in some ways marks a radical turnaround. For more than a year, Addis Ababa has been denouncing Asmara, and more recently its allies in the Sudanese army, for backing rebel groups in Ethiopia, particularly the TPLF. This antagonism stands in sharp contrast to what prevailed during the last Tigray war, which raged between 2020 and 2022, when Ethiopia and Eritrea had become friends rather than foes. That conflict came on the heels of Abiy’s ascent to power, which in turn dethroned the TPLF, a pivotal force in national politics for decades, and set the stage for a power struggle between the federal government and the TPLF high command in Tigray. Eritrea, which had fought its previous war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 while the TPLF was in charge in Addis Ababa, sought common cause with Abiy in confronting the group after Tigrayan forces attacked Ethiopia’s Northern Command in November 2020. A seesaw battle ensued, with Addis Ababa and its allies eventually beating back the TPLF ahead of the signing of the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022. This agreement left the TPLF largely intact, however, and its commitment to fully demobilise its armed forces was never fully enforced. Eritrea, which was not involved in the Pretoria negotiations, had been pushing for the group’s complete elimination. Asmara was incensed at the outcome. In its view, its critical national interests had not been respected during the talks. Eritrea’s relations with Ethiopia subsequently began to deteriorate. Some say Abiy was quietly courting the TPLF in order to establish a new alliance with it against Eritrea in the acrimonious aftermath of the peace deal. TPLF leaders apparently rebuffed these advances. Abiy also began to argue in public that Ethiopia needed to restore sovereign access to the sea. He said Ethiopia had a historical claim to the Red Sea coastline, which it had lost when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Since then, Ethiopia, the world’s largest landlocked country by population size, has been relying almost exclusively on Djibouti to export goods by sea. Officials in Abiy’s government have stressed that Ethiopia will not be satisfied merely with access to a wider range of ports, a course some have suggested it pursue, but needs a sovereign seaboard with a naval base. Asmara has viewed this rhetoric as a threat to seize Eritrea’s coastline, especially its southern port of Assab, by armed force. With bilateral relations souring, Eritrea and the TPLF began to explore establishing a common front against Addis Ababa. With bilateral relations souring, Eritrea and the TPLF began to explore establishing a common front against Addis Ababa. Asmara appears to have seen Tigray in the TPLF’s grip as a potential geographic buffer between it and the Ethiopian heartland, as well as a military counterweight to Addis Ababa. The TPLF, for its part, was keen to break the encirclement it endured in the 2020-2022 war. As a sign of their strengthening ties, Eritrean and Tigrayan authorities promoted new cross-border “people-to-people” exchanges known as tsimdo (“engagement” in Tigrinya), providing further ballast for their switch from adversaries to allies. Meanwhile, the 2022 peace deal began to fray. The TPLF complained that the government had failed to resolve major issues stemming from the conflict, including the status of disputed territories occupied by Amhara forces during the war and the return of displaced people to their homes in these areas. Little effort was made to remedy the antipathy between the TPLF and Abiy: Addis Ababa never reintegrated Tigray back into the national political federation, with the region remaining without representation in parliament or other institutions in the capital. In March 2025, the TPLF ousted the first post-war interim Tigray administrator, Getachew Reda, who had been a lead negotiator in the Pretoria peace negotiations for the TPLF and was chosen ahead of TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael. The group claimed that Getachew was too close to the federal government and had not defended Tigray’s interests sufficiently during his time in office. (Getachew fled to Addis Ababa, where he joined Abiy’s administration.) Abiy then appointed Tadesse Werede, a top Tigrayan general, in Getachew’s place, but the relationship between Tigray’s new ruler and the TPLF also began to worsen. In May 2026, the TPLF retook power in Mekelle, dismantling the interim administration, reinstalling its leader Debretsion as regional president and placing Tadesse under house arrest. The federal government responded by tightening its economic restrictions on the region and launching a campaign of airstrikes inside Tigray. In August, a major clash broke out between TPLF and federal ground forces before quickly subsiding. Shuttle diplomacy by the African Union and others aimed at restarting negotiations failed to gain traction. Simultaneously, mediators found their efforts thwarted by rising hostility among powers across the Horn. Addis Ababa began to denounce Asmara for trying to coordinate a transnational alliance against it, and accused the Sudanese army , an ally of Eritrea and Egypt (another Ethiopian foe), of supporting meetings of a nascent alliance of opposition groups in eastern Sudan. Ethiopia also complained that Sudan was harbouring a group of Tigrayan troops, known as Army 70, in Sudanese territory, where they were said to have stood alongside the army in fighting its enemy, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Ethiopia, on the other hand, began allowing the RSF to base itself in its Benishangul-Gumuz region close to the Sudanese border, from where it could launch attacks into Sudan’s Blue Nile state. Ethiopia’s relations with the Sudanese army, which had continued to function despite the chill between them, became icy as a result. Sudan has also claimed that drones attacking Khartoum were dispatched from Ethiopian territory. Neighbours at Loggerheads This mosaic of enmities and alliances has come into sharp relief since war broke out in Tigray. As hostilities have intensified, Ethiopia and Eritrea have edged ever closer to conflict. Ethiopia considers Eritrea to be masterminding the TPLF’s war effort. Soon after fighting broke out, Ethiopian federal officials and Afar’s regional president accused Eritrea of deploying forces in the Afar region. On 1 October, Ethiopia expelled all Eritrean diplomats from the country, accusing Asmara of “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence”. All diplomatic ties between the two states have since been severed. After Ethiopian federal forces began advancing north of Mekelle, the first reports emerged of alleged Eritrean deployments in northern Tigray, seemingly with the aim of bolstering the TPLF’s defensive lines. Several media reports indicated on 7 October that Eritrean units had passed through Adigrat, 30km south of the Ethiopian border. Accounts also suggest that Eritrean forces took up positions south of Adigrat in the Edaga Hamus area. A day later, after reported drone strikes on Eritrean vehicles, some of its forces reportedly withdrew to the border. With Ethiopian forces currently approaching the frontier at several points, the two armies are positioned in alarmingly close proximity. Asmara’s apparent gamble to intervene more directly in the war, even if the incursion was brief, could well backfire. On 9 October, Ethiopia wrote a letter to the UN Security Council saying it was “taking measures” of self-defence in response to Eritrea’s deployment of infantry and mechanised units across the border and occupation of Ethiopian territory. The letter also accused Eritrea of “harbouring, supporting, financing, arming and directing armed insurgent groups operating within Ethiopia”. On 10 October, Eritrea responded with its own letter, accusing Ethiopia of declaring a “war of aggression” against it three years ago and using self-defence as a pretext for acts of war. The Security Council has scheduled a closed-door session to discuss the crisis on 13 October. A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events. A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events. The last major interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa, in which hundreds of thousands perished in trench warfare, was fought along precisely the same border. One flashpoint could be Eritrean military positions inside Ethiopian territory; another could be disputed territory along the border. Should Eritrean forces fully withdraw to their side of the border, Ethiopia could point to Eritrea’s apparent incursion and alleged harbouring of TPLF fighters as justification for seeking to cross into Eritrea. Even if Ethiopia stops short of a land invasion of Eritrea (and Ethiopian officials maintain that they have no intention of fighting a war on Eritrean soil), aerial warfare using drones and other long-range strike weapons could cause devastating harm. Ethiopia possesses the larger air force and drone arsenal, and it could try to quickly overwhelm Eritrea’s air defences. Should the two states lock horns, war could also extend across the region. The Sudanese army and Egypt look primed to jump to Eritrea’s defence, though it is uncertain how much support they would be willing or able to give. On the other side, the United Arab Emirates could be expected to back Ethiopia with more arms transfers. Saudi Arabia is keen to prevent a new front from emerging along the Red Sea, especially one involving the UAE, and has tried in the past to de-escalate tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. On this occasion, however, Riyadh might be tempted to throw its weight behind Eritrea should a larger conflict erupt, given that its own Red Sea security would be at stake. That said, Saudi Arabia is also embroiled in a fresh round of fighting in Yemen and may not want to rally to the side of what might be a losing cause. Halting the Slide to War Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea back from the brink of war should be the priority for all those interested in preventing a deadly chain of interconnected conflicts from snaking across the Horn of Africa and Red Sea regions. Capitals such as Washington, Nairobi, Pretoria, London, Paris, Rome, Riyadh, Ankara and Abu Dhabi should press both sides to avoid escalation. In particular, they should urge Abiy to refrain from advancing into Eritrean territory. They should also appeal to Asmara to respect Ethiopian sovereignty and withdraw any remaining troops from Ethiopian territory, should they still be stationed there. Despite their rift, Saudi Arabia and the UAE could also use this moment to work together to staunch a new conflict along the Red Sea, which could otherwise cause even more trouble in their bilateral relations. Should efforts to avert an outright war prevail, diplomats should not desist until they manage to achieve a durable de-escalation of tensions between the two capitals. The heart of any settlement between the two countries is likely to be respect for each other’s sovereignty and restoration of diplomatic ties. In focusing on calming regional tensions, mediators should not forget the dispute between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF, should the latter manage to avoid complete collapse following its reversals. African leaders still look best placed to restart the Tigray peace track, even if neither federal officials nor TPLF leaders appear ready for direct talks any time soon. Prior to the start of hostilities, former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who oversaw the Pretoria negotiations that ended the last Tigray war, had been acting as the African Union’s peace envoy for the region. He visited Addis Ababa and Mekelle several times earlier in the year but had little success in bringing the two sides together. Efforts should be made to reactivate Obasanjo at the earliest opportunity. Other African leaders or ex-leaders could also be dispatched, such as South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, who made a quick stop in Addis Ababa on 5 October to speak with Abiy, or former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, who also played a key role in the Pretoria negotiations in 2022. The U.S. or European powers could also play a part behind the scenes in trying to rekindle peace talks. At a minimum, all sides should press the federal government and the TPLF to abide by humanitarian commitments under international law. The UN Security Council, which as noted will discuss the crisis on 13 October, should make a clear call for both sides to respect the UN Charter and instruct the Secretary-General to undertake urgent diplomacy to prevent a new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Another war in the Horn of Africa may lie around the corner. Outright conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea would likely spread to the Red Sea, disrupting the African side of this strategic waterway. It could also prove to be yet another front in the Horn that is easy to open and hard to close, especially once it becomes entangled in the mesh of disputes among neighbours and across the region. The best time to stop the looming Ethiopia-Eritrea war is now, before any more damage is done. Mandate of the UN Special Rapporteur on Russia Extended for Another Year. The UN Human Rights Council on October 6 extended the mandate of the Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in Russia for another year. Russia withdrew its amendment that attempted to delete renewal of the mandate. Click to expand Image The "Broken Chair” in front of the Palais Nations, Geneva, September 22, 2026. © 2026 Tanya Lokshina/Human Rights Watch The extension is welcome news. The Russia mandate provides an essential independent voice to document the Russian government’s grave human rights violations and serves as a lifeline for the country’s besieged civil society. The mandate was established in 2022 when, along with its war against Ukraine, the Kremlin launched a draconian crackdown on human rights defenders, independent journalists, political opponents, and other Russian based critics of the war. With the Ukraine war now in its fifth year, the Kremlin continues to escalate the crackdown on virtually all forms of dissent. There are over 1,800 political prisoners in Russia. The authorities have branded more individuals and organizations “undesirable” or “foreign agents”—labels used to stigmatize critics as enemies of the state—and targeted leading international human rights groups. They have also expanded the use of “extremist” designations against Russian human rights organizations, as well as LGBT people and their supporters. The crackdown has also intensified on digital freedoms, as authorities seek to isolate Russians from information critical of the government and to restrict access to online services and information they perceive as “hostile.” As UN Special Rapporteur Mariana Katzarova highlighted in her latest report, the Kremlin has increasingly resorted to transnational repression against exiled critics. Russia adopted in August legislation imposing restrictions on Russians abroad who have been convicted of offenses that are predominantly used in politically motivated prosecutions. The restrictions include denying consular services, such as passport renewals and notarial services; blocking access to government digital services; and freezing bank accounts and other assets in Russia. With human rights defenders, journalists, and activists imprisoned, forced into exile, or otherwise silenced, the Special Rapporteur’s mandate is more important than ever. Its renewal recognizes that intensifying repression inside Russia—and efforts to extend it beyond Russia’s borders—requires sustained international scrutiny. The Council should ensure that the Special Rapporteur has the support necessary to document these abuses, engage with Russian civil society, and ensure that repression is not rendered invisible.

Malaysia: Press Myanmar Junta Leader to End Abuses. Click to expand Image Myanmar nationals to be repatriated from Malaysia sit inside a bus, at Lumut, Malaysia, September 29, 2026. © 2026 Hasnoor Hussain/Reuters (Bangkok) – Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim should press Myanmar’s junta leader, Min Aung Hlaing, to end human rights abuses during his visit to Kuala Lumpur on October 7, 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The Malaysian government should also halt plans to forcibly return ethnic Rohingya and other people from Myanmar, where they face persecution and other rights violations. Malaysian authorities deported about 1,500 Myanmar nationals on September 29 in coordination with junta authorities, the first batch in a series of phased returns. “Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s invitation to Min Aung Hlaing to coordinate the forced return of people who fled military atrocities in Myanmar is an invitation for further abuse,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Malaysian government, which has provided protection to Rohingya and other refugees from Myanmar for decades, should halt any more returns and urge the junta leader to stop the abuses that have caused millions to leave the country.” On September 16, Prime Minister Anwar announced that he was inviting Min Aung Hlaing, who led the February 2021 military coup, to discuss the return of Myanmar nationals from Malaysia. This is Min Aung Hlaing’s sixth bilateral visit to an Asian country since he installed himself as president in April following sham elections and after stepping down as commander-in-chief of the Myanmar military. Min Aung Hlaing has been implicated in many abuses, and the International Criminal Court prosecutor has requested an arrest warrant for his alleged crimes against humanity. On September 29, Malaysian authorities sent back 1,476 Myanmar nationals—1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys, and 7 girls, ages 8 to 60—according to Malaysia’s state news agency, Bernama, aboard two Myanmar navy ships and a hospital ship from Lumut naval base in Malaysia’s Perak state. The deportations come amid a wave of public hostility in Malaysia toward refugees, particularly Rohingya, that government officials have fomented. The Home Ministry has described refugees as a financial burden, a social problem, and a security threat. Online hate speech and misinformation targeting Rohingya and migrants generally have surged this year, leading to harassment and the closure of community schools. The transfer was the first phase of an arrangement between the Malaysian government and the Myanmar junta to return 5,000 people, initially announced by Malaysian officials in July. Based on media reports, Malaysia’s Home Ministry said the Myanmar junta authorities had identified those slated for return. It did not disclose their ethnicity or refugee status, or say whether Rohingya were among them. The ministry was quoted as saying that further phased returns would follow once identification, documentation, and verification were complete. Malaysian authorities have claimed the returns were strictly voluntary. But those deported were taken directly from immigration detention centers—where former detainees have reported physical abuse and psychological harm—raising serious concerns about whether consent was freely given. The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) said it had no role in the operation and was not involved in identifying those deported. Since 2019, the Malaysian government has denied UNHCR access to immigration detention centers, preventing the agency from reviewing asylum claims or assisting detainees who are registered refugees. Consent given while in indefinite detention, without access to UNHCR or a meaningful protection assessment, cannot be truly voluntary, Human Rights Watch said. A representative of the ethnic Chin refugee community in Malaysia told the media that community leaders knew of several asylum seekers among those deported, including one who had been recognized by UNHCR as a refugee. There are no authoritative figures on the number of Myanmar migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers in Malaysia. More than 224,000 refugees and asylum seekers are registered with UNHCR in Malaysia, about 90 percent from Myanmar, the vast majority ethnic Rohingya. Since Myanmar’s 2021 military coup, Malaysia has summarily deported thousands of asylum seekers to Myanmar without assessing their asylum claims or other protection needs, and in violation of a Malaysian court order. In May 2024, UNHCR issued guidance stating that people fleeing Myanmar “are likely in need of international refugee protection.” Conditions for safe, dignified, and voluntary return to Myanmar do not currently exist, Human Rights Watch said. The Myanmar military continues to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity. Junta authorities have arbitrarily arrested tens of thousands of people since the coup, and thousands have experienced torture and ill-treatment or died in custody. A day before the September deportations took place, Myanmar’s military carried out an airstrike near a market in the town of Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, killing 50 people. Rohingya face particular danger if they are forcibly returned. Myanmar authorities have long denied them citizenship and subjected them to atrocity crimes, including the ongoing crimes against humanity of apartheid, persecution, and deprivation of liberty. In Rakhine State since late 2023, Rohingya civilians have been caught in the fighting between the junta and ethnic Arakan Army forces. Both parties have carried out grave abuses, including extrajudicial killings, widespread arson, and unlawful recruitment. Malaysian Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil said on September 30 that 3,524 people had been approved for a second phase of deportation from a list Myanmar authorities submitted in a diplomatic note dated August 13. Malaysia is awaiting a date from Myanmar. About 10,400 Myanmar nationals are held in Malaysian immigration detention, according to recent reports from the Malaysian Home Affairs Ministry. Malaysia has not ratified the 1951 UN Refugee Convention or its 1967 protocol, but it is still obligated to respect the international law principle of nonrefoulement, which prohibits countries from returning anyone to a place where they would face a real risk of persecution, torture or other serious ill-treatment, a threat to life, or other comparable serious human rights violations. The Malaysian government should immediately suspend all deportations to Myanmar, including its planned second phase, and grant UNHCR full and unimpeded access to all immigration detention centers. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) should maintain the ban on Min Aung Hlaing and other junta leaders participating in the regional bloc’s meetings. ASEAN members should refrain from organizing bilateral visits that undermine their collective ban on junta officials. Concerned governments should press Malaysia to halt the returns, and expand resettlement places and support for countries hosting refugees from Myanmar. They should not treat returns arranged with Myanmar’s military-backed authorities as evidence that the country is safe. “The Malaysian government should not be outsourcing the decision about who can safely return to Myanmar to the junta authorities,” Pearson said. “Prime Minister Anwar should stop the next ships before they set sail, and provide the UN refugee agency access to refugees and asylum seekers.”

El Salvador: Mass Trials a Mockery of Justice. Click to expand Image A woman holds a sign reading "We demand due process for the innocent. No to injustice" during a protest against the state of emergency imposed by the government since March 2022, in San Salvador, El Salvador, on March 24, 2026. © 2026 AFP via Getty Images (Washington, DC) – Since early 2026, Salvadoran courts have begun convicting people in mass trials of hundreds of defendants at a time, relying on weak evidence and giving them no real chance to defend themselves, Human Rights Watch said today. For months, courts in El Salvador have held mass trials of people detained under the state of emergency, which has been in place for over four years. Many people have been sentenced for “unlawful association,” a vaguely defined crime, on the basis of weak evidence in closed proceedings that are kept under judicial seal. Lawyers representing the accused say they have had no meaningful chance to contest evidence or prepare an adequate defense. The prosecutors and judges involved have little, if any, independence from the executive branch. “El Salvador’s mass trials are a mockery of justice,” said Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch. “These hearings are designed to produce guilty verdicts, not to weigh evidence under due process. The result is not accountability for the victims of gang violence, it is simply rubber stamping the mass incarceration under four years of the state of emergency.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 15 private defense lawyers representing people detained during the state of emergency and reviewed four indictments covering over 600 defendants and one judicial decision sentencing over 120 people. Researchers also interviewed members of civil society organizations with direct knowledge of the proceedings and, for a prior publication, several police officers whose descriptions of investigations were generally consistent with those of defense lawyers. Human Rights Watch also reviewed publications by the Salvadoran government and by Salvadoran and international news outlets describing the mass trials. Human Rights Watch also requested information from the Salvadoran Supreme Court and the Attorney General’s Office about the criminal proceedings of people detained under the state of emergency, including the total number of convictions and the number of people held in pretrial detention. The Attorney General’s Office responded that the requested records “were not found.” The Supreme Court had not responded at time of writing. Since March 2022, El Salvador has been under a state of emergency that suspends some due process rights, a measure cast as a necessary tool to fight gang violence. Security forces have detained over 93,000 people, including more than 3,000 children. Human Rights Watch has documented widespread abuses, including arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, torture and other forms of ill-treatment in detention, and severe due process violations. Many people with no connection to gang activities have been detained. Lawyers said they were routinely blocked from mounting an adequate defense. They said judges denied them access to case files, saying that the cases were under “seal.” They also said they could not speak with their clients privately. Some lawyers also said that prosecutors had threatened proposed defense witnesses with criminal prosecution. Defense lawyers said that judicial proceedings are conducted at such a fast pace that respecting due process is virtually impossible. “It is macabre,” one said. “They need the machine to run like clockwork.” They described being given only minutes at hearings to present a defense: about 10 minutes at the initial hearing and just 15 minutes at the sentencing hearing. Public defenders, they said, were given a few minutes to represent dozens and, in some instances, hundreds of defendants at a time. The lawyers interviewed said that prosecutors routinely relied on police reports to seek convictions. Police officers have previously told Human Rights Watch that many police reports are based on fabricated or uncorroborated evidence, such as anonymous calls, and that police were pressed to produce them to comply with an arrest quota. Prosecutors have also relied on anonymous testimony by witnesses who entered plea agreements. These witnesses testify behind screens or wooden partitions, with their voices distorted. “You don’t see them,” one lawyer said. “They are covered in a little box; you see a wooden board. The voice is distorted. Only the judge, the court clerk, and the prosecutor have access.” “We presented witnesses, family members, neighbors, who would testify he was not a gang member,” a lawyer said about her defense of a young man who has been in detention for more than four years accused of being a “gang collaborator.” “They are intimidated by the prosecutor’s office, which threatened to detain them.” The trials have been conducted before the Tribunals Against Organized Crime, which have been staffed by the Supreme Court through an ad hoc, opaque process. The identity of these judges has not been disclosed, even to the lawyers involved in the proceedings. One lawyer said that a judge opened a mass hearing by saying: “We are here to convict all MS-13 members.” An estimated 120,000 people are incarcerated in El Salvador today. That amounts to roughly 2 percent of the population, one of the highest incarceration rates in the world. Salvadoran prisoners have long suffered from overcrowding, violence, and inadequate access to food, water, and medical care. The state of emergency has sharply worsened these dire detention conditions by tripling the prison population, pushing it to more than double the system’s capacity. At least 513 people have died under state custody during the state of emergency, according to Cristosal, a human rights organization. Over 90 percent of people behind bars have been imprisoned for years awaiting trial, in part because of recent legal reforms that extended pretrial detention terms. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the American Convention on Human Rights, to which El Salvador is a party, guarantee everyone charged with a crime the right to be informed promptly and in detail of the charges against them, to have adequate time and facilities to prepare a defense, and to examine prosecution witnesses and present their own on equal terms. Salvadoran authorities should ensure proceedings comply with fair trial standards, carefully assess the evidence and charges against each individual, end the excessive use of pretrial detention and judicial seals, and disclose how the specialized tribunals were appointed. The Salvadoran government should also establish an independent, transparent mechanism to review the cases of people detained during the state of emergency and identify people who have been detained without adequate credible evidence, whom authorities should promptly release. The mechanism should prioritize reviewing cases of children, people with disabilities, pregnant women, and people with serious health conditions. “The government has built a system designed to convict hundreds at once, with no mechanism to separate the innocent from the guilty,” Goebertus said. Vague Accusations, Weak Evidence Many of the people sentenced in El Salvador’s mass trials have been accused of the vaguely defined crime of “unlawful association,” based on weak and uncorroborated evidence. The offense criminalizes not only those who create, lead, or finance gangs, but also anyone who “promotes, helps, facilitates or favors” such groups, or receives a direct or indirect benefit from a relationship “of any nature” with them, even without being a member. Human Rights Watch found that prosecutors have classified defendants by their alleged rank or role in gangs, in most cases as “collaborators” or “lookouts,” but have not further specified what activities specific defendants allegedly engaged in as part of the gang, or during what time periods. The indictments reviewed relied heavily on a set of recurring documents produced by the police: the arrest report, a police report about the defendant, and photographs taken when the detainee enters prison. In many cases, prosecutors also relied on testimony from one or two anonymous witnesses who entered plea deals. Lawyers said that the crime has at times been applied to sentence people who were gang victims. “In El Salvador, many people were coerced into ‘collaborating’ with gangs,” one lawyer said. “For example, prosecutors accused one woman of being the girlfriend of a gang leader, when in fact she had been forced into the relationship out of fear for her own life and the lives of her family members.” Human Rights Watch reviewed a judgment of a single mass trial in which over 120 people were convicted for “unlawful association.” Nobody was acquitted. Defendants were sentenced to either 30 or 45 years in prison. Almost all of those sentenced to 30 years were accused only of being “collaborators,” the lowest level of gang association under Salvadoran law. For the vast majority, the only evidence connecting them to a gang was a statement by one of two anonymous witnesses, who had received immunity from prosecution, together with police paperwork recording the arrest and a police-generated “criminal profile” of the defendant. Even when witnesses said that some of the defendants were fishermen, housewives, farmers, or students, and had no connection with gangs, the judge concluded, without explaining why, that the anonymous witnesses were more credible and convicted the defendants. Lawyers said that prosecutors frequently rely on the police report as the key piece of evidence, even though the defense is often unable to verify how it was created or the underlying sources used to create it. “Prosecutors say a person is a gang member because a police officer says so,” a lawyer said. “The prosecutor relies on the police report, and the police report relies on unspecified official intelligence or public rumors,” he added. Lawyers said police logs of the anonymous calls that allegedly trigger many arrests are not disclosed to the defense, making it impossible to even verify what was said. Several lawyers said prosecutors have also relied on witnesses who reached plea bargain agreements and then put forward broad, unverifiable allegations of gang membership. Lawyers said that in many cases the witnesses are unable to provide any meaningful details that might give credibility to their allegations. One lawyer said a protected witness described his client as a “lookout who moved drugs,” but was unable to specify when, where, with whom, or what kind of drugs. Severe Restrictions on the Right to Defense Lawyers consistently described a series of severe limitations on their ability to defend their clients. Many said that defense lawyers, especially public defenders, are given just minutes to present a defense at multiple stages of the proceedings—from initial hearings on pretrial detention to opening and closing arguments during trials—in some cases for hundreds of defendants at a time. One lawyer described an initial pretrial detention hearing in which a single public defender was given 10 minutes to defend 102 defendants. Another described a pretrial detention hearing, which he attended, where a public defender had between 20 and 30 minutes to present his defense for 200 defendants. A private defense lawyer said that in one hearing he was given between 30 and 40 seconds to defend his client. Defense arguments are “a mere formality,” one said. Defense lawyers said they are not given an opportunity to contest much of the evidence presented by prosecutors. They said courts have routinely denied requests for independent judicial assessments of whether a particular defendant had a stable job prior to their arrest and was therefore unlikely to be a gang member. Many requests to present witnesses for further information about police reports have gone unanswered, lawyers said. In some cases, prosecutors also are allowed to introduce written records of police interviews as evidence, giving defense lawyers no opportunity to cross-examine the officers. Prosecution witnesses who offer testimony as part of plea deals, defense lawyers said, testify behind screens or wooden partitions, with their voices distorted. “As defense lawyers, we don’t know who they are,” one said. “There is no control [by the defense] over protected witnesses. We don’t know what their motivations are besides getting a reduction of their sentence.” Several lawyers said that court clerks routinely deny them copies of case files, contending that they are subject to seal on “public security grounds.” “If you ask for a copy of the case file, they don’t give a copy,” one said. “The secrecy is generalized.” Defense lawyers also said that they are unable to meet in a confidential setting with their client to prepare their defense. One lawyer said that on the few occasions she was allowed, through virtual means, to speak with her client, the conversation was recorded and prison guards were nearby. “You are careful with what you can ask and what you can say,” she said. Another lawyer said she had never been able speak with her client, a young woman who has been detained since 2024. Climate of Fear Lawyers said that the widespread arrests under the state of emergency have created a climate of fear that dissuades many lawyers and witnesses from getting involved in these cases. As one lawyer put it: “Neighbors, friends, family members, co-workers, bosses are afraid to serve as witnesses because of the state of emergency, that there could be reprisals, police harassment.” Defense lawyers also said that in some cases, prosecutors threaten the best positioned people to contest accusations of gang membership—family members, neighbors, and employers—with criminal prosecution. This contrasts with the voice distortion, physical screens, and sealed identities for anonymous prosecution witnesses. Because the crime of “unlawful association” criminalizes “relationships of any nature” with a gang, anyone who vouches for a defendant risks being portrayed as a collaborator themself. One lawyer said: “In the hearing [prosecutors] question them, but before questioning them, they say ‘if you’re lying to me you can go to prison too’… ‘stop going around defending gang members.’ … This is a tool to intimidate, to instill fear, and it’s generalized.” Lack of Judicial Independence, No Meaningful Judicial Recourse Since President Nayib Bukele’s Nuevas Ideas (New Ideas) party won a supermajority in the Legislative Assembly in 2021, the legislature has approved a series of changes that have weakened judicial independence. The assembly replaced the attorney general and justices on the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court with loyalists and then gave them broad powers to remove or relocate judges and prosecutors. The Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court has since stopped ruling in a timely manner when lawyers file habeas corpus petitions to protect the rights of their clients. According to the University Observatory of Human Rights at the Central American University (Observatorio Universitario de Derechos Humanos, Universidad Centroamericana, OUDH), the number of habeas corpus petitions the chamber admitted, which ranged between 24 and 46 percent in the years before the state of emergency, collapsed to 3 percent in 2022 and fell below 1 percent in 2023. A law passed in 2022 allows courts to hide the name of the judge handling the case to the defendants and the general public. The provision was employed in the ruling Human Rights Watch reviewed. While protecting a judge’s life and physical integrity is fundamental to ensuring the proper administration of justice, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights has ruled that “faceless judges” make it impossible for defendants to assess whether judicial authorities have a conflict of interest and are independent and impartial, violating due process protections. One lawyer said she has filed seven habeas corpus petitions in the cases she has handled since April 2022 and has received no meaningful response. “We are using the available remedies,” she said, “but we are not getting answers.” Severe staffing capacity shortfalls have also undermined access to a meaningful defense. The OUDH reported that, as of 2024, there were 165 public defenders for over 93,000 people detained during the state of emergency, an average of 550 cases per defender. The Public Defender’s Office’s budget fell from US$38 million in 2024 to $34 million in 2025, a cut of nearly 10 percent, before an increase to $35 million in 2026. In the 2026 budget, the Criminal Public Defense Unit (Unidad de Defensa Pública Penal), responsible for the defense of everyone charged with a crime including people detained under the state of emergency, was allocated approximately $9 million, a small increase from the $8.7 million it received in the 2025 budget.

Countries Demonstrate Record Support for UN Sudan Probe Renewal. Click to expand Image The remains of fighting in the abandoned village of Bakri, about 35 kilometers (22 miles) from El Fasher, Sudan, where homes and fields were left deserted after residents fled escalating violence across the region, February 24, 2026. © 2026 Giles Clarke/Avaaz via Getty Images A record number of countries at the United Nations Human Rights Council this week voted to support a resolution renewing the mandate of the UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan. For the first time, the Gambia, Mauritius, and Malawi joined South Africa and countries from other regions voting in favor of the resolution. The fact-finding mission is mandated to investigate human rights violations and abuses committed by Sudan’s warring parties and advance accountability, including by collecting and preserving evidence to identify those responsible and to use in future prosecutions. Over the past year, the mission has presented various reports, including a special inquiry on the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) assault on El Fasher, which it concluded bore the hallmarks of genocide, as well as a recent exposé on the role of external actors in fueling the conflict. It has worked with the joint Fact-Finding Mission of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) to ensure their work is complementary. The Human Rights Council resolution also highlighted the mission’s identification of a “transnational network” of support for the RSF, including the provision of weapons, logistics, training, and foreign personnel. It underlined the need for heightened scrutiny and accountability of external support that sustains operations involving serious violations and international crimes, “across the full chain of responsibility.” The resolution’s increased support this year signals growing recognition of the need to combat atrocities in Sudan, and the impunity fueling them, underscoring that justice is central to resolving the crisis. In a powerful statement, the Gambia recalled their own national legacy to insist that “truth, justice, and accountability are the foundation on which sustainable peace and reconciliation must be constructed.” However, while the resolution acknowledges the importance of collection and preservation of evidence to support accountability, states did not act to strengthen the mission’s capacity to do so, a key recommendation by civil society. States that led and supported this resolution should further consider how to ensure evidence is preserved and prepared in real time to support prosecutions against all those responsible for serious international crimes amid Sudan’s conflict. African states that supported the initiative and others should also work to ensure the African Union Peace and Security Council considers the ACHPR mission’s own report.

Bahrain: Authorities Rearrest Pardoned Detainees. Click to expand Image Human rights defender, Naji Fateel. © Private (Beirut) – Bahraini authorities have rearrested at least nine men who had previously been released from prison by royal pardon, the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) and Human Rights Watch said today. The men, who were previously detained on politically motivated charges, were arrested in July and August 2026 for allegedly failing to pay fines dating back a decade. Bahraini authorities should immediately release them and cease all efforts to collect the dubious unpaid fines. “King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa’s decision to pardon over 3,000 prisoners in the last two years earned immense praise from the international community, but these new arrests call into question whether the pardons were genuine,” said Niku Jafarnia, Bahrain and Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Those who praised the pardons should call on Bahrain to stop rearresting people and release those again detained.” BIRD and Human Rights Watch spoke to three people, including Naji Fateel, a prominent Bahraini human rights defender who was among the nine rearrested and who spoke from detention. They also spoke to Mustafa al-Jamri and Hassan Burwase, who have not yet been rearrested, but who said the authorities were trying to detain them. The arrests are happening against the backdrop of one of the biggest crackdowns by Bahrain’s authorities on freedom of expression and assembly since the widespread arrests following the 2011 pro-democracy protests. Since March, authorities have arrested over 600 people on various charges, including “supporting and endorsing a state hostile to Bahrain” and espionage, and at least 69 people of Iranian descent have been stripped of their Bahrain nationality, including many children. Those interviewed said the issue was alleged unpaid fines imposed on them and 48 others accused of causing damage during a major protest in Jau Prison in 2015. Human Rights Watch and BIRD have documented that the authorities imposed physical and psychological abuse on the protesters and denied them needed medical care. In 2016, the authorities added 15 years to their sentences and fined them a total of 507,187.97 Bahraini Dinars (approximately US$1.35 million), for offenses including damaging public property, attacking police, arson, and resisting authorities. At the time, BIRD, along with several other human rights organizations, called into question the convictions, saying the Bahraini government had sentenced 57 people to lengthy prison terms amid allegations of abuse, torture, and due process violations, and called on security officials involved in the abuse to be held accountable. The 2024 royal pardons included 33 of those men. All three men interviewed said that their understanding was that the royal pardon also included the charges and fines imposed under the 2016 sentence following the protests. However, in early June, the authorities contacted many of the men to say that they had to pay fines without specifying what the fines were in relation to or how much they should pay. Al-Jamri said that a security official who called him simply said that he had “amounts of money due.” When he asked for clarification, the man said there were “amounts due related to the case,” without any details, and he was told to go to a police station in Manama, the capital. “I was surprised,” al-Jamri said. “What are these amounts? I mean, I hadn’t had any problems; there was nothing against me. I was approaching two years [since my release].” Burwase said the papers linked with his and the rest of the men’s pardons indicated that they had been cleared of “everything, completely,” and that the authorities had also issued him a “good conduct certificate,” meaning there were no outstanding cases against him. On June 16, after hearing from the authorities, 14 of the pardoned men, including the 3 interviewed, wrote to the crown prince, stating their belief that the royal pardon had “brought to an end all consequences arising from the judgments,” including the financial penalties. “This understanding was reinforced by the official measures that followed the pardon and were intended to reintegrate us into society, including government directives to provide training and employment opportunities to those covered by the pardon.” In the letter, the men asked the authorities to recognize the effect of the pardon on the outstanding penalties, halt enforcement measures that could result in their return to prison, clarify their legal position, and ensure that those released under the pardon were not imprisoned simply because they could not afford to pay any outstanding fines. The men received no response. But in July and August, the authorities arrested 8 of the 33 convicted in 2016 and pardoned in 2024. Among them, three were signatories to the letter. Fateel said that on August 16, officials contacted him regarding the fine. He had asked them to provide documentation establishing the amount to be paid and whether he should go to the police station to discuss the matter. He said that the officials had told him to instead contact the public prosecution and the sentence enforcement judge, who oversees sentencing for convicted individuals.
